articles.title: Zelensky Enacts Sanctions Targeting Russian Ballistics and Drones Makers
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky has signed decrees enacting decisions by the National Security and Defense Council (NSDC) to impose sanctions on Russian entities and individuals involved in manufacturing ballistic missiles and supplying critical components to Moscow’s military-industrial complex, the Office of the President of Ukraine announced.
The statutory measures target Russian enterprises and executive leadership providing raw materials, specialized machine tools, precision optics, and electronic modules required to produce standoff strike systems – such as Iskander, Kalibr, Kh-101, and Kinzhal missiles – alongside military aviation, armored vehicles, and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We are systematically identifying and imposing sanctions on enterprises involved in the production of Russian ballistic missiles and other strike weapons,” said Presidential Advisor and Commissioner for Sanctions Policy Vladyslav Vlasiuk.
“We are working to coordinate these sanctions with other international jurisdictions. Cumulatively, this should significantly degrade the Russian defense sector’s capacity to manufacture weapons.”
Ballistic missile supply chains and research institutes
The primary sanctions list targets 51 individuals and 44 corporate entities directly linked to the development and serial production of Russian ballistic and cruise missiles deployed against Ukrainian civilian settlements and municipal life-support systems.
Russian Border Strikes and EU EES Challenge Checkpoints
Key institutions designated under the presidential decrees include the Petrov Plastics Institute, identified as the sole manufacturer in Russia of specialized composite polymer components supplied to defense, aerospace, aviation, and naval shipyards.
The measures also target the Komet Corporation of Special Purpose Space Systems, the lead enterprise of a scientific and production consortium manufacturing surface-to-air missile systems, radar equipment, and airborne avionics suites, alongside VitaReaktiv, an industrial enterprise specializing in chemical raw materials integrated into ballistic missile propulsion systems and warheads.
Additional designations focus on research bodies and high-technology developers.
Among them are Promenergo, a defense contractor that develops optical, laser, and optoelectronic targeting systems alongside avionics testing facilities; the Kirov Biochemical Plant, engaged in the chemical synthesis and technical modernization of military armaments; and the Mendeleev All-Russian Research Institute of Metrology, a national scientific body that provides metrological research, precision measurement systems, and software architectures for military equipment.
Industrial tooling, electronics, and RUSAL aluminum imports
A second decree enacts sanctions against an additional 32 Russian citizens and 35 commercial entities embedded in supply chains for precision machine tools, microelectronics, and tactical communication components.
The measures target Gagaring, a commercial enterprise specializing in communications hardware and flight controllers for first-person view (FPV) strike drones; Virgin-EK, which procures foreign electronic components for the Russian armed forces; and the Pressmash Machine Tool Association, a wholesale distributor of metalworking machinery that supplies factories producing Kh-101 and Kh-59 cruise missiles alongside Orion medium-altitude UAVs.
The sanctions package also designates corporate entities belonging to the Russian metals group RUSAL. According to Ukrainian government data, between April 2024 and March 2025, United Company RUSAL Trading House and the RUSAL Taishet Aluminum Smelter imported aluminum oxide valued at nearly 150 million rubles ($1.6 million) into Russia.
Ukrainian authorities confirmed that these raw materials were diverted into manufacturing pipelines for military aircraft, armored combat vehicles, missile systems, and loitering munitions.
Air defense strains and transatlantic divergence
The enactment of domestic sanctions follows recurring Russian ballistic missile barrages against Ukrainian regional infrastructure ahead of the winter season.
On Monday, Oct. 19, Russian forces launched 16 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and surrounding districts without advance radar notification, damaging over 10 energy facilities and cutting electricity to at least 550,000 households. The strike underscored operational risks amid conflicting accounts between Washington and Kyiv over early-warning missile tracking feeds.
President Zelensky previously stated that Ukraine receives roughly 12 Patriot PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors per month – approximately one-quarter of the volume delivered under the Biden administration – despite paid commitments through NATO’s Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) and calculated domestic operational requirements of 350 interceptors monthly.
The Ukrainian sanctions push also unfolds amid transatlantic friction over economic deterrence. On Oct. 16, US President Donald Trump issued an executive order invoking Section 115 of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 to waive mandatory statutory penalties, including 500 percent tariffs on Russian imports and 100 percent duties on third-party petroleum purchasers.
EU leaders expressed regret over the suspension of US energy penalties during their Brussels summit, pledging to maintain European sanctions and expand coordination with Kyiv to close secondary procurement loopholes underwriting Moscow’s defense manufacturing base.

articles.title: United Kingdom and France Conducted Their First Joint Nuclear Airstrike Drill
articles.body:
The United Kingdom and France conducted their first joint exercise simulating a nuclear airstrike, involving Rafale and Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jets.
This was reported by the Ministry of Defence of the United Kingdom.
The exercise, codenamed Rummy, took place on October 20–21, 2026, over the Mediterranean Sea.
French Rafale fighter jets took off from the Saint-Dizier Air Base in northeastern France to carry out the simulated strike. British Eurofighter Typhoons provided cover for the strike group.
During the maneuvers, the crews practiced coordinating the air operations of the two countries.
It is worth noting that the Rafale can carry ASMP-A supersonic cruise missiles equipped with nuclear warheads.
The countries’ participation in these nuclear exercises marked the first practical example of such cooperation. Previously, London and Paris had conducted nuclear deterrence operations independently of one another.
The maneuvers took place as part of the implementation of the Northwood Declaration, adopted by the United Kingdom and France in July 2025.
The document provides for deeper cooperation in the field of nuclear deterrence; however, each state retains independent control over its own arsenal and the right to make decisions regarding its use.
The range of French missiles is estimated at approximately 500 kilometers. The United Kingdom currently maintains strategic nuclear deterrence using Vanguard-class submarines armed with Trident II ballistic missiles. At the same time, London plans to acquire 12 F-35A fighter jets to participate in NATO’s nuclear mission.
Earlier, Militarnyi reported that in late September 2026, the French Air and Space Forces conducted the Poker exercise, during which they practiced a simulated nuclear air strike. Rafale crews trained to penetrate the air defenses of a simulated adversary, fly at low altitudes, and refuel in flight.
In addition, on July 16, France and Germany conducted their first-ever joint exercise as part of France’s nuclear deterrence concept. During that exercise, two French Rafales and two German Eurofighters conducted a joint flight, refueling from a French Airbus A330 MRTT Phénix, after which they landed at Nörvenich Air Base in Germany.

articles.title: Iran says US military not allowed to enter Gulf
articles.body:
Houthis attack Yemen's Aden, say Saudi strikes kill 16
Yemen’s Houthi attacks, Saudi-led missile interceptions, Iran’s warning to the US and Israeli displacement of Palestinians escalate Middle East tensions.
This live blog has now ended. Make sure to follow us for the latest news on Facebook, X, and Instagram.

- Yemen's Houthi group said it launched attacks at Saudi oil facilities and airports on Saturday including a Saudi Aramco facility in Yanbu, the Rabigh oil refinery and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.
- - Iran said on Saturday that US military ships would never be allowed to enter the Gulf "under any circumstances" and that President Donald Trump will "take that dream to his grave".
- The Israeli military forced around 1,200 Palestinians to leave their homes in Hebron in the occupied West Bank, a Palestinian official said on Saturday, a day after an attack killed two Israeli soldiers.
Houthis say they attacked Saudi oil facilities, airports
Yemen's Houthi group said it launched attacks on Saudi oil facilities and airports on Saturday, including a Saudi Aramco facility in Yanbu, the Rabigh oil refinery and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.
The group's military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said it also targeted King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, Najran airport, and an air base in Khamis Mushait.
Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm the attack.
Iran's Pezeshkian blames US for interim deal failure,
Iranian President Massoud Pezeshkian, in remarks broadcast on state TV on Saturday, blamed the United States for the failure of an interim deal with Iran, but said there should be a new attempt at concluding it.
"We were having negotiations, the cowards (Americans) messed everything up...I still think we should go and conclude it," Pezeshkian said.
Iran remains open to talks with the US under a Pakistan-brokered interim deal reached in June to end the conflict, Tehran’s ambassador to Islamabad said Saturday, accusing Washington of undermining diplomacy and prolonging the standoff over the Strait of Hormuz.
Ambassador Reza Amiri Moghadam said Iran recently told Pakistan it was prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if Washington lifted its naval blockade, but accused US President Donald Trump of rejecting the proposal and insisting the blockade of Iranian ports would continue.
Palestinian Authority calls for intl pressure on Israel
The Palestinian Authority called on Saturday for international pressure on Israel to protect Palestinians after some residents of the West Bank city of Hebron were displaced from their homes in response to an attack that killed Israeli soldiers.
Confronting "the growing threats to expand the scope of forced displacement and destruction requires urgent international action that goes beyond condemnation to adopt tangible and deterrent measures", the PA's foreign ministry said in a statement.
Yemen's Houthis claimed an attack on Saturday on a naval base and a military camp in Aden, the interim seat of the internationally recognised government, after blasts were heard there.
"Our armed forced targeted Saudi enemy concentrations at the so-called Al-Nasr camp and the naval base in Aden," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said, adding that the sites were overseen by Saudi forces.
Saudi strike kills five members of same family in Hodeida
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis on Saturday said a Saudi strike on Hodeida killed five members of the same families, as both sides press attacks.
"Five people, the head of the family, two of his children and his two wives, have been martyred and his daughter wounded as a result of a Saudi enemy air strike on the home of citizen Abdulwahed al-Wasabi in the Al-Tuhayta district" of Hodeida, the Houthis' Al-Masirah TV channel reported.
Houthi media reported that Saudi strikes killed 11 people in Yemeni capital Sanaa on Saturday, shortly after the Saudi-led coalition fighting them said it had intercepted two missiles targeting Saudi cities.
The Houthis' Al-Masirah outlet reported a series of "Saudi enemy airstrikes" targeting Sanaa, including one on a house that killed at least four people and wounded several others.
A separate strike at a residence building for cement factory workers in the Sanaa governorate killed six women and one child and wounded three others, the broadcaster said.
Two people wounded in Friday's attack on a church in southern Jordan have died of their injuries, bringing the number of people killed to nine, health minister Ibrahim al-Bdour told AFP on Saturday.
"The number of victims who died in the terrorist attack on the church in the village of Al-Hamoud in Karak has risen to nine following the death on Saturday of a second casualty who had been in a critical condition," the minister said.
The Israeli military forced around 1,200 Palestinians to leave their homes in Hebron in the occupied West Bank, a Palestinian official said on Saturday, a day after a Palestinian attack killed two Israeli soldiers.
Yousef Zouhair Al-Jabari, the head of Hebron's municipality, said around 1,300 faced losing their homes in addition to the 1,200 already displaced.
He also said the Israeli operations were motivated by parliamentary elections on Tuesday, when Netanyahu's right-wing coalition may lose its majority, opinion polls show.
Jordan's king orders security forces to respond firmly to
Jordan's King Abdullah chaired a security meeting on Saturday and ordered security forces to respond firmly and pursue those behind a church attack in Karak Governorate that killed and wounded civilians, the royal court said.
A person wounded in Friday's attack on a church in southern Jordan has died of their injuries, bringing the number of people killed to eight, Health Minister Ibrahim al-Bdour told AFP on Saturday.
"The number of victims who died in the attack on the church in the village of Hammoud in Karak has risen to eight following the death of one of the injured who was in critical condition," the minister said.
Another 26 people remain hospitalised, including one in critical condition, he said.
Gunmen stormed the compound of a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hammoud in Karak governorate during a funeral procession on Friday and opened fire, Jordanian authorities said.
"A terrorist group has carried out a horrific act, one that is condemned in every respect, and the security services are working round the clock to track them down," Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya told a press conference.
Turkey's foreign minister will tell his Yemeni counterpart on Saturday that Houthi attacks on civilians are "unacceptable" and express hope the conflict can be resolved through dialogue, a Turkish foreign ministry source said.
Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan is due to meet Yemen's Afrah al-Zouba in Istanbul, a day after hosting talks with senior European and regional diplomats.
The Houthis have been at war since 2014 with Yemen's internationally recognised government.
Following an uneasy four-year truce, fighting reignited in July, months into the US-Iran conflict that has plunged the wider region into crisis.
Iranian President Massoud Pezeshkian will meet his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin in Moscow next week, Iranian media reported.
Pezeshkian is due to visit Russia for a meeting of gas-exporting countries.
Russia and Iran, two of the most sanctioned nations on earth, have grown closer together in the years since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
"The Iranian president will visit Moscow to attend the summit of gas-exporting countries that will take place on Tuesday, October 27," the Tasnim news agency reported, citing Tehran's ambassador to the country, Kazem Jalali.
The two leaders will discuss economic cooperation as well as "questions of geopolitics", Jalali was quoted as saying.
Saudi-led coalition says it destroyed Houthi missiles
A Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said it destroyed two ballistic missiles firedby the Iran-aligned group towards Taif and Yanbu on Saturday, as fighting between the sides continued.
Saudi Arabia's Civil Defence briefly issued alerts on Saturday warning of potential danger in Taif and Yanbu, as well as the holy city of Mecca and its second-largest city, Jeddah.
The service issued notices around 10 minutes later saying the danger had passed.
Saudi civil defence issues 'potential danger' warning
Saudi Arabia's civil defence agency broadcast warnings of "potential danger" for four of its western provinces, including that of Mecca, home to Islam's holiest city, on Friday, without saying why.
The alerts, which also covered the major Red Sea city of Jeddah, nearby Taif and the coastal oil hub of Yanbu, were all rescinded minutes later.
Residents were instructed to "proceed to the nearest safe place" by the agency. The agency also repeated a legal warning against sharing images or information related to "countering missiles and drones".
Netanyahu says Palestinian Authority in for 'big surprise'
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that the Palestinian Authority was in for a "big surprise" after he ordered a major military operation in response to an attack on soldiers in the West Bank.
Netanyahu, days ahead of elections, declined to answer directly when he was asked if he would dismantle the Palestinian Authority but said he favoured "ruse and surprise".
"We transformed the Middle East. I said that we would change things and we have," Netanyahu told i24News in an interview conducted late Friday.
"There is a very big surprise for the Palestinian Authority as well."
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said on Saturday it had intercepted a ballistic missile launched towards Riyadh by the Iran-backed group.
Two explosions rang out in Riyadh early Saturday, an AFP journalist in the Saudi capital said, as the Houthis keep up strikes on the kingdom.
An early warning system was activated to alert residents to a potential threat, the Saudi civil defence said.
"Air defences intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthi terrorist militia toward Riyadh," coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki posted on X.
Iran said on Saturday that US military ships would never be allowed to enter the Gulf "under any circumstances" and that President Donald Trump would "take that dream to his grave".
The remarks came amid mounting US and Israeli threats of renewed attacks on Iran, as US ambassador to Turkey Tom Barrack warned that Washington could "absolutely" strike Iran as soon as this weakened.
"We will not allow US military ships in the Persian Gulf under any circumstances and at any time," said Iran's armed forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi, according to Iranian state television.
"The US president must dream of seeing the armed forces enter the Persian Gulf. He will take that dream to his grave."

"A terrorist group has carried out a horrific act, one that is condemned in every respect, and the security services are working round the clock to track them down," Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya told a press conference.
Turkey's foreign minister will tell his Yemeni counterpart on Saturday that Houthi attacks on civilians are "unacceptable" and express hope the conflict can be resolved through dialogue, a Turkish foreign ministry source said.
Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan is due to meet Yemen's Afrah al-Zouba in Istanbul, a day after hosting talks with senior European and regional diplomats.
The Houthis have been at war since 2014 with Yemen's internationally recognised government.
Following an uneasy four-year truce, fighting reignited in July, months into the US-Iran conflict that has plunged the wider region into crisis.
Iranian President Massoud Pezeshkian will meet his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin in Moscow next week, Iranian media reported.
Pezeshkian is due to visit Russia for a meeting of gas-exporting countries.
Russia and Iran, two of the most sanctioned nations on earth, have grown closer together in the years since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
"The Iranian president will visit Moscow to attend the summit of gas-exporting countries that will take place on Tuesday, October 27," the Tasnim news agency reported, citing Tehran's ambassador to the country, Kazem Jalali.
The two leaders will discuss economic cooperation as well as "questions of geopolitics", Jalali was quoted as saying.
Saudi-led coalition says it destroyed Houthi missiles
A Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said it destroyed two ballistic missiles firedby the Iran-aligned group towards Taif and Yanbu on Saturday, as fighting between the sides continued.
Saudi Arabia's Civil Defence briefly issued alerts on Saturday warning of potential danger in Taif and Yanbu, as well as the holy city of Mecca and its second-largest city, Jeddah.
The service issued notices around 10 minutes later saying the danger had passed.
Saudi civil defence issues 'potential danger' warning
Saudi Arabia's civil defence agency broadcast warnings of "potential danger" for four of its western provinces, including that of Mecca, home to Islam's holiest city, on Friday, without saying why.
The alerts, which also covered the major Red Sea city of Jeddah, nearby Taif and the coastal oil hub of Yanbu, were all rescinded minutes later.
Residents were instructed to "proceed to the nearest safe place" by the agency. The agency also repeated a legal warning against sharing images or information related to "countering missiles and drones".
Netanyahu says Palestinian Authority in for 'big surprise'
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that the Palestinian Authority was in for a "big surprise" after he ordered a major military operation in response to an attack on soldiers in the West Bank.
Netanyahu, days ahead of elections, declined to answer directly when he was asked if he would dismantle the Palestinian Authority but said he favoured "ruse and surprise".
"We transformed the Middle East. I said that we would change things and we have," Netanyahu told i24News in an interview conducted late Friday.
"There is a very big surprise for the Palestinian Authority as well."
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said on Saturday it had intercepted a ballistic missile launched towards Riyadh by the Iran-backed group.
Two explosions rang out in Riyadh early Saturday, an AFP journalist in the Saudi capital said, as the Houthis keep up strikes on the kingdom.
An early warning system was activated to alert residents to a potential threat, the Saudi civil defence said.
"Air defences intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthi terrorist militia toward Riyadh," coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki posted on X.
Iran said on Saturday that US military ships would never be allowed to enter the Gulf "under any circumstances" and that President Donald Trump would "take that dream to his grave".
The remarks came amid mounting US and Israeli threats of renewed attacks on Iran, as US ambassador to Turkey Tom Barrack warned that Washington could "absolutely" strike Iran as soon as this weakened.
"We will not allow US military ships in the Persian Gulf under any circumstances and at any time," said Iran's armed forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi, according to Iranian state television.
"The US president must dream of seeing the armed forces enter the Persian Gulf. He will take that dream to his grave."

articles.title: North Korea improves ballistic missiles and mass-produces drones with Russian support – NYT
articles.body:
North Korea improves ballistic missiles and mass-produces drones with Russian support – NYT
North Korea is continuing to upgrade its ballistic missiles and has launched the mass production of attack drones, largely thanks to its cooperation with Russia.
Source: The New York Times
Details: The Russians are sharing their developments with Pyongyang in exchange for soldiers, workers and weapons.
North Korea is modernising its armed forces and weapons with the help of Russia, having renewed military cooperation following the start of the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine.
In early October, Pyongyang tested a tactical ballistic missile that it claims is capable of carrying a nuclear payload. South Korea and Japan estimated it flew about 700 km (430 miles), while North Korea claimed a range of 1,000 km (621 miles).
"South Korea usually responds to North Korean missile tests with brief statements condemning them as provocative. But five days after the North's launch, it test-fired its own hypersonic ballistic missile for the first time, observed by President Lee Jae Myung, indicating that Seoul has grown increasingly uneasy over the rapid advancement of North Korea's missile technology," the NYT writes.
Specifically, Pyongyang has access to Russian deployment data and feedback. Anton Ponomarenko, an analyst, noted that this has allowed them to improve the accuracy and manoeuvrability of their weapons, making the threat to South Korea "more substantial".
Russia has also helped North Korea develop its own unmanned systems and their mass production.
"Pyongyang has learned from the conflict in Ukraine and the Middle East that inexpensive drones can overwhelm costly air defence systems. During a North Korean drill last month, a drone swarm attacked a target island, while cruise and ballistic missiles struck simultaneously from different directions. North Korea's evolving tactics will eventually force South Korea and its allies to redesign their air defences at exorbitant costs," the NYT explained.
Background:
- Bloomberg reported this September that Russia is involving North Korean citizens in the production of military drones, particularly at facilities in Alabuga, Tatarstan. Up to 25,000 North Koreans are believed to be working at Russian military plants.
- In addition, a North Korean missile forces unit, which could be equipped with 120 ballistic missiles and six launchers for strikes against Ukraine, has begun deploying in western Russia.
- Ukrainska Pravda previously reported that in August, Russia had asked North Korea to provide KN-30 ballistic missiles. In June 2026, North Korea announced the testing of a modernised 240mm multiple-launch rocket system, a tactical ballistic missile and a 155mm long-range artillery shell.

articles.title: Russian-Indian BrahMos missile is getting future-ready
articles.body:
Russian-Indian BrahMos missile is getting future-ready
The BrahMos corporation is working to add more destructive power and reach to its namesake supersonic cruise missile, following its spectacular combat successes last year.
The operational and functional parameters of the missile are being upgraded, and new versions are in the works, the CEO and managing director of the joint venture between India and Russia, Jaiteerth Joshi, told local media recently.
Named after the Brahmaputra and Moskva rivers, the BrahMos is engineered for high-precision, long-range strikes. The missile offers militaries the versatility to engage threats using land, sea, and underwater platforms.
BrahMos earned its stripes last year when the Indian and Pakistani militaries briefly clashed with missiles and drones, following a terrorist attack on civilians in India’s Jammu and Kashmir state.
As the two militaries tested each other with drones, India fired BrahMos missiles to strike hardened high-value targets, including hangars reportedly housing Pakistan’s US-made F-16 fighter jets.
India has said there was not a single interception of the BrahMos during the clashes, dubbed Operation Sindoor, and buyer interest has risen since.
BrahMos Aerospace is a joint venture between India’s DRDO and Russia’s NPO Mashinostroyeniya.
BrahMos’ trajectory into the future
BrahMos started as a land-launched cruise missile, but its developers have worked to give it more flexibility and lethality as battlefield needs evolved and expanded.
The missile, which flies at nearly three times the speed of sound and carries a 200 to 300 kg warhead, had an initial range of 290 km but continuous upgrades have extended its reach.
In 2023, the Indian Air Force (IAF) successfully tested a version with a 450 km range. Mated to the Su-30MKI fighter, this variant, called the BrahMos-A, offers the IAF a standoff precision strike capability that few air forces in the world can match.
There is also a Block III land-attack variant, which can fly very low and approach targets from unexpected angles – dodging any defenses the enemy may try to throw at it.
The BrahMos corporation is working on a long and ambitious list of upgrades. At the top of the current development efforts sits a lighter, air-launched variant.
Christened the BrahMos-NG, it can be flown on the IAF’s other fighter jets, including the domestically produced Tejas light combat aircraft. The Su-30MKI will be able to sortie armed with three of these missiles.
The BrahMos-NG will feature higher domestically-produced content and advanced materials. The Indo-Russian joint venture expects to unveil this prototype by 2027-28.
The BrahMos corporation is also working on a very long-range missile. This version would be able to strike targets up to 1,500 km away, far more than the 290 km range of the original missile unveiled in the early 2000s.
This long-range version is at the conceptual stage, and the company is discussing further upgrades with its Russian joint venture partner. Joshi has told Indian media outlets in recent interviews that the range-extension program will proceed in phases, with test firings from land, sea, and air to validate the missile’s operational capabilities.
Also, on the missile maker’s drawing board is a hypersonic version – the new frontier of modern warfare – currently called BrahMos II.
The concept aims to integrate advanced technologies, state-of-the-art design, and smart materials to field a hypersonic futuristic weapon that will dominate fast-evolving battlefield technology.
BrahMos II will have an “air-breathing” scramjet engine that would boost it to a top speed of Mach 5.
BrahMos is seeing high global interest
The missile has already been sold to multiple countries, and many others have shown an interest in buying it.
One of the first foreign customers of the Indo-Russian missile was the Philippines, with Manila signing a $375 million contract in 2022. The first batch of BrahMos missiles was delivered to the country in April 2024, and the second in April 2025.
In June this year, India confirmed it had a deal with Vietnam to supply the missiles.
Indonesia, which has also evinced interest, has moved forward with procurement plans.
In addition, over a dozen nations including Malaysia, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Chile, and South Africa have evaluated or expressed a formal interest in the BrahMos missile system.
BrahMos is gearing up for a demand surge
The BrahMos project is a trailblazer in India’s defense industry. It broke the shackles of excessive bureaucratic controls that were once the hallmark of Indian state-owned defense corporations that had forced the country to remain a major arms importer.
Effective management and the synergizing of commercial viability, strike capabilities, and indigenization have helped the missile become the battlefield success it is, whie making inroads into the global arms market.
With a burgeoning order book, BrahMos corporation is prioritizing the fulfillment of orders received from the Indian armed forces, for whom the missile is a primary strike weapon. India recently contracted for more BrahMos launchers and fire-control systems, so more of its warships can be armed with the missile.
The missile maker now has production facilities in four Indian cities: Hyderabad, Nagpur, Pilani and Lucknow. Research and development clusters, nicknamed ‘tech-bricks’ have been set up to work on niche technologies for the next generation missiles.
The supply chain is being expanded to make it more robust and resilient – and to meet an expected surge in demand. For this, the company will expand the industry partners for each system and subsystem to up to 45, from the current one or two partners.
India’s arms export ambitions ride on BrahMos
New Delhi is gradually setting its sights to make a complete transformation from being one of the biggest arms importers to a major defense exporter.
It also simultaneously wants to see more domestically produced components and technology being used in its products. Indian defense exports registered an impressive 67% annual growth to reach $4 billion in the financial year ended March.
The federal government’s annual defense production target is $31 billion by 2029, of which defense exports are pegged at $5.5 billion.
BrahMos will be key to New Delhi’s ambitious goals to emerge as a major global arms exporter.

articles.title: Iraq believes Israel may have struck militia weapons supplied by Iran - report
articles.body:
Iraq believes that Israel was behind recent strikes on two sites where Iran-backed militias had stockpiled “Chinese-made shoulder-fired air defense systems” sourced from Tehran, sources told London-based Arabic international newspaper Asharq Al-Awsat on Saturday.
It was unclear which specific type of system the report referred to. One source told the newspaper that “the armed group that identified this location for storing air defense systems believed it was extremely difficult to access or detect…the suspected attack occurred shortly after the shipments arrived at the two storage sites.”
The report, which said the strikes occurred last week, did not provide evidence for the claims and noted that parts of the claims could not be confirmed.
Asharq Al-Awsat added that the Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), an umbrella group that contains numerous Iranian-backed militias and is also an Iraqi government paramilitary force, had said one of their bases suffered an explosion on October 17.
However, the PMF claimed at the time that this was an accident, and Iraq’s government vowed to investigate. The explosion had affected a stockpile of obsolete ammunition inside one of their headquarters in Baghdad's East Canal, injuring five people, according to Asharq Al-Awsat.
Not first time Iraq has blamed Israel for strikes
This is not the first time that Iraqis have sought to blame Israel for strikes in the country. Iranian-backed militias also blamed Israel for strikes in 2019 and a strike in Albukamal in Syria on the Iraqi border. In May, The Wall Street Journal reported that Israel set up a secret airstrip in Iraq in the midst of the Iran campaign.
Iran has been supplying Iraqi militias with weapons for many years. This has included missiles and drones capable of threatening Israel. The militias also carried out numerous attacks on Israel, especially after Hamas began its war on Israel on October 7, 2023.
The Asharq Al-Awsat report further cited an anonymous Iraqi government official who said that relevant authorities are still investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident, with the report noting that over a week had passed since the incident without any update.
Other sources said that the explosion in mid-October followed another incident on October 1. In that incident, warehouses belonging to Iran-backed groups in and around Baghdad had apparently been affected, “including warehouses containing drones intended for suicide attacks and reconnaissance.”
The report also reveals that the Iran-backed militias appear to be preparing for escalation. Iran has sought to make Iraq a frontline of the war since the US and Israel began airstrikes in February. For instance, Iran has carried out more than 1,000 strikes on the Kurdistan Region of northern Iraq since February. It has used drones and missiles.
In addition, Iran and the Iranian-backed militias carried out 600 attacks throughout Iraq, some targeting US diplomatic sites. The US withdrew forces from Iraq on September 30, a deadline that had been agreed to with Baghdad over the last years. Also, the US has warned Americans not to travel to Baghdad and noted the terror threats from the militias.
Asharq Al-Awsat appears to try to connect earlier reports about China supplying Iran with weapons to the movement of the same systems to Iraq. However, the report admits that this is “unconfirmed.” It further notes that on July 28, the Chinese Foreign Ministry denied these reports.
At the time, Iran was expected to receive, within weeks, its first shipment of up to 400 Chinese-made shoulder-fired air-defense missile launchers as it rebuilt its defenses after its war with the United States, three sources familiar with the deal told Reuters.
The militias may be preparing for what comes next. It should be noted that an Iran-backed militia targeted Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline in a drone attack. It is believed, according to a report at Al-Hurra and other reports, that the attack was carried out from Iraq’s Maysan province near the Iranian border. That border crossing has now been closed amid US pressure and Iraq’s concerns apparently over trafficking.
Asharq Al-Awsat further noted conflicting reports describing sorties by Israeli fighter jets through Iraqi airspace near the Iranian border, supported by midair refuelers, an operation it said had not been independently confirmed.
A security official told Asharq Al-Awsat that Iraqi authorities have not yet determined the nature of the strikes, but have seen sufficient evidence to believe Israel was behind them.
Strikes suggest the start of a new round of conflict, Asharq Al-Awsat reports
The report concluded that the strikes suggest the start of a new round of conflict. This seems sensational because the alleged incident took place in mid-to-early October. On the other hand, a source within the Shi’ite Coordination Framework told Asharq Al-Awsat that “leaders of ruling parties had been predicting for weeks that the resumption of war between Washington and Tehran would begin with the complete destruction of the capabilities of the Iraqi factions.”
The Shi’ite Coordination Framework includes the Shi’ite parties in Iraq. Many of the parties have armed wings that are part of the PMF. For instance, the Badr Organization has numerous brigades within the PMF. Other groups include Kataib Hezbollah, Asaib Ahl al Haq and Harakat Hezbollah al Nujaba. Most of these groups, except Badr, have been sanctioned by the US as terrorist groups.
Meanwhile, the Islamic Resistance in Iraq, which includes many of the militias and has been responsible for attacks on Israel and the US in the past, published a report claiming Iraq’s airspace was being violated.

articles.title: British jets escort French jets on ‘nuclear strike’
articles.body:
RAF Typhoons have escorted French Rafales simulating a nuclear strike mission over the Mediterranean, the first time British aircraft have taken part in a French nuclear exercise, according to the government.
Exercise Rummy ran on 20 and 21 October, with the Rafales launching from Saint-Dizier air base in eastern France, the home of the French air force’s airborne nuclear component. No nuclear weapons were involved, and the Ministry of Defence said the exercise was conducted under robust safety and security arrangements and focused on how the two air forces work together.
Wes Streeting, the Defence Secretary, said: “This exercise marks a new chapter in the defence nuclear relationship between the United Kingdom and France.
“As Europe’s nuclear powers, we have a shared responsibility to contribute to the security and stability of the Euro-Atlantic region. This exercise demonstrates the depth of our partnership, the credibility of our deterrents and our determination to stand together in the face of emerging threats.
“In an increasingly dangerous world, our adversaries should be in no doubt: the UK and France remain united in our commitment to European security and to maintaining the deterrence that has helped preserve peace for generations.”
Catherine Vautrin, the French Minister of the Armed Forces and Veterans, said: “Having independent nuclear forces does not exclude coordination. Our nuclear cooperation with the United Kingdom keeps deepening: on Tuesday night, UK Typhoons participated for the very first time to a French nuclear exercise alongside Rafales.
“Through coordination, our nuclear forces demonstrate that they can contribute even more significantly to the overall security of the Alliance and to the peace and stability of the Euro Atlantic area.”
The exercise falls under the Northwood Declaration, the agreement signed last year under which the two countries said that no extreme threat to Europe could arise which would not prompt a response by both, while each retains sovereign and independent nuclear forces and national decision making. Britain and France are the only nuclear armed states in Europe, and the declaration established a joint nuclear steering group to coordinate their policy, capabilities and operations.
Saint-Dizier is the base of the 4th Fighter Wing, which operates Rafales carrying the ASMP-A supersonic stand-off missile that forms the airborne half of the French deterrent. The French maintain both an airborne component and ballistic missile submarines, while Britain has relied on submarines alone since the WE.177 bomb was withdrawn in 1998.
That changes with the purchase of twelve F-35A aircraft and British entry into NATO’s nuclear mission, which will return a nuclear role to the Royal Air Force after more than a quarter of a century. Air Marshal Johnny Beck told a committee this year that the aircraft were not bought for the nuclear role, while the government has presented the purchase as the means of joining the mission.
The Defence Investment Plan commits £63 billion over four years to the nuclear enterprise, funding the Dreadnought ballistic missile submarines, SSN-AUKUS attack submarines, a new sovereign warhead and the supporting infrastructure. The refreshed Lancaster House agreement between Britain and France covers an expanded joint deployable force, deeper nuclear cooperation and work on the next generation of weapons.

articles.title: The Arctic giant: How Russia dominates the frozen frontier
articles.body:
The Arctic giant: How Russia dominates the frozen frontier
“Russia’s future... lies in the Arctic,” President Vladimir Putin declared last year, portraying the frozen north as a cornerstone of national prosperity for generations to come.
One look at a map shows why: The country accounts for approximately 53% of the Arctic Ocean’s coastline, according to the Arctic Council, making it the world’s largest Arctic power in geographical terms.
However, the stakes go well beyond geography, as Russia’s Arctic territories contain enormous oil, gas, and mineral reserves, host vital elements of its nuclear deterrent, and accommodate multiple military bases.
As climate change and retreating sea ice gradually open new opportunities for maritime navigation, Moscow is also seeking to transform the Northern Sea Route into a lucrative trade artery connecting Europe and Asia.
Meanwhile, both NATO and the EU are increasingly challenging Russia’s traditional presence in the Arctic. On October 20, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas described the region as the “frontline of global power competition,” accusing Moscow of militarization while setting course on expanding cooperation with NATO, developing military logistics corridors, and catching up with Moscow in its icebreaker capacity.
Russia maintains that it has “never threatened anyone in the Arctic” but vowed to safeguard its sovereign interests while accusing NATO of escalating tensions.
But what exactly makes the Russian Arctic so special, and why is Moscow so determined to stand its ground there?
What defines the Arctic?
Unlike Antarctica, which is a continent surrounded by ocean, the Arctic is an ocean surrounded by the northern reaches of Eurasia and North America, Greenland, and numerous islands. The region’s generally accepted geographical boundary is the Arctic Circle, beyond which the sun can remain above the horizon for 24 hours during summer and disappear entirely for at least one day during winter.
Eight countries have territories in the Arctic: Russia, Canada, the United States, Denmark through Greenland, Norway, Sweden, Finland, and Iceland, with the first five having coastlines directly bordering the Arctic Ocean – which gives them an important role in determining maritime boundaries and access to resources.
The region is characterized by extreme cold, extensive sea ice, permafrost, prolonged polar darkness during winter, and continuous daylight during summer. Temperatures can fall below -40C in continental areas, while thick sea ice, storms, and limited infrastructure make transportation and industrial operations exceptionally challenging.
However, the Arctic is warming nearly four times faster than the global average, creating unprecedented opportunities for maritime trade and resource exploitation, even if thawing permafrost threatens existing infrastructure.
Who owns what in the Arctic?
Russia, Canada, the US, Denmark, and Norway – countries bordering the Arctic Ocean – exercise sovereignty over their established land territories and islands, as well as their territorial waters extending up to 12 nautical miles offshore. Coastal states also enjoy exclusive rights to natural resources within a 200-nautical-mile exclusive economic zone.
However, their rights can extend considerably farther if they establish that the seabed beyond this limit forms part of their continental shelf. This is where high-stakes game begins, as countries with rights over an extended continental shelf can exclusively explore and exploit its oil, gas, and mineral resources.
The Arctic is estimated to hold 90 billion barrels of oil and 1,669 trillion cubic feet of natural gas in undiscovered and recoverable reserves alone, on top of abundant deposits of nickel, copper, palladium, iron ore, zinc, lead, phosphate, and bauxite. To put it into perspective, OPEC estimates Russia’s entire proven reserves at 80 billion barrels of crude oil and approximately 1,483 trillion cubic feet of natural gas.
At the same time, extended continental shelf rights are not equal to territorial sovereignty, with the waters remaining open to international navigation.
Russia was the first country to formally seek recognition of an extended Arctic continental shelf, submitting several claims to a UN commission since 2001. The commission requested additional scientific evidence, prompting Moscow to conduct extensive Arctic expeditions.
Other countries joined the Arctic race: Denmark submitted claims in 2014, followed by Canada in 2019. After Russia significantly expanded its proposed continental shelf in 2021, Canada responded with an enlarged claim in 2022, complaining that Moscow’s move had tripled the area overlapping with its own submission.
However, Moscow has made significant strides in defending its claims. In 2023, the UN Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf largely endorsed Russia’s geological arguments, supporting an extended shelf encompassing an estimated 1.8 million sq km.
Yet UN recommendations alone do not settle the dispute. Russia, Canada, and Denmark must still resolve their overlapping entitlements through negotiations or other lawful means. The outcome is not entirely without precedent, as Russia and Norway managed to settle a decades-long disagreement over approximately 175,000 sq km of the Barents Sea in 2010.
What does the Russian Arctic look like?
Russia’s Arctic stretches from the Kola Peninsula near Norway in the west to Chukotka opposite Alaska in the east, with the total coastline spanning more than 24,000 km. Russia’s officially designated Arctic Zone covers approximately 4.8 million sq km, or 28% of the country’s territory, and encompasses entire administrative regions, from Murmansk in the west to northern Yakutia in the east.
The landscape varies from rocky coastlines and tundra plains to frozen wetlands and vast taiga forests. Farther north lie remote archipelagos, including Novaya Zemlya, Franz Josef Land, Severnaya Zemlya, and the New Siberian Islands, some of which are extensively covered by glaciers and permanent ice. Novaya Zemlya also served as a major Soviet nuclear weapons testing ground.
The Russian Arctic is home to nearly 2.5 million people, with the region generating an estimated 7% of national GDP and 11% of its exports as of 2025.
Despite its unforgiving climate, the Russian Arctic is far from an empty wilderness. Its major population and industrial centers include Murmansk – the world’s largest city north of the Arctic Circle with a population of 260,000 which is also a major ice-free port – and Norilsk, a powerhouse of nickel, copper, and palladium production.
Other important Arctic Zone centers include Arkhangelsk and Severodvinsk, known for maritime industries and nuclear submarine construction, as well as Vorkuta, Salekhard, and the gas-producing hub of Novy Urengoy.
Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous District is also the site of Novatek’s Yamal LNG plant, the largest of its kind in Russia, which exports gas through the port of Sabetta. Farther east, Pevek is home to the Akademik Lomonosov, the world’s only floating nuclear power plant.
The unique design is dictated by necessity: Western Chukotka is cut off from Russia’s national power grid, while the NPP was built at a shipyard and transported to the remote location by sea, avoiding major problems associated with construction of an ordinary nuclear facility.
How important is the Arctic to Russia, and vice versa?
Russia’s Arctic Zone is an economic powerhouse, underpinning its energy exports and supplying critical raw materials, hosting more than 80% of national natural gas production, alongside substantial shares of its oil, nickel, and platinum-group metal output. Major industrial complexes, including the Yamal gas fields and Norilsk mining operations, are central not only to Russia’s welfare, but also to global energy and commodity markets.
As for trade, Russia’s ports, major Siberian rivers, and icebreaker fleet – the largest in the world – form an extensive transportation network connecting resource-rich territories with international markets.
In this vein, the Northern Sea Route is now emerging as the most important Arctic itinerary due to climate change, having handled more than 37 million tons of cargo in 2025, including 5.4 million tons transported between Russian and Chinese ports.
Despite tensions with the West over the Ukraine conflict, Russia continues to participate in limited Arctic Council cooperation, including technical work on environmental monitoring and other shared regional challenges.
Why is the Arctic a key military stronghold for Russia?
Beyond its economic importance, the Arctic is a cornerstone of Russia’s national security, hosting crucial elements of its nuclear deterrent and providing strategic access to the Atlantic and Pacific oceans.
The Kola Peninsula, bordering Norway and Finland, anchors the Northern Fleet and its nuclear-armed submarines, while an extensive network of airfields, radar installations, missile defenses, and military bases protects Russia’s northern approaches. Since the early 2010s, Moscow has also been restoring numerous Soviet-era facilities across remote Arctic islands.
The importance of the Arctic only increased after Finland and Sweden acceded to NATO in 2023 and 2024, respectively, leaving Russia as the only non-NATO member among the eight Arctic states.
Moscow subsequently sounded the alarm about the bloc’s expanding presence near its strategic naval bases. This year, NATO launched the so-called Arctic Sentry initiative, aimed at strengthening military coordination and surveillance, with joint drills involving tens of thousands of troops.
The EU, meanwhile, is also looking to interfere in regional affairs, with the bloc’s new Arctic Strategy envisaging the development of military logistics, upgrading ports and airports for military use, expanding icebreaker fleets, and increasing satellite surveillance of the region and tracking of Russian oil tankers.
In light of Western countries’ saber-rattling, Putin accused NATO of increasingly treating the Far North as a “springboard for potential conflicts,” warning that “we will proceed from current realities and will respond to all this.”
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov went further, accusing NATO of deliberately militarizing the Arctic, stressing that “such military activity in the Far North poses a direct threat to Russia’s security.” He also warned that escalating tensions could trigger an armed clash with “potentially disastrous consequences.”
How powerful is Russia’s icebreaker fleet?
Russia’s icebreaker fleet is in a league of its own, comparable in numbers to the rest of the world combined. The country operates 43 icebreakers, including eight nuclear-powered vessels and 35 diesel-electric ships.
Nuclear icebreakers are particularly formidable as they can operate for extended periods without refueling, maintaining access to remote ports, and escorting commercial ships through heavily ice-covered waters. Russia’s four modern 60-megawatt Project 22220 icebreakers are designed to break through ice up to approximately 2.8 meters thick.
Moscow also continues to press its icebreaker advantage, with plans to commission four additional nuclear icebreakers that are now at various stages of development. These include the behemoth Project 10510 Rossiya, designed to deliver 120 megawatts of propulsion power and support navigation through even thicker Arctic ice. The icebreaker is expected to be ready for operations in late 2029.
Russia’s icebreaker fleet is far ahead of the American one, which only operates three polar icebreakers – a shortcoming several US administrations described as a national security concern.
As for the EU, it collectively operates around ten icebreakers, depending on classification. The bloc’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, acknowledged the gap, declaring that “in the Arctic, icebreakers are the measure of power,” with plans to explore joint procurement, though these efforts are unlikely to yield results for many years.
How does Russia govern the Arctic?
Given the region’s undeniable importance, Moscow has built an extensive state apparatus dedicated to managing its northern territories.While overall priorities and strategic vision are set by Putin personally, much of the federal coordination falls to Deputy Prime Minister Yury Trutnev, who chairs the State Commission for Arctic Development. Established in 2015, the body brings together senior officials, regional governors and representatives of major companies to coordinate economic, infrastructure and security policies.
The region is also overseen by the designated Ministry for the Development of the Russian Far East and Arctic, headed by Aleksey Chekunkov, which handles Arctic development policy, investment incentives, and socioeconomic programs.
As for the Arctic’s maritime portfolio, it is supervised by former Russian Security Council Secretary Nikolay Patrushev, now a presidential aide, who chairs the Maritime Board, established in 2024 to coordinate maritime strategy and defend Russia’s interests at sea.
Russia’s state nuclear corporation, Rosatom, also plays a significant role in the region while managing the Northern Sea Route infrastructure and nuclear icebreaker fleet. Murmansk Governor Andrey Chibis also chairs a dedicated State Council commission on the Northern Sea Route and the Arctic, helping coordinate regional development proposals.
The Russian government has also for years run several incentivizing special programs in the region, including a preferential business regime offering qualifying companies multi-year tax breaks and reduced social insurance contributions.
Moscow also operates the Arctic Hectare program, allowing eligible citizens to obtain up to one hectare of land for development completely free of charge, with the possibility of subsequently obtaining ownership, and the Arctic Mortgage scheme, offering qualifying borrowers subsidized housing loans at rates of up to 2%.
Some of the Arctic Zone regions boast the highest average salaries nationally. According to Rosstat, average gross monthly salaries in 2025 reached approximately 215,000 rubles ($2,570) in Chukotka and 178,000 rubles ($2,130) in the Yamal-Nenets Autonomous Area – a level exceeding or comparable to Moscow’s and higher than the national average of 100,000 rubles ($1,200). However, the financial advantages are partly offset by higher living costs.
The region also benefits from a dedicated Soviet-inherited Northern Delivery system that coordinates supplies of essential goods to remote settlements.
How did Russia develop its Arctic frontier?
While indigenous peoples inhabited the region for thousands of years, Russian Pomor seafarers first began exploring the White and Barents Seas in the Middle Ages, establishing trading and fishing settlements. However, a full-scale expansion picked up steam only in the 16th century and beyond.
The most dramatic transformation took place in the Soviet era, when Moscow poured major resources into polar exploration, industrialization, and transportation infrastructure. In 1932, the Soviet icebreaking steamer Alexander Sibiryakov became the first vessel to traverse the Northern Sea Route in a single navigation season.
Another landmark achievement came in 1959 when the Soviet Union commissioned the Lenin, the world’s first nuclear-powered icebreaker, allowing ships to operate in the Arctic for extended periods of time. During the Cold War, Moscow also heavily invested in naval and submarine bases in the region.
Following the Soviet collapse in 1991, investment plunged, infrastructure deteriorated, and northern shipping declined. However, Russia began rebuilding its Arctic presence in the 2000s, developing major energy projects, reviving military facilities, and expanding its icebreaker capabilities.
How is Russia investing in the Arctic?
Moscow has made Arctic development a long-term national priority, with the current strategy running through 2035. According to Russian officials, more than 1,000 state-supported projects have been launched in the region since 2020, attracting approximately 2.6 trillion rubles ($32 billion) in investment. Moscow expects total investment over the coming decade to exceed 30 trillion rubles.
Much of the effort is focused on natural resources, as major companies, including Gazprom, Rosneft, Novatek, and Nornickel, are expanding oil, gas, and mining operations, while the government offers preferential tax arrangements and other incentives to attract investors.
Moscow is also modernizing Arctic ports, expanding railway connections, and developing specialized cargo fleets. Apart from building icebreakers, it plans to construct at least ten rescue vessels and launch 12 weather-monitoring and radar satellites by 2035 in a bid to support more reliable navigation along the Northern Sea Route.
The military development remains another priority, with Russia continuing to modernize airfields and bases, strengthening the Northern Fleet and expanding the number of personnel deployed in the region. Last year, Putin also ordered the extension of a military-town renovation program through at least 2030, with a minimum of 10 billion rubles in annual federal funding.
Bottom Line
While the Arctic race has been overshadowed by the Russia-West standoff over Ukraine, the region remains crucial to Russia’s long-term interests. The Arctic’s enormous natural reserves underpin the national economy, and its military bases form an indispensable part of Russia’s nuclear deterrent, while the Northern Sea Route promises lucrative trade opportunities along the country’s vast northern coastline.
As both NATO and the EU hanker after influence in the region, Russia has made clear that it has no intention of surrendering its longstanding position. For the Arctic giant, the frozen frontier is far more than a distant outpost or a peripheral prize – it is a cornerstone of its security, prosperity, and future.

articles.title: Denmark to Purchase New U.S.-Made Anthem Cruise Missiles
articles.body:
Denmark will purchase Norwegian Joint Strike Missiles from Kongsberg to arm its F-35s, as well as new Anthem cruise missiles from the American company Covenant for launch from ground-based launchers. The Anthem was first publicly unveiled in early September.
The Danish Ministry of Defence announced the procurement.
According to the ministry, the goal of the procurement is to strengthen national and collective deterrence. These are weapons that NATO needs and that contribute to Denmark’s security.
The missiles are among various types of long-range, high-precision weapons that, thanks to advanced navigation technologies, can strike targets at great distances with high accuracy.
Covenant is an American defense company with an Israeli engineering and manufacturing base, founded in 2024 by Michael Kaufman and Ofir Dayan. Kaufman, an American-Israeli entrepreneur who previously worked with Peter Thiel, became the company’s CEO, while Dayan became the CTO. Covenant is headquartered in Washington, D.C., and operates a research and development and manufacturing complex covering approximately 3,000 m² in northern Israel.
Over the past two years, Covenant has raised more than $250 million in investments. Its investors include Andreessen Horowitz, Peter Thiel’s Founders Fund, Lux Capital, 8VC, Lightspeed, Altimeter, and the Israeli fund Aleph. The company has brought together more than 200 employees in the U.S., Germany, and Israel, including engineers with experience working at major defense corporations.
Covenant publicly unveiled its flagship product—the Anthem long-range cruise missile—only on September 9, 2026, after two years of development. At the time of the presentation, the company had already reported over 200 test flights of the missile and approximately $150 million in orders. Among its customers, the company named the U.S. Army and Navy, as well as international partners.
The Anthem is a ground-launched missile capable of carrying a payload weighing over 200 kg. It uses a solid-fuel rocket engine for launch. The developer has not publicly disclosed the exact flight range.
The missile is being developed with mass production and large-scale deployment in mind, alongside other long-range weapons such as the Tomahawk and JASSM-ER. According to Covenant’s management, once full-scale serial production begins, the target price for the Anthem will be several hundred thousand dollars.
To ensure mass production, Covenant has engaged three suppliers of solid-fuel rocket engines and has been working to bring on a fourth. The company has also signed long-term agreements for more than 4,000 rocket engines over the next two years. This approach is intended to reduce dependence on individual suppliers as production scales up.
The company is rolling out Anthem production in the U.S., Germany, and Israel. Once they reach full capacity, the facilities in Dallas and Saxony are expected to produce 5,000 missiles each per year, while the site in northern Israel will produce an additional 2,000.
The Joint Strike Missile (JSM) is a fifth-generation strike missile from Kongsberg, designed to overcome modern air defense systems.
It was developed based on the NSM naval missile. The air-launched variant, like the base version, is capable of engaging surface and ground targets, making it a versatile weapon.
The JSM’s stated range is 350 km. The warhead weighs 120 kg, and the missile’s total weight is 416 kg. It is 4 m long and has a diameter of 480 mm.
The missile can be stored in the internal bay of an F-35A fighter jet, preserving the aircraft’s low-observability characteristics.
The missile uses a high-precision navigation system that ensures a low-altitude flight profile. For terminal guidance, it employs a modern infrared seeker with imaging capability.
