articles.title: No Persian Gulf for old carriers
articles.body:
No Persian Gulf for old carriers
Top commander says American warships will never return as Strait of Hormuz becomes center of war
TEHRAN – The main confrontation between Iran and the United States in this war has been, and continues to be, in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, and senior Iranian commanders now say the era when American aircraft carriers cruised these waters with impunity is over for good.
In his strongest remarks to date on the naval war, Chief of the General Staff of the Armed Forces and Commander of the Central Khatam al-Anbiya Headquarters, Major General Ali Abdollahi, declared that the U.S. Navy has been rendered ineffective and will never be allowed back into the Persian Gulf.
Abdollahi said: The proud Armed Forces of Islamic Iran, with trust in Almighty God, have managed to render ineffective the U.S. Navy, which Trump and the leaders of that country regard as the pinnacle of American power and with which they threaten the region and the world, in such a way that it is no longer able to approach the seas surrounding the Persian Gulf and Iran’s territorial waters.
“The U.S. president must dream of his military and army once again entering the Persian Gulf. They will take this wish to the grave forever,” he added.
“We will under no circumstances and at no time allow American military vessels to enter the Persian Gulf,” he stressed.
From overthrow to reopening the Strait
His remarks, delivered as Washington and Tel Aviv openly speak of “finishing the job” and preparing a renewed offensive, underscore how far the war’s objectives have shifted. What began as an American-Israeli campaign to overthrow the Islamic Republic or force its surrender has now, after more than eight months of war, been reduced in practice to a struggle to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
When the war began in June 2025 with surprise strikes in the middle of negotiations, and escalated again in February 2026 and June this year, U.S. President Donald Trump promised swift collapse in Tehran, destruction of Iran’s nuclear program, and an end to its missile and regional power. None of that happened.
Instead, Iran survived, retaliated with massive missile, drone and naval operations against American bases and Israeli targets, tightened its control over the Strait of Hormuz, and imposed an unprecedented energy and military cost on Washington. Moody’s estimates the war has already cost American consumers $265 billion this year, about $2,000 per household, half of it from higher energy prices.
Today, American officials no longer speak of imminent regime change in Tehran. They speak of restoring freedom of navigation, reopening the Strait, securing detained vessels, and preventing oil prices from climbing beyond $110 per barrel after mine incidents involving tankers. In other words, the superpower that came to bring Iran to its knees is now fighting to bring its own ships back through a waterway guarded by Iran.
Abdollahi directly mocked that reversal: Trump has repeatedly claimed that they have destroyed Iran’s nuclear facilities, but at the same time they keep repeating that Iran must not have nuclear weapons, and this blatant contradiction has no end.
“If you have destroyed everything, then what is the meaning of repeating these hallucinations? These remarks are utterly meaningless, contradictory and repetitive, and are consumed to deceive world public opinion and especially the American people,” he said.
“If you are sure that you have destroyed all of Iran’s military facilities and capabilities, then why do your rusted carriers, vessels and cowardly military forces not dare to approach the Strait of Hormuz and Iran’s maritime and land borders?” he asked.
Fifth Fleet no longer functional
That question now defines the military map of the region. Iranian officials say U.S. forces, after suffering painful blows from the guardians of the Strait, no longer come forward from the Arabian Sea, and whenever they have taken that risk, they have harmed themselves.
Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyed Mojtaba Khamenei made the same point in his message of September 28, which Abdollahi’s statement echoed: These days [the enemy forces], because of the painful blows they have received from the guardians of the Strait of Hormuz, do not come forward from the Arabian Sea, and whenever they have risked this danger, they have inflicted damage upon themselves; and soon the Arabian Sea itself will rid itself of them.
Iranian commanders say this is not rhetoric but the result of sustained, heavy strikes on the very infrastructure that once sustained American dominance in the Persian Gulf.
According to Iranian military assessments, U.S. bases around the Persian Gulf — in Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait and Iraq — have been repeatedly targeted since the start of the war and have suffered extensive damage. Above all, the U.S. Fifth Fleet headquarters in Bahrain, the command center of American naval power in the region for nearly three decades, has been rendered completely destroyed and unusable by Iran’s heavy missile and drone attacks.
For years, the Fifth Fleet, with its destroyers, coastal combat ships, minesweepers and logistics hub at Manama, was presented as the guarantor of American order. Iranian officials now say its piers are empty, its command facilities inoperable, and its remaining vessels forced to operate from far outside the Persian Gulf, beyond the reach of Iranian anti-ship missiles, speedboats, submarines, mines and coastal defense systems.
U.S. carriers that once docked in Bahrain and sailed routinely through Hormuz now remain in the northern Indian Ocean and the Arabian Sea. Resupply requires long detours. Insurance rates have soared. Even Washington’s allies on the southern shore of the Persian Gulf, who hosted U.S. forces in hope of protection, have found their ports and airfields turned into targets and have quietly asked Washington to reduce its visible presence.
No return to pre-war order
Abdollahi said Iran’s strategy is to deepen that quagmire: Undoubtedly, with the firm resolve of the brave and wise Leadership, the will of the risen and resistant people, the self-sacrificing Armed Forces and the officials of Islamic Iran, it has been decided to drown you day by day deeper into the quagmire you have built with your own hands — America and its illegitimate offspring, the Zionist regime, and your feeble and aggressive armies.
“With the help of Almighty God and divine victory, the strategy of a strong Iran is that the longer this confrontation lasts, the deeper you will be dragged into the swamp of death and decline, God willing,” he added.
Regional and even Western analysts now concede that the security architecture of the Persian Gulf will not return to what it was before the war. For thirty years, that architecture rested on a simple assumption: unchallenged American naval supremacy, an open strait under American escort, and regional states sheltering under the U.S. umbrella while Iran was contained.
That assumption has collapsed. Iran has demonstrated it can close or control the Strait at will, strike any base in a 2,000-kilometer radius, impose costs on global energy markets, and survive direct American-Israeli bombardment. Host states have learned that hosting U.S. strike assets invites Iranian retaliation. Shipping companies have learned that transit without Iranian consent is a military risk, not a routine insurance matter.
Tehran therefore rejects talk of a return to the status quo ante through a ceasefire that merely reopens the waterway for American warships. Iranian officials insist any durable arrangement must recognize Iran’s legitimate security rights, end aggression and sanctions, and exclude U.S. military vessels from the Persian Gulf altogether.
For Tehran, the message is both military and political: the Persian Gulf is no longer permissive waters for aging carriers, rusted destroyers and expeditionary fantasies. It is, in Iranian doctrine, the front line of national defense and the lever that turned an intended war of overthrow into a war of attrition Washington cannot win.

articles.title: Ukraine receives only 24 Patriot missiles from USA over past three months - Zelenskyy
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that Ukraine has received only 24 interceptor missiles for its U.S.-made Patriot air defense systems over the last three months—a quantity far short of what is actually needed.
In an interview with ABC News on Friday, he noted that 30 ballistic missiles were fired at Kyiv just this past Thursday evening.
According to Zelenskyy’s estimates, Ukraine requires an average of 350 Patriot interceptor missiles per month.
Asked if he believes Putin requested that Trump to turn off intelligence-sharing between the U.S. and Ukraine, Zelenskyy responded, "I don't know. I hope, I trust and I hope God bless. No."
The President of Ukraine noted that he does not feel betrayed by the United States, but expressed regret over the lack of American aid. "I feel what I feel. It's not supportive," Zelenskyy said.
He emphasized that he is grateful for the partnership in the war against the Russian Federation, but suggested that, at times, he may not be as "polite" as other partners expect him to be. "Of course I'm a normal person, I'm just human, maybe not such a big humanitarian as Putin, of course … Like between friends, like in the family, you have to be honest, not to play games. I don't play games with Trump. This is my difference between me and Putin. I don't play with him any games. I'm direct, honest," Zelenskyy said.
The Ukrainian head of state believes that this is Trump’s personal decision “to be friends with Putin or not," but suggested that “they're in quite very good relations.”
Zelenskyy stated that the Ukrainian side is "ready to stop this war as quick as possible," but noted that the Russian Federation currently controls more than 19% of Ukrainian territory, and that Ukraine is not prepared to cede any further territory for the sake of ending the war.
As earlier reported, by June 2025, the U.S. military will likely have used up to two-thirds of its stockpile of missile-defense interceptors, even as American defense companies ramp up production. Specifically, Lockheed Martin is working to increase its annual production capacity for advanced PAC-3 interceptors, used in Patriot missile systems, from approximately 600 to 2,000 units. According to Bloomberg, the shortage in missile stockpiles has already affected supplies to other U.S. allies.
German authorities are seeking permission from the USA to assemble an advanced version of the Patriot interceptor missiles at facilities in Germany, stated German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius.
Zelenskyy has stated that Ukraine is not the top priority for suppliers of American PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles for Patriot air defense systems, as the majority of these have long been directed to the Middle East. According to the president, Ukraine is also working with European and other nations around the world to secure additional missile supplies to protect its population.
According to him, Ukraine received 675 missiles throughout 2023, and 364 in 2025—yet the number of Russian missile strikes has increased during this period. For 2026, the delivery of 264 PAC-3 and PAC-2 missiles was planned. The PAC-3 missiles are supplied by the United States through the PURL program. "All our partners—both Americans and Europeans—are aware of the sums they are contributing and know exactly how many missiles they are providing us. There are also separate bilateral agreements with various European nations and countries in the Middle East. But, unfortunately, you can see a downward trend, and this depends primarily on the American side," Zelenskyy stated in August of this year.
On October 21, Ukrainian Minister of Defence Yevhen Khmara and Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine Mykhailo Drapaty met with a delegation from the American defence company Lockheed Martin, led by Orlando Sanchez Jr., President of Lockheed Martin Aeronautics. The discussions focused on the importance of stable arms supplies and future cooperation. In particular, the parties addressed increasing the delivery of PAC-3 interceptor missiles to counter the threat of strikes by Russian ballistic missiles.

articles.title: US lawmakers urge Pentagon to expand Starshield contract for Ukraine
articles.body:
US lawmakers urge Pentagon to expand Starshield contract for Ukraine
Members of the US Congress have called on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the Pentagon to expand its contract under the Starshield programme and restore Ukraine's access to Starlink and Starshield satellite communications following recent disruptions.
Source: a letter from US lawmakers
Details: In a bipartisan, bicameral appeal, US lawmakers insist that services be restored without speed restrictions to ensure Ukraine has the technical capabilities it needs.
Quote: "Ukrainian forces depend on these services for command and control, intelligence sharing, battlefield communications, and the operation of unmanned systems. Any degradation in service, including reduced connection speeds, restricted geographic coverage, or interruptions in access, undermines Ukraine's military effectiveness and provides Russian forces with an operational advantage that will extend the conflict and put more civilians in harm's way."
Details: The lawmakers urged the US Department of Defense to maintain the coverage Ukraine needs to conduct legitimate military operations, including over Russian territory, and to ensure that the transition from the commercial Starlink service to the government-run Starshield programme takes place without any interruption to service.
"Decisions regarding service availability, coverage, and performance should not be left solely to the discretion of a private provider when they have direct consequences for Ukraine's ability to defend itself," the lawmakers added.
They also called on the Department of Defense to consider using its powers under the relevant provision of the Defense Production Act, which allows the federal government to require companies to prioritise government orders.
"The United States and Europe have made significant investments in Ukraine's defence because of how a Russian victory would put our security at risk. Those investments should not be undermined by preventable disruptions to the communications infrastructure on which Ukrainian forces depend," the lawmakers concluded.
Previously: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed on 23 October that speed restrictions for Starlink satellite communications terminals in Ukraine remain in force.
The New York Times reported that US senators had warned the White House they would withhold votes on nominees until President Donald Trump's administration ensured the restoration of the communications capabilities used by Ukrainian troops.
A bipartisan group of nearly 20 members of the US House of Representatives called on Trump to ask Elon Musk to give Ukraine access to Starlink systems to target missile launchers on Russian territory.
US Democratic Senator Chris Coons had previously contacted Elon Musk's SpaceX, asking the company to explain who had decided to restrict Starlink's operation in Ukraine and why.
Background:
- The Wall Street Journal reported that Elon Musk had ordered Starlink services to be slowed down. It is unclear to what extent Trump was involved in discussions about the slowdown.
- US Republican Senator Thom Tillis is seeking an investigation into the Pentagon's actions with regard to problems with Starlink satellite communications systems encountered by the Ukrainian Armed Forces.
- US House of Representatives member Joe Wilson and nearly two dozen of his colleagues prepared a letter calling for Ukraine to be permitted to use Starlink for strikes on launch sites within Russian territory.
- The Wall Street Journal, citing US and Ukrainian officials familiar with the matter, reported that Trump had called Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on the military version of Starlink in Ukraine.
- On the evening of 22 October, Trump said Musk had already lifted speed restrictions on the military version of Starlink in Ukraine but declined to say whether he had personally called him about the issue.
- Ukraine's Defence Ministry said it was recording disruptions to Starlink and Starshield services on the line of contact.

articles.title: Ukraine’s military says Starlink satellite connection stable after recent restrictions
articles.body:
Ukraine’s military has a “stable connection to Starlink”, the Ukrainian government said, 10 days after its ability to use the satellite communications system was suddenly restricted.
But hours after the announcement, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, whose company owns Starlink, accused the Ukrainian military of violating the company’s terms. Neither Musk nor the US government, which operates Starshield using Starlink technology, took responsibility for imposing the curbs.
“Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week,” Musk said in a social media post.
Serhiy Beskrestnov, a Ukrainian presidential adviser, said on the Telegram app that the country is “physically unable” to use Starlink for long- and medium-range attack drone operations.
Ukraine’s general staff and defence ministry did not immediately comment.
The Starlink satellite terminals, which are produced by Elon Musk’s SpaceX but managed by the US government, are a key component of Ukraine’s military operations. Sudden speed restrictions on the terminals, which capped operations at speeds of 160km/h (99mph), led to the failure of several Ukrainian combat missions earlier this month.
The military’s ability to intercept Russian attack drones was hampered and some Ukrainian operations to strike behind enemy frontlines were cancelled. Russia was able to launch ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US.
The speed restrictions coincided with the announcement by Donald Trump of a US deal to buy Russian diesel, although the US president initially denied that his administration was behind the decision to cut intelligence sharing with Ukraine.
“I don’t know if it was anybody, but it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” Trump said, referring to Musk, SpaceX’s chief executive.
However, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, appeared to throw suspicion on Musk when he defended Trump last Wednesday. “The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr Musk,” Rubio said. “That’s a private company. The president doesn’t run that company and can’t direct that company to do anything.”
Musk was quick to blame the limits on Starshield on the Trump administration, writing on X last week that the systems were “owned and controlled by the US government”. “Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately Potus [president of the United States],” he wrote.
The US vice-president, JD Vance, backed Musk on Thursday, saying the billionaire “doesn’t want to get in the middle of what is a war between two state actors without the United States government effectively directing him on what to do”.
Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, blamed both parties: “It was a message from [the] American government to limit the speed … And technically, SpaceX did it.”
There were no similar restrictions on Starshield terminals in EU countries and that they applied only to Ukraine, he added. “In other words, this is a planned operation.”
He said the decision would “bring a lot of human losses … of course people would die”.
Announcing the restoration of the system on Saturday in a diplomatic video address on the Telegram app, Zelenskyy expressed his gratitude to his US allies, including Trump and the US state department, for resolving the operational issue: “The most important development for today is that Starlink and Starshield have resumed operations at their pre-restriction speeds. The speeds are now at the level we need.”
The restoration began overnight. “By this morning, the speeds were already sufficient for operational use,” Zelenskyy said. “This is very important and significant for our frontline logistics and for defending Ukraine against jet-powered Shaheds.”
On Thursday, Trump had claimed the service was running again at full speed, but a European official speaking to the Associated Press denied the service was fully functioning.
When asked by reporters whether he would tell Musk to stop “messing around” with Ukraine’s access to Starlink on Friday, the US president said: “I’ve not spoken to him. I might have to … I’ve heard it was fixed. But if it’s not, I’ll speak to him … If there is a problem, I’ll get it straightened out.”
He then described Musk as a “very brilliant” and “very good” person.
Reuters contributed reporting

articles.title: Bipartisan US Lawmakers Push Back On Trump's Russia Policy, Vow Support For Ukraine
articles.body:
WASHINGTON -- A bipartisan group of US lawmakers is stepping up efforts to defend Ukraine, challenging President Donald Trump’s decision to ease restrictions on Russian energy imports and demanding guarantees that Kyiv will retain access to critical American military and intelligence support.
In a series of legislative initiatives, congressional inquiries, and appeals to the administration, Republicans and Democrats have warned that decisions benefiting Moscow or disrupting Ukraine’s battlefield capabilities could undermine US national security, weaken congressional authority, and prolong Russia’s war.
The pushback comes after the administration authorized transactions involving Russian diesel fuel, amid reports that Ukraine’s access to SpaceX’s Starlink and military-grade Starshield satellite communications systems had been restricted.
Ukrainian officials say the disruptions have affected military operations, although they reported on October 24 that satellite connection speeds had been restored. Questions remain about who imposed the restrictions.
A Ukrainian official familiar with the matter told RFE/RL that SpaceX had not responded to Kyiv about the previous restrictions. The official added that although Kyiv had been in touch with the US government, "no one has explained what happened or what will happen next."
The developments have exposed growing divisions over the administration’s Russia policy, with some Republicans joining Democrats in demanding accountability and stronger safeguards for Ukraine.
Bill Targets Russian Oil Waiver
Representative Brian Fitzpatrick, a Pennsylvania Republican and co-chair of the Congressional Ukraine Caucus, has introduced the Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act of 2026, alongside Republican Representative Don Bacon of Nebraska and Democratic Representative Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington.
The bill would nullify a Treasury Department waiver issued on October 9 that authorized transactions involving Russian diesel fuel, including imports into the United States. The temporary authorization is due to expire on April 7, 2027.
Trump has defended the agreement with Russia as a way to increase global diesel supplies and bring down fuel prices. Announcing the deal on October 9 following talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, he said Russia had agreed to immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to US and global markets, with further shipments to follow. Diesel prices have risen sharply amid disruptions to global energy supplies linked to the war in Iran.
The proposed bill would also prohibit future waivers allowing Russian energy imports and require intelligence agencies to provide support for Ukraine’s defense, notifying congressional intelligence committees within 24 hours of any interruption.
The legislation seeks to reinforce a 2022 federal law prohibiting Russian oil imports, which the sponsors say the administration has undermined through its latest decision.
“Congress must be a check to the president’s egregious appeasement to Putin,” Bacon told RFE/RL.
In a statement announcing the bill, Fitzpatrick argued that Washington could not credibly demand accountability from Russian President Vladimir Putin while allowing American markets to support the energy revenues sustaining his war.
“We must not import a single drop of Russian oil,” Fitzpatrick said, adding that Congress had approved the prohibition with overwhelming bipartisan support in 2022.
He invoked the late President Reagan’s foreign policy doctrine, arguing that strength was necessary to secure peace and that aggression must carry a cost greater than its rewards.
Bacon accused Trump of reversing his own criticism of European countries for purchasing Russian energy.
“For years, President Trump criticized Europe for buying Russian energy and propping up Putin’s war economy,” Bacon said. “Now, Trump wants to make it easier for Putin to sell diesel fuel. He is wrong.”
Gluesenkamp Perez also condemned the waiver, saying it ran roughshod over American national interests and the bipartisan will of Congress. She argued that if Trump wanted to reduce gasoline prices, he should pursue policies that end the war in Iran rather than direct American money toward Russia.
The bill has been referred to three House committees for consideration. Its introduction marks one of the first legislative responses to the administration’s recent Russia-related decisions.
Lawmakers Press Pentagon Over Ukraine Satellite Access
Concern over Ukraine’s military capabilities has also brought together lawmakers from both parties in the House and Senate.
Eight lawmakers -- Representatives Marcy Kaptur (Dem.-Ohio), Brian Fitzpatrick (Rep.-Pennsylvania), Mike Quigley (Dem.-Illinois), Jim Costa (Dem.-California), and Jimmy Panetta (Dem.-California), along with Senators Mark Kelly (Dem.-Arizona), Thom Tillis (Rep.-North Carolina), and Elissa Slotkin (Dem.-Michigan) -- have urged Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to expand the Pentagon’s Starshield contract and ensure uninterrupted access to Starlink and Starshield services.
The lawmakers called for the restoration of unrestricted service speeds, sufficient geographic coverage for Ukraine’s lawful military operations, including over Russian territory, and a seamless transition from commercial Starlink to government-contracted Starshield.
“Any degradation in service, including reduced connection speeds, restricted geographic coverage, or interruptions in access, undermines Ukraine’s military effectiveness and provides Russian forces with an operational advantage that will extend the conflict and put more civilians in harm’s way,” they wrote.
They also urged the Defense Department to consider using its authority under the Defense Production Act to ensure reliable access to the satellite communications on which Ukrainian forces depend for command and control, intelligence sharing, battlefield communications and drone operations.
“Decisions regarding service availability, coverage, and performance should not be left solely to the discretion of a private provider when they have direct consequences for Ukraine’s ability to defend itself,” the lawmakers said.
The appeal followed Ukrainian reports that restrictions introduced on October 13 disrupted communications for drones and other military platforms moving faster than 100 miles per hour (160 km/h), affecting Ukraine’s ability to guide defensive drones and conduct operations against Russian positions.
Musk Faces Questions Over Ukraine Satellite Restrictions
The satellite dispute has prompted additional congressional investigations into who ordered the restrictions and whether the US government has sufficient oversight of the communications systems it relies on.
New York Representative Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and Democratic Senator Peter Welch of Vermont have led a group of six Democratic lawmakers demanding answers from SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk.
Their letter questions Musk’s public assertion that restrictions were determined by the US military and ultimately the president, citing reports that Musk himself proposed limiting Ukrainian communications.
The lawmakers have asked whether Musk or SpaceX officials discussed restricting access with Trump, Putin, or their representatives; who ordered any limitations; what conditions Ukraine must meet to regain full access; and who will control future operational decisions.
They also raised concerns about corporate governance and the implications of a private company exercising decisive influence over a foreign military’s communications.
Connecticut Senator Richard Blumenthal, the top Democrat on the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, has separately opened a congressional inquiry, demanding written answers from Musk by November 5 and a briefing from SpaceX officials by November 12.
Blumenthal is seeking details about who authorized the restrictions, whether Ukraine received advance notice, and whether SpaceX can degrade Starshield service for US or allied forces without Pentagon authorization. He has also requested information on the value of SpaceX’s government contracts since 2020.
Separately, Democratic Representatives Sam Liccardo and Ro Khanna of California, along with Panetta, have called on White House chief of staff Susie Wiles to initiate a government-wide investigation and provide a briefing within two weeks.
“Either a private contractor independently made life-and-death national security decisions, or President Trump directed the restriction of critical military communications supporting a US ally,” they wrote.
The demands for answers come amid conflicting accounts of who authorized the restrictions.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio has denied that Trump or other administration officials ordered them or knew about them in advance. Musk, meanwhile, has said Starshield systems are controlled by the US government and that decisions on restrictions ultimately rest with the military and the president.
Trump has said service was restored following contact with Musk, but Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has disputed that account, saying restrictions remain in place.
The uncertainty has also drawn criticism from Republican Senator Thom Tillis, who wrote on X: “Whoever is handing Putin the gift of a more vulnerable Ukraine should at least have the guts to put their name on it.”

articles.title: Moscow Eyes European Security Overhaul in Talks With US Envoys
articles.body:
As expected, talks on ending Russia’s war against Ukraine have shifted to talks on a new division of Europe.
In his statement on 22 October, Putin said that future negotiations should determine guarantees for Russia as well as the broader rules of European security. According to him, it was Witkoff who proposed widening the agenda.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Europeans are not yet being invited to the conversation about European security. Peskov specified that representatives of Ukraine, Russia and the US will meet in Abu Dhabi. He acknowledged that European countries cannot be left out going forward, but tied their participation to the position they take (whether they behave themselves).
Revival of December 2021 ultimatum and territorial claims
Some Russian experts have a quite concrete picture of what the coming talks should cover. Valdai Club expert Stanislav Tkachenko speaks openly of a return to the demands of December 2021: limiting NATO’s military presence to pre-enlargement levels, removing new bases and military facilities from the Baltic states and Eastern Europe, and halting further enlargement. To this he adds recognition of territorial seizures, the lifting of sanctions and the return of frozen assets. His reasoning is that Moscow regards the European Union as a losing party as well, and therefore expects concessions from it too. Tkachenko even suggests new claims on Odesa, Mykolaiv and Kharkiv, arguing that Putin’s references to “historical territories” leave room for them.
Russian Border Strikes and EU EES Challenge Checkpoints
At the same time, it is possible to negotiate and continue the war.
Frontline combat alongside protracted diplomacy
Dmitri Trenin, president of the Russian International Affairs Council, believes that freezing hostilities along the current front line does not suit Russia. Talking to the US is nevertheless worthwhile, since it is already producing some results. He notes that Moscow has agreed to discuss, first and foremost, the future post-war security system. The fighting itself, he predicts, may continue into 2027. He links the concrete terms of any agreement to the situation on the battlefield: talks can happen now, while decisions will depend on military outcomes.
Explanations for the case that negotiations once again lead nowhere are also already being prepared. Fyodor Lukyanov interprets the new Ukrainian proposals as Zelensky’s attempt to ease pressure from Trump. He suggests that Kyiv may walk away from agreements already reached, with the Europeans backing it. For that reason, in his view, Witkoff’s arrival with new ideas does not yet mean anything.
Political messaging ahead of US midterms
Meanwhile, Moscow is finding reasons to celebrate even before any deal. Duma deputy Oleg Matveychev considers it a success in itself that the US talks to Russia as an equal and discusses a wide range of global issues with it. A concrete outcome of the meeting is not even necessary for this assessment. He takes the comparison of a possible Putin–Trump–Xi meeting with “Yalta-2” as recognition of Russia’s special status: it is once again among the states that shape the future order.
Practical gains are added to the symbolic success. Duma deputy Leonid Slutsky calls the meeting with Witkoff a diplomatic “master class” by Putin and points to sanctions relief and the diesel deal with the US. For him, this is already evidence of a successful restoration of relations with Washington. He envisions further negotiations taking Russia’s interests fully into account.
Trump is also seen as a partner for exerting influence on Ukraine and Europe. Political commentator Gevorg Mirzayan suggests that Moscow and Washington are discussing a coordinated policy towards them. In his view, Trump wants to show voters a foreign-policy success, bring the Europeans back into greater obedience, and establish energy cooperation with Russia.
The rush ahead of the US elections is also viewed as an opportunity for Russia. Boris Mezhuev openly calls Trump an ally on the question of a settlement. He believes the US president needs a peace plan he can present to voters, even if it has not yet been signed. Russia can help him secure such a political result while advancing its own demands.
And yet there are still some in Moscow who remain dissatisfied, such as Dugin, Malofeev and Karaganov, united by a shared mental disorder: a passion for using nuclear weapons. In their latest interviews and publications, they openly call on Putin to use nuclear weapons against Ukraine and Europe.

articles.title: Germany in talks with Ukraine to purchase Bars jet-powered drones – Bloomberg, photo
articles.body:
Germany in talks with Ukraine to purchase Bars jet-powered drones – Bloomberg, photo
Germany plans to replenish its stockpile of precision-guided weapons with several thousand missiles from European arms manufacturers. In particular, the country is in talks with Ukraine regarding Bars jet-powered drones.
Source: Bloomberg
Details: According to Bloomberg, the Ukrainian jet-powered UAVs are among four main options being considered by the German Defence Ministry. In addition to Bars, Germany is discussing a contract worth more than €1 billion to purchase Anthem ground-launched cruise missiles from US company Covenant.
Germany is also considering Ruta missiles from the Dutch company Destinus, which have been used in Ukraine, and the HS1 high-speed missile being developed by German-British defence start-up Hypersonica, the financial news agency's sources said.
"They are also in talks with Ukraine to co-produce and acquire the Bars cruise missile, whose manufacturer has not been made public, people familiar with the negotiations said," Bloomberg reported.
The Bars jet-powered drone has a strike range of up to 1,000 km and can carry a warhead weighing up to 60 kg. The UAV can reach speeds of more than 700 km/h. Bars operates as a modular platform which, depending on its fuel load and warhead weight, can be used for long-range and mid-range strikes as well as strikes near the front line.
The manufacturer of Bars drones is capable of producing around 600 jet-powered drones per month. The company is also working on upgrading the drone to the Bars 2.0 version.
Background: Earlier, Ukrainska Pravda reported that Ukraine and Germany signed an agreement in July 2026 on the joint production of Bars UAVs. During the first stage of the project, Germany will finance drone production, with all the systems produced to be supplied to Ukraine's defence forces.

articles.title: Zelenskyy imposes sanctions on suppliers to Russia’s defense industry
articles.body:
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy has signed decrees enacting decisions by the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine (NSDC) to impose sanctions on Russian entities and individuals. These parties are involved in the production of Russian ballistic missiles or supply equipment and components to Russian defense industry enterprises for use in military aircraft, armored vehicles, missile systems, and drones.
Relevant decrees, Nos. 1058/2024 and 1059/2024, are dated October 24 and have been published on the head of state’s official website.
The first sanction list includes 51 individuals and 44 legal entities involved in the manufacture of ballistic missiles—weapons that the Russian Federation uses to attack critical and civilian infrastructure, as well as to shell Ukrainian cities and communities. These entities produce and supply raw materials, equipment, and tools used to create long-range strike systems, including the Iskander, Kalibr, Kh-101, and Kinzhal.
The sanction package specifically targets Russian enterprises that manufacture weaponry, components, and related software, as well as the executives of these companies.
All individuals subject to these sanctions are citizens of the Russian Federation. Of the 44 entities on the first list, 42 are registered in the Russian Federation, while two are registered in the People's Republic of China.
Additionally, sanctions have been imposed on 32 Russian citizens and 35 Russian companies that are part of the production and supply chains for high-precision industrial equipment, tools, components, electronics, and raw materials intended for entities that serve Russia’s defense-industrial complex.
Sanctions have also been imposed on enterprises belonging to the Russian industrial group Rusal—entities that are significant to the aggressor state and involved in the production of military aircraft, armored vehicles, missile systems, drones, and other military hardware.
"We are systematically identifying enterprises involved in the production of Russian ballistic missiles and other weaponry, and applying sanctions against them. We are also working to extend these sanctions to other jurisdictions. Taken together, these measures should significantly weaken the capacity of the Russian military-industrial complex to manufacture weapons," noted Vladyslav Vlasiuk, Advisor and Presidential Commissioner for Sanction Policy.

articles.title: Ukraine continues to receive intelligence from CIA, despite strained relations between Trump and Zelenskyy – media
articles.body:
The U.S. intelligence community continues to assist Ukraine in defending itself against Russian aggression—notably by providing early warnings of incoming missiles and drones—even as relations between President Donald Trump and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy remain poor, reports The Atlantic.
Citing an unnamed high-ranking officer who frequently visits Ukraine, the publication notes that the CIA plays a leading role among American personnel in the country. The source also remarked that, with the CIA’s help, Ukrainians have become very adept at carrying out strikes against Russia.
Another intelligence official based in the Baltic states, who works closely with the USA to counter Russian influence, told the publication that CIA operations are currently much more aggressive than they were during the administration of former President Joe Biden, though you would never know it from Trump’s rhetoric.
“The administration’s policy is deeply conflicted, and perhaps no one understands that better than John Ratcliffe, the director of the Central Intelligence Agency. He has a foot in two worlds: advising a president who’s continuously at odds with Ukraine’s leadership, and running an agency that’s essential to Ukraine’s war for survival … ,” the article says.
Ukrainians do not view Ratcliffe as their defender. They know that he works for an unpredictable boss and that, should Trump carry out his recent threat to cut off intelligence support unless Ukraine stops attacking Russian oil refineries, Ratcliffe will follow that order, The Atlantic added.
Sources familiar with the matter describe Ratcliffe as someone who clearly understands the threat that the Russian Federation poses not only to Ukraine but also to the United States and its allies. The same can be said of U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, both of whom have now aligned themselves with Trump’s rhetoric.
According to the report, the CIA Director has likely advised Ukrainian President Zelenskyy on how to engage with Trump.
Commenting on disruptions to the Starlink satellite network and American early-warning systems, the publication notes that the USA has not yet officially cut off the flow of intelligence, though Trump could take such measures at any moment. The ezine says that should Trump decide to do so, those who have worked with Ratcliffe say he would not attempt to persuade the president to change his mind even despite concerns within CIA headquarters.

articles.title: Zelensky Says Starlink Speeds Fully Restored, Urges Interceptor Deliveries
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Saturday, Oct. 24, that SpaceX’s Starlink and Starshield satellite networks have had their operational speeds restored to pre-restriction levels, easing constraints that had affected counter-drone operations and front-line military logistics.
In a video address published on Telegram, the president confirmed that system diagnostics conducted by military specialists verified that bandwidth and velocity capabilities have returned to required operational thresholds.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The most important development for today: Starlink and Starshield operations have been restored to the speeds that existed prior to all these restrictions,” Zelensky stated.
“The restoration began overnight, and by this morning the speeds were already sufficient for operational use. This is very important and significant for our front-line logistics and for defending Ukraine against jet-powered Shaheds.”
Zelensky confirmed that Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara delivered an official briefing on Saturday morning verifying that technical testing demonstrated full network functionality.
The president expressed gratitude to American partners, lawmakers, media, the US State Department, and US President Donald Trump for addressing the operational issue.
Appeals for ballistic interceptor deliveries
Addressing broader security cooperation with Western allies, Zelensky emphasized that Kyiv is maintaining active consultations with Washington and European partners to restore regular deliveries of surface-to-air interceptors capable of neutralizing Russian ballistic missiles.
Technocracy Takeover
The president noted that several critical air defense aid packages, backed by existing political approvals from partner nations, remain pending delivery to Ukrainian armed forces.
“We continue communicating with partners so that other levels of our cooperation with America are restored,” Zelensky said.
“It is very important that deliveries of air defense interceptors – interceptors against Russian ballistics – are renewed. There are packages that we are still awaiting. These include packages from America and from European partners – packages for which political decisions have already been adopted.”
The appeal follows Zelensky’s recent disclosures that Ukraine received only 24 Patriot interceptors from the US over the past three months, despite facing coordinated ballistic barrages and maintaining an estimated operational requirement of roughly 350 interceptors per month.
European diplomatic coordination and Oleshky humanitarian access
Zelensky disclosed that Ukrainian delegations are preparing a series of diplomatic consultations in Europe with representatives of the US president and European allies, emphasizing that European capitals must remain directly involved in all stages of prospective peace negotiations.
“Europe must be involved in the diplomatic process,” Zelensky stressed. “Ukraine always involves European partners in diplomatic efforts and counts on their continuation next week.”
The president also revealed that an agreement has been reached to secure humanitarian access to the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in southern Kherson region, where an estimated 1,700 civilians have faced acute isolation, hunger, and severed medical supplies.
Zelensky explained that Russian forces have heavily mined access roads leading to the left-bank enclave, creating critical survival hazards for remaining residents ahead of the winter season.
“There is also an agreement regarding Oleshky. Its implementation should take place soon so that access to Oleshky is unblocked,” Zelensky said.
“In the temporarily occupied part of our Kherson region, the Russians have mined roads, making the situation difficult – extremely difficult. We hope this humanitarian operation will succeed: unblocking Oleshky, providing access to deliver food and medicine, and allowing people to leave this combat zone.”
Zelensky confirmed that the humanitarian framework had been under discussion across multiple institutional levels, emphasizing that Ukraine will fulfill all operational commitments and counts on the effectiveness of American diplomatic mediation to secure the corridor.

articles.title: Iran says won’t allow US warships to get close as Trump ponders new attacks
articles.body:
Iran says won’t allow US warships to get close as Trump ponders new attacks
Iranian officials, media and analysts sense war is closer, but signal there will be no backing down.
Tehran, Iran – Iran’s armed forces say they are prepared to fire on United States warships as President Donald Trump said Washington was still deliberating new attacks or continued pressure on Iran.
Trump told supporters at a rally in Florida on Friday that the US military “may do another Epic Fury”, in reference to the extensive bombing campaign against Iran at the start of the war. He had earlier questioned whether to end the conflict quickly through huge attacks on Iran or let pressure on Tehran from a naval blockade and sanctions persist.
But Ali Abdollahi, chief of general staff of the Iranian armed forces, asserted that the US Navy is incapable of re-entering Iran’s territorial waters or its periphery due to Iran’s ability to target any vessel in the region.
“The US president can only dream of their soldiers and military again entering the Persian Gulf. They will take this wish to the grave for good,” he said in a statement carried by state media on Saturday morning.
Abdollahi also said US rhetoric about the war pointed to a basic contradiction: US claims that Iran’s military capabilities have been mostly destroyed during the war were nullified by its refusal to bring its aircraft carriers and support vessels closer to Iranian territory.
He added that Iranian forces were determined to “drown” the US and Israel in a “quagmire” in retaliation for their surprise attack on Iran on February 28, starting an eight-month war and plunging the whole region into instability.
Strait of Hormuz
Vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz continue to be attacked by Iran. Together with the increased odds of renewed war, this has driven up oil prices and sent Brent crude to its highest price since April, at about $117.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said seven tankers were attacked or hit mines overnight into Thursday. It then claimed on Friday that two supertankers struck mines. The IRGC has said its military doctrine is now more offensive, and Washington has reportedly ordered many diplomatic personnel to leave Saudi Arabia, with others set to depart other countries in the region.
The Iran-allied Houthis in Yemen also continued to exchange attacks with Saudi Arabia, hitting Riyadh again on Saturday, with the international airport in Dammam and the Shaybah oilfield targeted in recent days. Saudi forces have bombed Marib, Taiz and several other Yemeni provinces under Houthi control.
In southern Lebanon, Friday brought further reported Israeli air attacks around Nabatieh and artillery fire near Zawtar ash-Sharqiyah. Iran has linked this front to its war with the US and Israel, in the past demanding that any ceasefire with Washington also cover Lebanon.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, facing an election on October 27 which comes days before the November 3 mid-term elections in the US, also ordered a lockdown of the occupied West Bank after a Palestinian attack killed two soldiers in Hebron. The Houthis have also launched attacks on Israel linked to events in Gaza and the West Bank, highlighting how wider regional peace now depends on events in multiple theatres, including Lebanon, the occupied West Bank and Gaza.
Netanyahu has reiterated his desire to overthrow the Iranian government, leading several state-linked media and analysts in Iran to claim that Tehran has activated a “dead hand” doctrine. That allegedly enables military attacks against US, Israeli and regional interests to continue from across the country’s 31 provinces if senior Iranian figures are again assassinated as at the start of the war.
The IRGC has threatened seabed internet and communication cables if Iran’s civilian infrastructure is again targeted by the US and Israel. US-based Axios on Saturday cited US intelligence claiming that Iranian authorities had “substantially increased” efforts to strike American officials in the Middle East and beyond.
Diplomacy in Istanbul
Mediated negotiations between Iran and the US are no closer to yielding results. But regional and European powers held a coordination meeting in Istanbul on Friday and announced their expectations for the future of the war.
Top diplomats from Turkiye, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt met with the United Kingdom, France, Germany and Italy, with neither the US nor Iran participating.
“We agree that a new attack on Iran would widen the war and spread the conflict across the region,” Turkiye’s Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said after the meeting. “Military intervention in Iran is by no means a solution. No one is endorsing it at this point.”
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said his government held Iran and the Houthis responsible for instability in the Middle East.
But the foreign ministers of the four regional countries issued a joint statement that said “Israeli occupation was the main source of instability in the region and beyond.”
In line with resolving the US-Israel war on Iran, the four regional countries supported the Islamabad memorandum of understanding signed in June and a negotiated settlement, while demanding unrestricted passage through the Strait of Hormuz. The group said they opposed attacks on civilians and commercial vessels, and condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and its Red Sea shipping interests.
The Istanbul meeting once again displayed a “gap between diplomatic claims and realities in the field”, Nour News, an outlet affiliated with Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, argued in an analysis on Saturday.
It said the US and European powers – not Iran – must make concessions first. The outlet presented reopening the Strait of Hormuz as conditional on the US accepting Tehran’s demands and acknowledging responsibility for attacking Iran and Yemen.
Most Iranian newspapers on Saturday focused on signs of war, including rising oil prices.
The headline from hardline Vatan-e Emrooz reported that the price of a barrel of Brent crude rising above $117 was “evidence of disgrace for Trump”. Reformist Etemad said US and Israeli actions were signalling that the “zero hour” of another intense round of the war was approaching.
Reza Nasri, a Tehran-based foreign policy analyst with links to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said that after being subject to decades of attacks, nuclear sabotage, sanctions and violated deals by the US, Iran’s strategy was now “enough is enough.
“Iran has reached its verdict. It will no longer negotiate under bombardment, honour agreements the other side treats as optional, or accept the killing of its children and the penury of its people as routine instruments of policy,” he wrote on X. “It will put an end to this cycle, and it will do so by all necessary means”.

articles.title: Iran-backed militias in Iraq accuse US of violating airspace, as threats grow - analysis
articles.body:
Iran-backed militias in Iraq accused the United States of violating Iraqi airspace. The statement comes amid tensions between the Iraqi government and Iran-backed militias over efforts to bring weapons under state control, according to a report by Rudaw.
"Standing with the forces of righteousness against the forces of evil is a duty dictated by sound human nature," the IRI said, according to Rudaw. The group sees the conflict involving Iran as a struggle against the US and Israel. The IRI has attacked Israel in the past during the conflict in Gaza.
The Islamic Resistance in Iraq, an umbrella group of Iran-backed militias, continues to support Iran. The group issued a statement amid speculation about a possible new war with Iran.
The militias also accused Baghdad of appeasing the US due to Washington’s pressure on Iraq. The IRI is unhappy that Baghdad has been reducing commercial flights and closing border crossings with Iran. The IRI claimed to have documented 171 violations of Iraqi airspace by US fighter jets and reconnaissance aircraft between September 30 and Friday. The allegations were not independently verified.
The accusations come after the US-led anti-ISIS coalition formally ended its military mission in Iraq on September 30. Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has sought to use the transition to bring militia weapons under government control. However, several powerful factions have rejected the initiative. The plan is set to take effect by June 2027. Some militias have agreed, while others have rejected the policy.
Some militias opposed to disarmament, others willing to cooperate
According to Rudaw, Kataib Hezbollah and Harakat al-Nujaba remain opposed to disarmament, while Harakat Ansar Allah al-Awfiya and Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada have expressed willingness to cooperate with government measures.
Zaidi has extended the disarmament deadline to June 30, 2027, by which time "no weapons will remain outside the framework of the state," he said in an interview with Iraqi state media, quoted by Rudaw.
The dispute illustrates a central challenge facing Iraq. Even after the US-led coalition's withdrawal, Iran-backed factions continue to portray their weapons as necessary for confronting Washington and Israel. This puts them increasingly at odds with Baghdad's efforts to assert state authority over armed groups.
The tensions come as the US State Department has warned of increasing regional threats that could affect security in Iraq. On Saturday, the US Embassy in Iraq published an update to the State Department's travel advisory, citing the threat of increased attacks by the Iranian-backed Houthis. The warnings also cite terrorist threats in Iraq, including those posed by Iran-backed militias.
The advisory maintained the existing warning against all travel to Iraq. It noted that Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, including strikes on civilian airports and critical infrastructure, could lead to wider regional escalation.
"The hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area," the State Department warned. It also noted that "the Iraqi government cannot guarantee the safety of US citizens against sudden outbreaks of violence and armed conflict."
The advisory specifically highlighted threats from armed groups inside Iraq. "Terrorists, including ISIS and Iran-aligned militias, encourage and conduct attacks against US persons and interests in Iraq," the State Department said.
State Department warns of threats to US citizens, companies
It also warned that militias threaten American citizens and international companies, citing attacks involving drones, indirect fire, and improvised explosive devices. Potential targets include airports, energy infrastructure, hotels, and diplomatic facilities.
The warning illustrates the broader security challenges facing Baghdad. While the Iraqi government seeks to consolidate control over armed factions, Washington continues to view Iran-aligned militias as a threat. The escalation involving the Houthis also highlights how regional conflicts could further complicate Iraq's efforts to maintain stability and avoid being drawn into new confrontations.
The tensions in Iraq come amid other developments involving Iran and Iranian-backed groups across the region. On Saturday, Rudaw reported that US intelligence had warned of increased Iranian efforts to assassinate American diplomats and officials in the Middle East and elsewhere. Citing an Axios report, Rudaw said a memorandum dated Friday from US National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton to Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned that some alleged Iranian plots had reached advanced stages. The report comes as Washington reduces staffing at several embassies amid concerns about regional escalation.
Meanwhile, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Saturday that it had targeted a gathering center belonging to the Kurdistan Free Life Party (PJAK), an Iranian Kurdish opposition group. The attack took place in Iran but could have implications for Iraq, where Tehran has previously targeted Iranian Kurdish opposition groups. According to Rudaw, clashes between the IRGC and PJAK's armed wing, the Eastern Kurdistan Units (YRK), have intensified over the last week. Iran has used drones and artillery against mountainous areas where the Kurdish fighters operate. Iran's Mehr News Agency described the latest operation as a preemptive strike against PJAK members allegedly preparing attacks.
These developments also come as Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi continues to insist that his government will end the presence of armed factions operating outside state control. In an interview quoted by Rudaw on Friday, Zaidi said that "Iraq will soon, God willing, be a state free of factions, like other countries in the world, and weapons will be exclusively in the hands of the Iraqi security forces."
The developments illustrate the competing pressures facing Iraq. Baghdad wants to consolidate state authority over armed groups, but Iran-backed militias continue to see themselves as part of a wider regional confrontation with the US and Israel. At the same time, Iran's operations against Kurdish opposition groups and reports of threats to American officials suggest that tensions could spread across several fronts.
One example of Baghdad's progress is a new agreement with a Yazidi armed group called YBS in Sinjar in northern Iraq. Baghdad also says it has reached a deal with Turkey for Ankara to leave a base near Bashiqa. However, these may be low-hanging fruit because Iran-backed militias are, in some ways, more powerful. Iran shares a long border with Iraq. It views Iraq as a "near abroad," basically meaning it feels it should control Iraq. It has carried out 1,000 attacks on the Kurdistan Region of Iraq, but also 600 on the rest of Iraq, using militias in some attacks.
For Iraq, the challenge is not only disarming militias. It is also preventing the country from becoming a battleground in a wider regional conflict. The coming months will test whether Zaidi can turn his government's commitments into reality, particularly as the June 2027 deadline approaches.

articles.title: Houthis claim 7 attacks on Saudi targets as heavy airstrikes hit Yemen
articles.body:
SANAA, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- Yemen's Houthi group said Saturday that it had launched seven missile and drone attacks on airports, oil facilities and a military base across Saudi Arabia, as heavy Saudi-led airstrikes hit various Houthi-held areas of Yemen.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said in a statement broadcast by Houthi-run al-Masirah TV that the group had used ballistic missiles and drones in the attacks targeting airports, oil facilities and a military base in the Saudi cities of Riyadh, Yanbu, Rabigh, Dammam, Najran and Khamis Mushait.
Sarea said King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh was targeted in two stages. Other attacks struck targets including Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu and King Fahd International Airport in Dammam.
There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of the claimed strikes.
Sarea said the attacks were launched after what he described as 100 Saudi airstrikes on Houthi-held areas of Yemen over the previous 24 hours. He claimed Saudi Arabia had carried out a total of 3,123 air and missile strikes on Yemen since the latest escalation began.
Meanwhile, al-Masirah TV reported on Saturday casualties from heavy Saudi-led airstrikes across Houthi-held areas. It said four people were killed and several others wounded when a house was hit in the Asr neighborhood of the capital Sanaa, citing a preliminary toll.
In the western province of Hodeidah, five members of one family were killed when an airstrike hit their home in the At Tuhayta district, while another child was wounded, according to al-Masirah.
The broadcaster also reported that eight people were killed and more than 10 others wounded in airstrikes on housing for cement factory workers in Hamdan district of Sanaa province.
Separately, Sarea said in a statement posted on social media platform X that Houthi forces had targeted what he called Saudi-backed "mobilizations" at Al-Nasr camp and a naval military base in the southern port city of Aden, where Yemen's internationally recognized government is based.
The strikes came amid an intensifying confrontation between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces backed by the Saudi-led coalition, with missile, drone and air attacks escalating across several parts of the country in recent days.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of the country's north. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government. ■

articles.title: US senators threaten to block Trump's nominees over Starlink restrictions in Ukraine – NYT
articles.body:
US senators threaten to block Trump's nominees over Starlink restrictions in Ukraine – NYT
US senators have warned the White House they will withhold their votes to confirm nominees until US President Donald Trump's administration secures the restoration of communications systems used by Ukrainian forces, The New York Times reports.
Source: The New York Times, citing sources
Details: According to three people familiar with the discussions, Republicans and Democrats in the Senate have told senior White House officials that they will block confirmation of Trump's nominees awaiting congressional approval until the administration restores critically important satellite communications capabilities used by the Ukrainian military.
The move, disclosed to the NYT by sources speaking on condition of anonymity because it has not yet been officially announced, will intensify bipartisan tensions over the White House's ever-more conciliatory approach towards Russia.
This will take place during the remaining congressional session scheduled for after the midterm elections, when Republicans are expected to try to confirm dozens of Trump's nominees before the current Congress's term ends.
The stance highlights growing divisions between the White House and Congress over Russia, with even senior Republicans showing increasing willingness to challenge Trump's policy positions. It also points to a possible shift after the midterm elections, when control of Congress could pass to the Democrats and lawmakers from both parties may be more resolute in using their leverage and oversight powers on the issue.
Congressman Brian Fitzpatrick, a Republican from Pennsylvania who is fighting to retain his seat in a highly contested district, has threatened to seek the dismissal of US officials responsible for the network disruptions as well as cuts to their departments' budgets. He said he doubts the problems were accidental.
A US Senate staff member told the NYT on condition of anonymity that the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations had approved several shipments of critical air defence interceptors that had still not been delivered to Ukraine, raising concerns about delays in aid already authorised by Congress.
Staff are also considering launching investigations into SpaceX in connection with the satellite disruptions and have asked companies involved in Russian diesel fuel transactions to retain documents in the event of possible congressional investigations, the source added.
Previously: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed on 23 October that speed restrictions for Starlink satellite communications terminals in Ukraine remain in force.
A bipartisan group of nearly 20 members of the US House of Representatives called on President Donald Trump to ask Elon Musk to give Ukraine access to Starlink systems to target missile launchers on Russian territory.
US Democratic Senator Chris Coons had previously contacted Elon Musk's SpaceX, asking the company to explain who had decided to restrict Starlink's operation in Ukraine and why.
Background:
- The Wall Street Journal reported that Elon Musk had ordered Starlink services to be slowed down. It is unclear to what extent Trump was involved in discussions about the slowdown.
- US Republican Senator Thom Tillis is seeking an investigation into the Pentagon's actions with regard to problems with Starlink satellite communications systems encountered by the Ukrainian Armed Forces.
- US House of Representatives member Joe Wilson and nearly two dozen of his colleagues prepared a letter calling for Ukraine to be permitted to use Starlink for strikes on launch sites within Russian territory.
- The Wall Street Journal, citing US and Ukrainian officials familiar with the matter, reported that Trump had called Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on the military version of Starlink in Ukraine.
- On the evening of 22 October, Trump said Musk had already lifted speed restrictions on the military version of Starlink in Ukraine but declined to say whether he had personally called him about the issue.
- Ukraine's Defence Ministry said it was recording disruptions to Starlink and Starshield services on the line of contact.
