articles.title: Ukrainian forces reportedly strike Russian targets 2,500 kilometers from border
articles.body:
Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
Ukraine struck several targets, including a petrochemical plant and a warehouse in Siberia around 2,500 kilometers away from the border on Oct. 24, monitoring channels reported.
A fire first broke out at the Omsky Kauchuk petrochemical plant in the Russian city of Omsk, according to Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova Plus.
The facility is one of Russia's largest petrochemical plants, and the company behind Omsky Kauchuk says the site is a leading producer of synthetic rubber, organic synthesis products, and methyl tert-butyl ether, an additive used to refine gasoline.
The plant is part of Russia's supply chain for rocket fuel, including for the Iskander ballistic missile used in fatal attacks against Ukraine, Exilenova Plus said.
Russian ballistic missiles targeted Kyiv in a fatal attack on the night of Oct. 13-14, killing five people and injuring another 25. At least one person was killed, and 24 were injured in another Russian ballistic missile attack overnight on Oct. 22.
Later, a warehouse belonging to major Russian online retailer Ozon was also hit in the Ukrainian drone attack, Exilenova Plus reported.
Omsk Oblast Governor Vitaliy Khotsenko confirmed that the region was targeted by Ukrainian drones, saying that a logistics hub in the city of Omsk was hit.
"A logistics hub in Omsk was attacked by a drone. Personnel were promptly evacuated. Emergency services are working at the scene," he claimed.
Reports could not be immediately verified by the Kyiv Independent.
Ozon and its competitor Wildberries have been targeted by Ukrainian forces in recent months. The two are a major part of Russia's economy, with their broader ecosystems accounting for about 8.5% of Russia's GDP.
Ukraine has targeted facilities that often serve as storage sites for dual-use goods used in weapons production and other military purposes.
Ukraine regularly strikes military targets deep within Russia and occupied territories in an effort to diminish Moscow's ability to continue waging its war.
Omsk Oblast was also under fire in an attack on Oct. 8. Ukraine's General Staff confirmed that its forces struck the Omsk oil refinery.
"The destruction of such facilities is the exercise by Ukraine of its inalienable right to self-defense in accordance with Article 51 of the UN Charter and is aimed at reducing the military-economic potential of the Russian Federation," Ukraine's General Staff said.
More recently, on Oct. 24, the General Staff said that Ukrainian forces struck the Tolyattikauchuk petrochemical plant in the Russian city of Tolyatti, Samara Oblast, as well as an aircraft at the Yeysk airfield in Krasnodar Krai.
The synthetic rubbers are used to make solid rocket fuel for tactical and ballistic missiles, according to the General Staff.
"Damage to such objects affects the supply chain of raw materials for the Russian missile program," Ukraine's General Staff wrote.

articles.title: Silence about attacks on nuclear facilities is unforgivable
articles.body:
Silence about attacks on nuclear facilities is unforgivable
Jam-e-Jam criticized the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) for its response to attacks on Iranian nuclear facilities. The article argued that military strikes carried out by the United States and Israel against Iran’s nuclear sites in 2025 and 2026 constituted serious violations of international law and the prohibition on aggression.
According to the paper, both the governing bodies and the Secretariat of the IAEA failed to issue even a statement condemning these actions, a situation unprecedented in the agency’s history. The newspaper claimed this failure exposed a major institutional weakness and raised concerns about the consistent application of principles that the agency is supposed to uphold. It argued that the IAEA cannot credibly defend the integrity of safeguards while treating attacks on safeguarded facilities as a secondary concern. Therefore, the agency should clearly reaffirm that attacks on peaceful nuclear facilities are unlawful, unacceptable, and should never be tolerated under any circumstances.
Donya-e-Eqtesad: Decoding an Emirati flight to Tehran
Donya-e-Eqtesad examined the repeated landing of an Emirati aircraft in Tehran. These flights sparked speculation about possible contacts between the UAE and Iran ahead of a potential new phase of regional tensions. The visits occurred at a time of intensified diplomatic activity across the region. The newspaper also noted that Trump’s support for Netanyahu before Israel’s national elections increased concerns about possible new attacks against Iran. Since the UAE aligned itself with the United States and Israel after the outbreak of conflict and was reportedly targeted by Iranian retaliatory actions, the return of a government-linked Emirati aircraft to Tehran attracted attention. Combined with earlier reports regarding possible arrangements related to frozen Iranian assets, the flights fueled speculation about behind-the-scenes communication between the two countries. Nevertheless, the true purpose of the flights remains unclear, leaving open the question of whether they were intended to ease tensions or serve another mission.
Ettelaat: E3’s proposal for mediation amid tensions
Ettelaat discussed the announcement by Germany, France, and the United Kingdom (known as European trio) that they are prepared to act as mediators between Tehran and Washington over the Iran nuclear issue. According to the newspaper, these three countries possess extensive experience in talks concerning Iran’s nuclear program and have long participated in diplomatic efforts aimed at ensuring its peaceful nature. The European initiative remains focused on preventing Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons, a goal that Berlin, Paris, and London continue to regard as essential for reducing regional tensions. European governments are therefore seeking to keep the door open for negotiations while responding to the rapidly evolving security situation in the Middle East. At the same time, Iran’s response to the proposal remains uncertain. Since the European troika has largely been sidelined in recent phases of the nuclear dispute, it remains to be seen whether Iran and the United States will once again bring these countries back into the negotiating process.
Etemad: Washington’s messages not genuine diplomatic initiatives
Etemad interviewed former Iranian parliamentarian Heshmatollah 
 
Falahatpisheh about the likelihood of war versus successful negotiations. While diplomatic efforts to reduce regional tensions continue, assessments of potential Iran-US talks remain cautious. Falahatpisheh argued that Washington’s recent messages are not genuine diplomatic initiatives but rather ultimatums containing strict demands. He believes the United States seeks to restrict significant parts of Iran’s nuclear and military capabilities, and that its proposals appear closer to demands for surrender than a basis for agreement. At the same time, he noted that Iran is trying to highlight the costs and vulnerabilities of any military confrontation, taking into account both US electoral considerations and Iran’s military posture. In his view, this strategy can strengthen deterrence while keeping diplomatic channels open.
Javan: No violations in the Strait of Hormuz
In an article, Javan addressed developments in the Strait of Hormuz. Contrary to misleading narratives from Trump and CENTCOM, field reports indicate that vessels involved in oil smuggling or other violations have reduced or halted their activities. The newspaper suggested that military measures and restrictions may be influencing maritime calculations in this strategic waterway. Meanwhile, rising oil prices, with crude exceeding $117 per barrel, demonstrated that developments in the Strait of Hormuz are not merely military issues but also have immediate consequences for global energy markets and the international economy. In this context, warnings from the IRGC Navy about expanding responses to US actions, alongside statements from the speaker of Parliament regarding the costs of conflict with Iran, reflected two complementary messages: Iran’s ability to affect one of the world’s most important energy corridors and a warning about the broader economic and strategic consequences of escalating tensions.

articles.title: Is Iran planning attacks on Americans; why is the US on alert?
articles.body:
Is Iran planning attacks on Americans; why is the US on alert?
US intelligence memo warns that Iranian plots against US citizens in the Middle East ‘have reached advanced stages’.
United States intelligence agencies have warned that Iran is in “advanced stages” of plans to target US personnel abroad, prompting Washington to place staff on high alert in the Middle East, according to US officials and an official memo cited by Axios and The New York Times (NYT).
The alert comes as the US and Israel signal they may be preparing for a new military campaign against Iran, which Tehran has reportedly threatened to retaliate against, in part by targeting communications cables in the Gulf.
The heightened threat assessment has prompted Washington, already on guard over escalating attacks by Iran-backed Houthis, to trim Washington’s diplomatic presence in the Middle East, the NYT has reported, citing officials.
Here’s what we know about the latest US warning, and how it fits into the broader US-Iran conflict:
What has the US said about Iran’s alleged plans to attack Americans?
A warning about Iranian plans to target US citizens was detailed in a memo sent by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, first reported by US news site Axios.
In the memo, Clayton wrote that US agencies had received intelligence indicating that Iran has “substantially increased efforts to target US personnel” overseas, with lethal plots reaching “advanced stages” in the Middle East and other countries.
The NYT, which also reported on the memo, cited unnamed US officials as saying threats to American officials, including ambassadors, had been assessed in recent weeks, and that Iran had lined up potential targets in Europe.
The officials said some intelligence indicates Iranian operatives are already active within the US.
What evidence has Washington presented, and what remains unverified?
Washington has not publicly commented on the memo, although the NYT cited a US official as confirming its authenticity on behalf of President Donald Trump’s administration.
Another official cited by the NYT played down Iran’s ability to execute attacks inside the US and elsewhere, saying it lacks the capacity to follow through on all its ambitions.
Why have US officials raised the alarm now?
According to officials cited by the NYT, US agencies deem Iranian threats to US citizens in the Middle East to be “at the highest level” since the US-Israel war on Iran began in February.
This assessment is behind the US’s recent moves to withdraw staff posted in the region, the NYT added.
In the background are reported US and Israel plans to initiate a new military campaign against Iran following the US mid-term elections next month. On Friday, Trump said the US “may do another little epic fury”, using the codename for the US-Israel war against Iran that began on February 28.
Which countries has the US withdrawn diplomats from?
On Wednesday, the US Department of State announced it was removing non-essential staff in its embassy in Saudi Arabia, citing escalating attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen against Saudi infrastructure.
Staff levels have also been quietly reduced at other US diplomatic missions in the region, several US media have reported. That includes embassies in the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Jordan and Lebanon, according to CNN.
A US official cited by the NYT said the threat of Houthi attacks and “Iranian terror plots targeting US officials” were driving US staffing decisions.
Has Iran responded?
Iran has not responded to news of the US intelligence memo accusing it of planning attacks on US personnel.
However, Iranian officials have repeatedly threatened and carried out attacks against US bases and those of its allies in the region. The Pentagon has confirmed that 21 US military personnel have been killed in the Middle East since the war on Iran began.
On Wednesday, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) warned that Tehran would follow a new “offensive” strategy if the US renewed attacks.
That means Tehran would no longer limit its military operations to retaliatory strikes, said IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi, adding that the quality, range and power of Iranian missiles had improved.
Tehran also has in-depth plans to target undersea communications cables in the Gulf in the event of new US-Israeli attacks, the Reuters news agency reported, citing two senior Iranian security officials.
Previously, Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei warned that cables, data centres and artificial intelligence facilities across the region could come under attack if war with the US breaks out again.
Has Iran previously been accused of plotting attacks against Americans?
Yes, US authorities have long accused Iran of being behind plots targeting US citizens, including assassination attempts against Trump on US soil.
In March this year, a Pakistani national was convicted by a US court of plotting to assassinate Trump and other US politicians on the orders of Iran’s IRGC.
An Iranian IRGC member was charged in 2022 with trying to assassinate former US National Security Advisor John Bolton. The individual allegedly “attempted to pay individuals in the United States $300,000 to carry out the murder in Washington DC or Maryland”, according to the US Department of Justice.
Last year, the US intelligence community warned that Iran would “continue to directly threaten US persons globally”, specifically targeting officials it believed were involved in the 2020 assassination of IRGC Quds Force commander Qassem Soleimani.
This month, the US abruptly withdrew bombers from an airbase in England, United Kingdom, citing concerns about a potential attack. That followed a security incident at the base, after which the UK arrested several men on suspicion of working with Iranian intelligence.

articles.title: Protector drone flight over Channel was not for Home Office
articles.body:
An RAF Protector RG-1 that flew over the English Channel on 14 October was operating in support of defence aims and not in support of the Home Office, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, had asked for what reason the aircraft was tasked to support the Home Office in the Channel on that date.
Louise Sandher-Jones, the Minister for the Armed Forces, said: “The Ministry of Defence regularly and routinely monitors our waters to protect UK interests, contribute to domestic maritime security, and act as a deterrent against potentially malign activities.
“The deployment the hon. Member refers to was conducted in support of Defence aims, not in support of the Home Office.”
Protector RG-1 is the RAF’s version of the General Atomics MQ-9B SkyGuardian, and the United Kingdom has ordered sixteen of them to replace the MQ-9A Reaper fleet that was retired after two decades of operations over Afghanistan, Iraq and Syria. The aircraft has a wingspan of around twenty four metres, an endurance of more than thirty hours and a maximum altitude above forty thousand feet, and carries Brimstone 3 missiles and Paveway IV bombs alongside its electro-optical and infrared sensors and a maritime search radar.
The aircraft is built to a NATO airworthiness standard and fitted with a detect and avoid system, lightning protection and de-icing, and that certification allows it to fly in unsegregated British airspace alongside civil traffic without a reserved block of sky being set aside for it. The Reaper it replaced could not, and needed segregated airspace or a danger area for every domestic sortie. The fleet is based at RAF Waddington in Lincolnshire with 31 Squadron, and operations are flown from ground control stations on the station.
Surveillance of small boat crossings in the Channel has been contracted out by the Home Office to a commercial operator. The Portuguese company Tekever has operated its AR5 maritime surveillance aircraft over the Channel since 2020 under Home Office contracts, a framework worth up to £1 billion and renewed repeatedly since. The AR5 is a twin-engine fixed-wing aircraft that flies for more than twelve hours and carries maritime and synthetic aperture radars, day and night cameras and receivers for vessel identification and distress beacons.
Paul Webb, managing director of Tekever UK, has said of the work that “drones can identify humans in distress in a much faster way and help rescue teams.” The company has since sold the same system to the Portuguese government and has expanded into supplying uncrewed aircraft to Ukraine.

US taxpayer money laundered back through Ukraine – Musk
Billionaire Elon Musk has accused US politicians of putting Kiev’s interests ahead of their own country’s, alleging that American taxpayer money sent to Ukraine is being laundered back into political campaigns.
Writing on X on Friday, the SpaceX founder suggested that financial interests could explain why some American lawmakers remain staunch supporters of Kiev in its conflict with Russia.
“Some of that US taxpayer money comes back through multiple laundry machines to fund political campaigns in America, which is why you see some politicians caring more about Ukraine than America!” Musk wrote, without identifying the beneficiaries.
And some of that US taxpayer money comes back through multiple laundry machines to fund political campaigns in America, which is why you see some politicians caring more about Ukraine than America!
— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) October 23, 2026
In March, US outlet Just the News cited a declassified intelligence summary describing a plan to divert hundreds of millions of dollars in American aid earmarked for clean-energy projects in Ukraine into then-President Joe Biden’s 2024 reelection campaign.
Trump shared the report on Truth Social, while then-US intelligence chief Tulsi Gabbard reportedly asked officials at the US Agency for International Development (USAID) to investigate whether the alleged scheme had been carried out.
Musk also accused Ukrainian elites of profiting from Western assistance while ordinary Ukrainians bear the human cost.
“The former have grown very rich off the hundreds of billions flowing to Ukraine, while the latter’s children are conscripted to die in trenches,” he wrote.
Kiev’s increasingly coercive mobilization campaign has been marked by numerous documented cases of forced detentions and violent confrontations involving recruitment officers. Corruption investigations have also exposed schemes allowing wealthier Ukrainians to evade military service.
Ukraine has been rocked by major corruption scandals involving figures close to Vladimir Zelensky. One centered on his longtime associate Timur Mindich and an alleged $100 million bribery and money-laundering operation at state nuclear energy company Energoatom. The scandal forced senior officials from office, including former presidential chief of staff Andrey Yermak, while Mindich fled Ukraine.
Ukrainian investigators have also uncovered what they say is fraud to the tune of $5.6 million involving military drones purchased at prices up to 90% above market rates.
Even Kiev’s staunchest European backers have criticized its failure to deliver promised anti-corruption reforms, warning that billions of euros in assistance could be withheld.
Zelensky is seeking at least €70 billion ($81 billion) in additional foreign assistance for 2027, estimating Ukraine’s total conflict-related spending needs for next year at €155 billion.
European Council President Antonio Costa said on Friday that the EU expects to cover roughly two-thirds of the additional funding, or around €46.7 billion, with a decision potentially coming in November. That sum would come on top of the €45 billion already earmarked for Kiev next year.

articles.title: US updates Israel travel warning, cites growing threat from Iran-backed Houthis
articles.body:
The US State Department issued an updated travel advisory notice for Israel on Friday, warning of an increased threat of armed attacks by Iran-backed Houthi terrorists and the potential for a rapid escalation of regional hostilities.
The update did not change Israel's overall travel advisory classification, which remains at Level 3, urging American citizens to reconsider travel due to terrorism and unrest. The existing risk indicators and restrictions on travel to certain areas of the country also remain unchanged.
In its warning on armed conflict, the State Department cited previous Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, including strikes on civilian airports and critical infrastructure that resulted in civilian casualties and major travel disruptions.
The department warned that hostilities involving the Houthis could escalate rapidly beyond the areas immediately affected, potentially posing additional risks to travelers across the region.
The updated warning comes against the backdrop of previous missile threats originating from Yemen, which have required Israel to activate air defense systems and issue civilian alerts.
US maintains restrictions on travel to Israeli border areas
Despite the updated regional threat assessment, Washington has not raised its overall warning level for Israel. The State Department continues to advise Americans to reconsider travel because of terrorism and unrest, while maintaining stricter Level 4 restrictions in several designated areas.
These restrictions cover areas north of the Route 85, Route 90, and Route 87 boundaries in northern Israel; locations within 11.3 kilometers of the Gaza Strip; and areas within 2.4 kilometers of the Israel-Egypt border, except near the Taba crossing, also known as the Menachem Begin crossing.
The State Department said Israeli authorities restrict travel in the designated northern areas because of IDF activity and presence, and instructed Americans not to travel there for any reason.
US government employees working in Israel face the same geographical restrictions. Official travel to these areas requires approval from the US Embassy's security office.
The advisory also reiterated that, as of August 26, family members are permitted to accompany US government employees stationed in Israel. However, Washington warned that additional security measures affecting US personnel could be introduced as conditions evolve.
The State Department emphasized that Israel's security environment remains complex and can change rapidly, warning that violence could occur without advance notice.
Regional tensions could also prompt airlines to cancel flights or reduce services to and from Israel, potentially disrupting travel plans even in areas not subject to the highest-level restrictions.
Americans urged to prepare for missile and drone threats
The advisory urged American citizens planning to visit Israel to remain vigilant, avoid demonstrations and large gatherings, and familiarize themselves with emergency procedures.
Travelers were advised to identify nearby bomb shelters and download the Home Front Command's Red Alert application, or similar services, to receive real-time warnings about incoming rockets, missiles and armed drones.
Israel's Home Front Command emergency warning systems have been used during previous missile attacks, providing residents with alerts intended to help them reach protected areas.
The military has also updated its advance-warning capabilities to give civilians more time to prepare for certain missile threats.
The State Department encouraged American travelers to enroll in its Smart Traveler Enrollment Program, which enables the US Embassy to distribute security updates and contact citizens or their emergency contacts during a crisis.
Americans were also urged to develop independent evacuation plans that do not rely on US government assistance, follow instructions from local security officials, and exercise particular caution near checkpoints and areas with a significant security presence.
The advisory further recommended purchasing comprehensive travel insurance that covers emergency medical treatment, evacuation assistance, and trip cancellations.
The warnings underscore the continued importance of civilian preparedness amid regional missile and drone threats, with Israeli authorities having previously reviewed the timing and operation of emergency alerts during periods of heightened tensions.
Although the October 23 notice highlighted the increased potential for Houthi aggression, it did not announce additional restrictions on travel to Israel or a change in the State Department's assessment of the country's overall travel risk.

articles.title: Starlink in Ukraine Back to Normal After Week of Throttling
articles.body:
Ukraine said on Saturday that the Starlink satellite system and its military version Starshield were now fully functional after over a week of restrictions that disrupted military operations and intensified tensions with the U.S.
Problems with Elon Musk's SpaceX-owned systems came after U.S. President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel while pressing Kyiv to stop striking Russian oil refineries.
Ukrainian officials said the restrictions, which capped operations at speeds of 160 kilometers per hour (kph), hampered the military's ability to intercept Russian attack drones and forced the cancellation of some operations.
"The main thing for today is that Starlink and Starshield have resumed operations at their pre-restriction speeds. The speeds are now at the level we need," President Volodymyr Zelensky said on the Telegram app.
According to Zelensky, the speeds started returning to normal overnight. Ukraine's Defense Ministry said on Saturday the connection remained stable at over 400 kph.
Ukraine does not rely on the systems for long-range drone operations on Russian territory, including attacks on refineries.
But Starlink remains vital for frontline communications, and the deployment of Starshield-enabled medium-range attack drones has helped Ukraine gain the upper hand in several areas of the battlefield this year.
Limitations order
The restrictions sparked outrage in Ukraine, particularly as they coincided with disruptions to allied warnings about incoming Russian missile attacks. Kyiv later said it continued to receive U.S. intelligence.
Neither Musk nor the U.S. government has acknowledged responsibility for restricting Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine. Both have said publicly that any such decision could only have been taken by the other.
Reuters has reported that the order to throttle Starshield came from inside the White House. Previously, U.S. administrations had several times asked SpaceX to turn Starlink on or off in various countries, sources said.
On Friday, contradicting his previous statement that the services had been fully restored, Trump said that if problems persisted, he would "get it straightened out."

articles.title: Kyiv's power ring under attack: why the capital faces a winter of blackouts
articles.body:
Kyiv's power ring under attack: why the capital faces a winter of blackouts
Hopes for a mild winter or inaccuracies in Russian strikes will not help Kyiv get through this winter without problems with its electricity supply. The only question is how long the power cuts will last and whether air defence forces and power engineers will manage to prevent the worst-case scenario.
The Russians are continuing their systematic attacks on Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast, seeking to completely destroy the city's combined heat and power plants and break the so-called power ring in order to plunge the capital entirely into darkness and cold.
The city has already lost a significant proportion of its own power generation capacity, while strikes are destroying substations through which electricity is supplied from other regions. In the event of severe frosts and further hits, a scenario involving 20 hours without electricity no longer seems far-fetched.
What is Kyiv's power ring, what risks does damage to it pose, and what should the capital's residents prepare for?
What is Kyiv's power ring?
This article does not disclose any sensitive information. The configuration of the power system is no secret to Russia, as Ukrenergo, Ukraine's state-owned electricity transmission operator, has warned. What does remain secret are the protection systems, equipment redundancy arrangements and power restoration procedures following attacks.
In the narrow technical sense, Kyiv's power ring is a system of high-voltage power lines and 330-kilovolt (kV) substations that connects the capital to Ukraine's integrated power grid and enables electricity to be transmitted to the city from different directions.
A key element of the capital's power supply is the 750 kV Kyivska substation, through which electricity from the Rivne and Khmelnytskyi nuclear power plants can be delivered to the capital.
Given their strategic importance, these facilities are under constant attack by Russian forces. The aim is to cut Kyiv off from Ukraine's integrated power grid and cause a blackout.
Put simply, the ring is a kind of road network for electricity. Transmission lines carry electricity to the capital, while substations step down its voltage and feed it into distribution networks for consumers.
If one section of this "road" is damaged by attacks, electricity flows can be rerouted through other lines. This helps maintain the power supply after damage occurs.
The ring is a critically important element of Kyiv's energy supply because the city consumes far more electricity than its own sources generate.
How much electricity does Kyiv consume, and why have power cuts begun?
Kyiv is the largest consumer of electricity in Ukraine. According to estimates by energy experts, the city consumes 1-1.2 GW, or 12-15% of the national total. In winter, depending on the temperature, demand can rise to 1.8-2 GW.
In 2025, before the large-scale winter attacks, local generation played a key role in supplying electricity to the city. According to sources at one of the energy companies who spoke to Ekonomichna Pravda, it may have accounted for as much as 1.3 GW. This came primarily from Kyiv CHP-5, CHP-6 and Darnytsia CHP (CHP-4) – combined heat and power plants (CHP plants) that produce both electricity and heat for the city's district heating network.
These plants are now no longer able to generate electricity. Nevertheless, all three CHPs were hit again by the Russians during the large-scale attack on the night of 13-14 October.
The capital is now forced to rely more heavily on electricity supplied from other regions via the power ring. The problem is, however, that its key components have been under constant attack for more than a month. Some of these attacks result in damage to equipment.
To cause significant problems, the Russians do not necessarily have to destroy the entire power ring. It is enough to damage a few critical nodes through which a large share of the electricity flows.
As a result, a situation may arise where there is electricity in the system, but the grids cannot transmit it to the capital in the required volume. If the city lacks its own power generation, the situation becomes even more complicated.
Under such conditions, dispatchers are forced to restrict consumption, including by introducing emergency or scheduled power cuts. This makes it possible to maintain a balance between available capacity and consumption and to prevent a large-scale failure in the power system.
The time needed for repairs depends on the extent of the damage. Some equipment can be repaired quickly. Replacing a large power transformer or other complex equipment may take longer, especially if the necessary equipment is not held in reserve.
Further complications are caused by repeat attacks, air-raid warnings being in effect for long periods, risks to repair crews and government attempts to reduce the proportion of energy company employees eligible for deferral from mobilisation. Following emergency repairs, the situation can deteriorate again, as strikes have been relentless lately and power workers face the risk of further attacks.
What to expect this winter
The main risk for Kyiv is a combination of three factors: low air temperatures, high consumption and Russian strikes that restrict the ability to transmit electricity to the capital. Given this combination, even fully functioning power generation in other regions does not guarantee that Kyiv will receive enough electricity, making various scenarios possible.
In a relatively favourable scenario, energy workers will repair damaged equipment and new strikes will not cause critical losses. In that case, restrictions may be moderate, although avoiding power cuts altogether will be difficult. For consumers, this would mean 8-10 hours without electricity per day.
If the attacks continue and some equipment remains damaged, Kyiv could face longer power cuts during moderately cold spells. Under this scenario, outages could last 12-16 hours per day.
The worst-case scenario involves regular large-scale strikes on key substations and other elements of the power system amid severe frosts. In that case, restrictions could last up to 20 hours per day. However, sources in the energy sector interviewed by Ekonomichna Pravda do not believe in a scenario in which the Russians would manage to destroy everything and "plunge Kyiv into darkness".
The consequences will depend on which facilities are damaged, how quickly they can be repaired and how much electricity can be transmitted to the capital.
A separate challenge is keeping critical infrastructure running, including water supply pumps, heating systems, transport, hospitals and communications.
Read also: No electricity means no water: an interview with the deputy CEO of water utility Kyivvodokanal
The capital needs approximately 200 MW of generating capacity for these purposes, primarily from combined heat and power units and high-capacity generators. According to Ekonomichna Pravda's sources, 150 MW of distributed generation has been brought into operation in Kyiv. By the end of 2026, this is expected to increase to 180-185 MW. Private facilities accounting for another 55-60 MW could become operational before winter, around half of which are already ready.
* * *
It is clear that protecting energy facilities critical to Kyiv from ballistic missiles depends primarily on the effectiveness of air defence. The engineering protection built at most substations can reduce the impact of individual strikes, but it cannot guarantee the survival of critical equipment after a direct hit.
Amid a shortage of missiles for Patriot systems, it is important to have the necessary amount of backup equipment, trained repair crews and clear action protocols for crisis situations.
Experience from previous winters shows that energy workers have learned to work under conditions of large-scale destruction. However, this does not cancel out the physical limitations of the grid and does not guarantee an uninterrupted electricity supply under every attack scenario.
Three things will be decisive for Kyiv this winter: how much electricity can be delivered to the city, how quickly energy workers can repair damaged equipment and whether backup generation can sustain critical facilities.
How long the power cuts last will depend on this. Kyiv can get through the winter without a collapse of its power supply, but it would be naive to expect the capital to avoid prolonged power outages if constant attacks continue.
By Mykola Topalov
Translated by Anna Kybukevych and Solomiia Shvak

articles.title: Pakistan can mediate between Washington and Tehran, but it cannot manufacture trust
articles.body:
When Field Marshal Asim Munir, Pakistan’s army chief, met Iranian leaders in Tehran last Tuesday, he heard a familiar message in a harder form. President Masoud Pezeshkian said Washington must lift sanctions and pressure before talks resume. Security chief Mohsen Rezaei said no enriched material would leave Iran. After Munir left, a Qatari delegation arrived, a reminder that Islamabad no longer carries this file alone.
The real test is not whether Pakistan can soften Tehran’s opening position. It is whether it can help two adversaries negotiate commitments neither believes the other will honour.
The Islamabad Memorandum, signed on 17 June, extended the ceasefire for 60 days and promised to reopen Hormuz and lift the US blockade. It also pledged oil-export waivers. By 8 July it had collapsed after Iranian strikes on commercial vessels and a US response, and Washington reinstated the blockade six days later. The lesson is not merely that signatures are cheap. The text allowed each side to claim a different meaning. Iran read a “best efforts” clause on passage as giving it some authority over the strait, while the two sides disagreed over the strait provisions from the start. No neutral body existed to say who was right.
Pakistan deserves credit for building a channel between enemies. Few governments can speak to Iran, keep close ties with Washington and engage the Gulf capitals. But access is not leverage.
Islamabad cannot lift American sanctions, settle the enrichment dispute or guarantee that armed actors across the region will respect a ceasefire.
Nor is Pakistan an uninvolved broker. It shares a border with Iran, depends on Gulf energy and is a party to the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, under which it has pledged to defend Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks hit Saudi infrastructure. A mediator that has promised to defend one side’s partner cannot claim neutrality. It can claim something narrower and more useful: both sides have reason to keep its channel open.
That is why Pakistan should narrow its ambitions. It should not chase a grand reconciliation. It should help build a process in which limited cooperation does not require either capital to trust the other’s intentions.
The core problem is credible commitment. Tehran sees sanctions, blockades and strikes as proof that American assurances are unreliable. Washington sees enrichment and regional military activity as proof that Iranian promises are. Each wants the other to move first. Reuters has reported Iranian officials saying Tehran is deliberately slowing talks to weaken President Trump before the November midterms. If so, deadlock is a strategy for some, not just a failure.
The strongest objection to mediation is therefore serious: Islamabad cannot change either side’s strategic calculation, and its ties to Washington and Riyadh complicate any claim to impartiality. Iran’s decision-making is also fragmented. Munir’s August visit followed a change in Iran’s military hierarchy, so an understanding with civilian officials could fail elsewhere.
Even so, neutrality is not the only measure of a useful intermediary. What matters is whether messages are conveyed faithfully, whether the channel is trusted and whether steps can be independently checked.
A modest agenda would start at sea. Agreed procedures for reporting attacks on shipping, exchanging operational notices and investigating alleged violations would not need a nuclear settlement. But Iran’s claim to administer the strait is a sovereignty question, not an incident-management one. The June memorandum left the strait’s future administration to Iran in consultation with Oman and other Gulf states. That question must be put on the table, with partners such as Oman, which has facilitated US-Iran channels before, rather than papered over with vague wording.
The second track should pair reciprocal, time-limited steps. The June memorandum already linked the strait to sanctions waivers, so the difference this time must be design: smaller steps, explicit sequencing, reversibility and no side surrendering its main leverage on a promise.
The nuclear file needs different machinery. Iran’s refusal to export its stockpile and Washington’s demand for limits are substantive disagreements, not misunderstandings. The IAEA can verify agreed limits, but it cannot invent the bargain or inspect without a legal basis and access. Reports of a Qatari–Pakistani proposal linking inspections to interest on frozen funds rest on anonymous sources, and an Iranian parliamentary spokesman described Munir’s trip as bilateral only. Still, they point in the right direction: link access to relief.
READ: After Mecca, why Badr? Because this pact builds, not binds
Any new arrangement should specify who verifies compliance, how disputed incidents are judged and what happens after a breach. A joint implementation group with independent technical expertise could set deadlines, document performance and resolve accusations before they trigger retaliation.
Pakistan should also resist competing for credit. Qatar is already a co-mediator, and Oman has long experience with Gulf security channels. The goal is an effective process, not Pakistani ownership of it.
None of this guarantees peace. If either government believes time or escalation favours it, the best verification system will sit unused. Regional actors can also wreck understandings reached in negotiating rooms.
For the world, the stakes are tangible. Threats to Gulf shipping unsettle energy markets and raise costs for households and importers everywhere. For Pakistan, the danger is closer still.
Islamabad has shown it can bring adversaries toward an agreement. The harder, less theatrical task is helping them build one that survives the next crisis. Pakistan can open the door to diplomacy. It cannot supply the trust Washington and Tehran lack. What it can help supply is a system that makes cooperation possible without it.

articles.title: What to know about Melania Trump’s Oleshky ceasefire deal
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
What to know about the Melania Trump-brokered ceasefire in Russian-occupied Oleshky
A small city in southern Ukraine, cut off for months by fighting, is set to get a brief pause in the 4 1/2-year-old war so that aid can get in and residents can get out.
US First Lady Melania Trump brokered the localised ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine around Oleshky, a Russian-occupied city she said is "on the brink of disaster."
Ukrainian, Russian and US negotiators reached the deal Friday. Officials on all sides have confirmed it, but they have not released many details.
Oleshky has been without power, heat or water
Oleshky is located in Ukraine's partially occupied Kherson region. It sits on the Dnipro River, which separates Ukrainian forces from the city's Russian occupiers. Moscow's forces captured it on the first day of the full-scale invasion in February 2022. Its buildings were shelled and burned.
In June 2023, floodwaters swamped the city after the Kakhovka Dam collapsed in an explosion that an Associated Press investigation found was likely caused by the Russian military. Hundreds of residents were killed.
Once home to about 24,000 people, the city has had scarce food and medical supplies for months. There is no electricity, heat or running water. Roads out of town are mined and lined with burned-out cars, and drones buzz overhead. With another harsh winter approaching, those still there face death from hunger or disease.
Ukraine has repeatedly appealed for a local ceasefire to organise evacuations. As the occupying power, Russia is obligated under international law to make sure civilians under its control have what they need to survive.
Ceasefire, aid, then evacuations
The deal sets out three stages: a ceasefire, then humanitarian aid delivery, then the evacuation of civilians who want to leave Oleshky, according to Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's human rights ombudsman and chief negotiator in the talks.
Before any aid moves, Lubinets said, mines will be cleared on the routes into the city.
Russia's human rights ombudswoman, Yana Lantratova, who took part in the negotiations, said they plan to establish what residents need and then deliver food, medicine, hygiene products and other essentials. She said anyone who wants to leave the combat zone will be guaranteed safe passage.
The pause begins Tuesday and will last several days
Lubinets told the AP that the ceasefire will begin Tuesday, two days before the humanitarian mission starts, and will last several days.
Russia's chief of the general staff, Gen. Valery Gerasimov, said Russian forces "will cease fire on the Kherson axis" from 4 AM Tuesday Moscow time, which is late Monday in the United States. He said Russian forces would also carry out "engineering reconnaissance" and ensure the "humanitarian convoy" can move safely into the city.
Ukraine's General Staff said the ceasefire will begin at 3 AM Tuesday Kyiv time, since Ukraine moves its clocks back an hour on Sunday while Russia does not.
Lubinets said the pause would apply across the Kherson region and neighbouring areas essential to the operation.
Key details have not been released 
Lubinets gave no details on how the ceasefire or the aid mission would be monitored or carried out, citing the sensitivity of the negotiations. He declined to say whether Melania Trump would travel to Ukraine.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said people who want to leave Oleshky can do so. He would not say whether they would be taken to Russian- or Ukrainian-held territory. Asked how long the evacuation would last, he said only that it would most likely take several days.
"The operation will be carried out gradually and is extremely challenging to implement," Lubinets said.
The first lady took up the issue at the UN
The first lady began talks on Oleshky after she heard about the situation at one of her events during the UN General Assembly session in September, the White House said. She and a representative then worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to set the terms. She had already been working with officials from both countries on a separate matter.
"When Melania Trump learned about the situation in Oleshky, the negotiation process began under her coordination," Lubinets said. He said the sides spent several weeks discussing ideas and developing "new approaches, mechanisms and tools" to help civilians there survive.
Helping children in conflict zones has become one of her signature issues during her husband's second term. She hosted a UN Security Council meeting on the issue earlier this year.
Last year she wrote to Russian President Vladimir Putin about efforts to reunite families with children she described as "displaced by the war." Her senior adviser, Marc Beckman, says she has helped reunite nearly three dozen children.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has lobbied various world leaders for help reuniting children he says were taken by Russia after the invasion began in 2022. The International Criminal Court in 2023 issued an arrest warrant for Putin for war crimes, accusing him of personal responsibility for the abductions of children from Ukraine.
Tensions between Washington and Kyiv are rising
The development comes as tensions have increased to new highs between the Trump administration and Ukraine's government. Kyiv has faced restrictions on the satellite internet system it relies on to knock down Russian attacks, with President Donald Trump and other top US officials sending mixed messages about who was responsible for throttling the Elon Musk-made Starshield system.
Trump also recently waived new Russia sanctions, agreed with Russia to import diesel fuel, and pushed Zelenskyy to make a deal to end the war. In renewed efforts to revive the peace process, Trump envoy Steve Witkoff travelled to Norway this week for talks with Zelenskyy before meeting Putin in St. Petersburg, Russia.
Zelenskyy did not mention the Oleshky ceasefire during a remote appearance at the Hudson Institute, a Washington think tank, on Friday. He did note that American Patriot missile interceptors were still on hold.
He also stressed the importance of the United States in renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war, including a possible joint meeting with Trump and Putin.

articles.title: Iran Has Prepared Plan to Destroy Submarine Cables in Persian Gulf in Event of New U.S. Strikes
articles.body:
Iran has developed a detailed plan to attack submarine telecommunications cables in the Persian Gulf in the event of renewed military strikes by the U.S. and Israel.
This was reported by Reuters, citing two high-ranking officials from Iranian security agencies who agreed to speak on condition of anonymity
Tehran also plans to hinder repairs to damaged lines in order to prolong communication disruptions as long as possible.
The agency’s sources did not disclose the methods to be used for the operations or the exact locations of the planned targets.
On October 21, the deputy head of the political department of the IRGC stated that seven major internet cables laid along the seabed of the Strait of Hormuz could become potential targets.
According to data from the United Nations International Telecommunication Union, approximately 99% of global internet traffic passes through undersea cables. At the same time, less than 1% of international network bandwidth passes through the Strait of Hormuz, so the global consequences of any damage would be limited.
For Gulf countries, however, simultaneous damage to several lines could cause slower internet connections and disruptions to financial transactions, e-commerce, and cloud services. The extent of the disruptions will depend on operators’ ability to reroute traffic via alternative routes.
Restoring communications amid hostilities may also be complicated by limited access for repair vessels to territorial waters, rising insurance costs, and the need to obtain special permits. This creates the risk of prolonged disruptions even after the attacks cease.
In addition to cable networks, Tehran is considering strikes against U.S. digital infrastructure in the region. Data centers and facilities related to artificial intelligence have previously been cited as potential targets.
Similar attacks have already occurred. In March 2026, Iranian strikes damaged two Amazon Web Services facilities in the UAE, as well as infrastructure near the company’s data center in Bahrain. At that time, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps named American technology companies—Microsoft, Google, Apple, and Nvidia—among potential targets.
Iran expects that concerns over multibillion-dollar investments in the region’s technology infrastructure will prompt them to oppose a resumption of hostilities.
Earlier, Militarnyi reported that Iran is strengthening the protection of its nuclear facilities, rebuilding its military capabilities, and preparing the population for a possible escalation with the U.S. In particular, Mohsen Rezaei estimated the value of technology infrastructure linked to American companies in the Middle East at over $2 trillion and warned of the possibility of its destruction in the event of a new war.

The Atlantic: CIA director would not dissuade Trump if he decided to cut off intelligence to Ukraine
The US has not officially suspended intelligence sharing with Ukraine, but CIA Director John Ratcliffe would not try to talk President Donald Trump out of it if he decided to do so.
Source: The Atlantic; European Pravda
Details: Last week, Ukraine got a glimpse of what it could be like to have less intelligence support from the US. Reports emerged about disruptions to the Starlink satellite network and US early-warning systems, which blinded Ukraine to some incoming Russian missiles and limited its ability to intercept them, people familiar with the matter told The Atlantic.
A Ukrainian intelligence official pointed the finger at the Americans, but technical failures may also have played a part in Ukraine's inability to intercept some of the incoming missiles.
Officially, the Americans have not yet turned off the flow of intelligence, although Trump could act at any time. If Trump were to do so, people who have worked with Ratcliffe said that he would not try to convince the president to change his mind, despite misgivings at CIA headquarters.
The Atlantic notes that while relations between the leaders of Ukraine and the US may have reached a personal nadir, the US intelligence community has not ceased its fight to defend Ukraine against Russian aggression.
Armed with information provided by the US, the Ukrainian military is launching strikes deep inside Russia. Meanwhile, US spy satellites provide early warning about incoming missiles and drones.
Among US personnel on the ground, "the CIA is in the lead", a retired senior officer who travels frequently to Ukraine said. The Atlantic notes that the Ukrainians, with the CIA's help, have become too adept at striking Russia for Trump's liking.
An intelligence officer in the Baltics, who works closely with the Americans to counter Russian influence, revealed that although you would never know it from Trump's rhetoric, CIA operations are now "much more aggressive" than they were during the Biden administration.
"The Ukrainians don't see Ratcliffe as their advocate. They know he works for a mercurial boss, and that if Trump were to follow through on his recent threat to halt intelligence support unless Ukraine stops attacking Russian oil refineries, Ratcliffe would carry out the order," The Atlantic noted.
However, the CIA helped create the modern Ukrainian intelligence apparatus after Russia annexed Crimea in 2014. Partly owing to this long history, officials in Kyiv stated that they trust Ratcliffe to tell Trump the truth about the war, and not simply what the president wants to hear.
More than a dozen current and former intelligence officials The Atlantic spoke with in the US and Europe described Ratcliffe, who served as the director of national intelligence in Trump's first term, as a person who is clear-eyed about the threat Russia poses not just to Ukraine, but to the US and its allies.
Background:
- The Washington Post reported that the US had threatened Ukraine with a halt to intelligence sharing if the Ukrainian military launched further strikes on Russian energy facilities.
- President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed in an interview with NPR on 14 October that the Ukrainian military had received warnings and threats regarding intelligence sharing, but they have not yet been acted upon.

A drone attack struck the Tolyattikauchuk petrochemical plant in Russia’s Samara region overnight on October 24, triggering a large fire at a facility producing synthetic rubber, gasoline additives, and chemicals with applications in solid rocket propellants.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the monitoring channel Exilenova+ on October 24, the attack targeted the industrial complex in the city of Tolyatti. Local residents reported a significant fire around 6:30 a.m., while drones were reportedly still flying over the city.
Footage circulated on social media showed thick black smoke rising from the industrial area. Russian authorities issued a drone threat warning across the Samara region, while a local airport temporarily suspended operations.
Local reports also indicated that workers at the nearby AvtoVAZ automotive plant were evacuated following the attack. The extent of damage to Tolyattikauchuk and any casualties have not been independently confirmed.
According to the OSINT-Varta database, Tolyattikauchuk is one of Russia’s largest petrochemical facilities, with an estimated annual synthetic rubber production capacity of approximately 260,000 metric tons.
The plant manufactures butadiene, isoprene, hydrocarbon products, and methyl tert-butyl ether (MTBE), a chemical additive used to increase the octane rating of gasoline.
Several of these products have military applications. Butyl rubber is used in tires for military vehicles, while synthetic rubber compounds can serve as polymer components in composite solid rocket propellants.
These materials connect the facility to supply chains supporting Russia’s defense industry, although the proportion of its production used for military purposes remains unclear.
The facility was previously targeted on April 4, when long-range drones struck both the Tolyattikauchuk and KuibyshevAzot chemical plants in Russia’s Samara region. The attack triggered explosions and a major fire.

articles.title: How Ukrainians in US advocate for Ukraine’s interests
articles.body:
How Ukrainians in US advocate for Ukraine's interests
For decades, the Ukrainian community in the U.S. has been working to ensure that relations between Ukraine and the U.S. remain strong and that Ukraine has reliable partners in Washington.
The Ukrainian Congress Committee of America (UCCA), a nonpartisan organization of Ukrainian Americans, has represented the community's interests since 1940. Our position does not depend on which party is in power; our mission is to defend Ukraine's interests. In our work and communications, we consistently explain to the American public that supporting Ukrainian sovereignty is important for America itself.
One focus of our advocacy is increasing economic pressure on Russia. As part of this effort, we have supported legislative initiatives by Senators Lindsey Graham and Richard Blumenthal to strengthen sanctions against the Kremlin.
The latest decisions by U.S. President Donald Trump's administration – in particular, regarding the return of Russian diesel fuel to the global market and the easing of sanctions against Russia – contradict our position on the need to increase economic pressure on the Kremlin, as they provide Russia with additional resources to continue the war.
While the U.S. Administration might couch the rationale for the diesel deal to 'lower fuel prices' for American consumers, the easing of sanctions should be evaluated in light of their consequences. A decision that claims to offer only minor benefits for U.S. citizens but simultaneously increases Russia's revenues – which it uses to finance the war – runs counter to the long-term security interests of the U.S., and most importantly to worldwide democratic values and principles.
Similarly, we disagree with the U.S. government's criticism of Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure as an argument in favor of making concessions to the Kremlin. Ukraine is defending itself against a state that launched a full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, and still shows no willingness to end its aggression. Unilateral concessions by partners do not, in and of themselves, guarantee peace.
Moreover, the experience of recent years shows that Vladimir Putin is not seeking a compromise for the sake of a just peace, but rather the opportunity to continue the war on terms favorable to himself. Therefore, in its communications with the American audience, the UCCA strives to clearly explain Russia's true intentions and outline the real mechanisms for deterring the aggressor.
At the same time, we see that concerns about such decisions are shared not only by Democrats but also by Republicans in Congress. This is important because support for Ukraine must not become a pawn in intra-party struggles.
Not just protests
When talking about the influence of the Ukrainian community in the U.S., it is important to understand the unique characteristics of the American political system. American democracy has its own mechanisms for influencing the government, and mass street protests are just one of them. They can draw attention to an issue, but they do not guarantee a change in political course.
Large-scale demonstrations on various domestic and foreign policy issues take place regularly in the U.S.. However, our experience shows that if we want to achieve concrete results for Ukraine, we must work simultaneously on many levels – in Congress, in the media, with civil society organizations, business representatives, and various ethnic communities.
The UCCA's activities are not limited to public events; we also maintain regular contact with members of the House of Representatives and the Senate, convey our position to political circles in both parties, collaborate with journalists, and strive to ensure that Ukrainian issues remain on the American public agenda.
We have developed partnerships with other communities, including Polish, Baltic, Georgian, Jewish, and Cuban. For example, in 1994, the UCCA was instrumental in founding the Central and East European Coalition (CEEC), which unites the concerns of over 20 million Americans citizens of Central and East European descent. Many of them have their own historical reasons to take a close interest in Russian aggression, authoritarianism, and international security issues. Working together helps us better explain to the American public why supporting Ukraine is in the interests not only of Ukrainians, but also of the U.S. and its allies.
We also work with business leaders. When influential businesspeople publicly support decisions that could weaken Ukraine's ability to defend itself, it is important for Americans to understand the consequences of such decisions, especially in bringing attention to the American businesses that have been targeted by Russian attacks in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022. We view public communication and peaceful protests near commercial facilities as one way to draw attention to the responsibility businesses have for their influence on societal processes.
Our task is not simply to express disagreement, but to convey our arguments to as broad an audience as possible and to translate public support for Ukraine into concrete policy decisions.
We see a basis for this work. According to the sociological studies on which we rely, the majority of Americans supports aid to Ukraine and views Russia as an existential threat to American interests. At the same time, this support cannot be taken for granted – it must be constantly reinforced by explaining to Americans what is at stake.
Strength lies in unity
The Ukrainian community in the U.S. is not homogeneous; among Ukrainian Americans, there are supporters of both Democrats and Republicans, representatives of different generations of immigrants, and people with diverse experiences and views on US domestic policy.
From the very beginning, the UCCA has been an organization that unites the community around shared national interests, rather than party affiliation. We have contacts with people who have worked in both Republican and Democratic administrations, and we collaborate with representatives of both parties. This allows us to convey the Ukrainian position to various political circles, regardless of who is in the White House or leading Congress.
The diversity of our community is not a weakness but a strength. It enables us to speak to different audiences in the language of their values and interests. For some, the main argument is the defense of democracy; for others, it is national security; and for still others, it is the need to prevent aggressive authoritarian regimes from changing international borders by force.
Ukrainians who arrived in the U.S. after the start of the full-scale invasion deserve special attention. The issue of their future and immigration status remains critical, and we are working with our partners in Congress and other government officials to advocate for their interests.
At the same time, their contribution to supporting Ukraine is already extremely significant. The Ukrainian community in America is raising funds, organizing humanitarian aid shipments, and assisting hospitals and the civilian population. Since the start of the full-scale war, tens and hundreds of millions of dollars in aid have been sent to Ukraine through various community initiatives and charitable projects.
Not everyone can attend a demonstration or speak out publicly against a particular political decision. But helping Ukraine takes many forms, and each one is important. Our goal is to create opportunities for everyone who wants to get involved, regardless of their background, political beliefs, or life circumstances.
One area of our work is direct humanitarian support for Ukraine. I recently joined the Ukraine Focus mission to deliver ambulances that were collected in Europe and transported to Ukraine. This time, there were about fifty vehicles intended for the needs of Ukraine's territorial defense forces and other units requiring medical transport.
Another important area is political advocacy. As early as 2000, the UCCA launched Ukrainian Days in Washington so that representatives of Ukrainian communities from across the country could meet with their congressmen and senators, representatives of research centers, diplomats, and other influential figures. Following Russia's aggression in 2014, we stepped up this work.
We also collaborate with other initiatives to strengthen U.S. support for Ukraine. Overall, our guiding principle is that the voice of the Ukrainian community must be heard consistently, not just when another crisis arises.
Ukraine's security is America's security
For decades, American leadership and cooperation with European allies have been key factors in the stability of the democratic world. If the U.S. distances itself from its partners in Europe or gives the impression that aggression can be rewarded with concessions, the consequences will be felt not only by Ukrainians. This will affect allies' confidence in American commitments, the ability to deter future conflicts, and the international system, in which the sovereignty of states should not depend on the strength of their neighbors.
We work earnestly to ensure that cooperation between the White House and Congress will pave the way for a more consistent policy toward Ukraine. It is important that our security issues not be turned into a tool for domestic political struggles, and that support for Ukraine remain a shared strategic interest of the U.S.
I often recall the words of American pastor Mark Burns, who, after visiting Ukraine and seeing things with his own eyes, said: "Ukraine is America First". These words are particularly telling in the context of the "America First" slogan frequently used by President Trump. Their meaning is that defending Ukraine does not conflict with American interests. On the contrary, Ukraine is part of the democratic world, and the outcome of this war will affect security, stability, and the future far beyond its borders.
That is why we will continue to explain to Americans that aid to Ukraine is not just a matter of solidarity, but an investment in international security and the protection of the principles of American democracy.
To the people in Ukraine, I want to say that we are constantly working for victory for Ukraine. Ukraine remains in our thoughts, in our humanitarian work, in our meetings with politicians, and in every effort to convince the American public that our struggle matters to the entire democratic world.
Having been to Ukraine several times since Russia's full-scale invasion, I, and my organisation, understand how difficult it is to live under constant rocket and drone attacks and how much depends on the support of our partners, so we will continue to work – in the humanitarian sphere, in political advocacy, and in building partnerships that help Ukraine endure.
I would like to thank Ukrainian Americans for their tireless work. Regardless of when they or their families arrived in the U.S., what political views they hold, or how they choose to help, their contribution is of great importance.
We must remain united around a common goal. We don't have to agree on every issue of the American domestic policy to understand that a free, democratic, and sovereign Ukraine is in the interests of both Ukraine and the U.S.
Our task is to continue our work, expand our circle of partners, find new ways to convey our position, and turn support into concrete actions. I am convinced that a strong, democratic, and sovereign Ukraine will remain an important strategic partner of the United States for infinity. And that is precisely what we are working toward.
Michael Sawkiw, President of the Ukrainian Congress Committee of America (UCCA) and Director of its Washington, DC bureau – the Ukrainian National Information Service (UNIS), Chair of the Ukrainian World Congress (UWC) Foreign Policy Council, and recipient of the Order of Merit II degree.

articles.title: Russian attacks on three Ukrainian oblasts kill two people and injure 27
articles.body:
Russian attacks on three Ukrainian oblasts kill two people and injure 27
Two people have been killed and another 27 injured in Russian attacks on Donetsk, Kherson and Kharkiv oblasts on 23 October.
Source: Donetsk Oblast Military Administration; Kherson Oblast Military Administration; Kharkiv Oblast Military Administration
Details: Russian forces killed two people in Donetsk Oblast: one in Kramatorsk and one in Sloviansk. Another 18 people were injured: 14 in Kramatorsk and four in Sloviansk.
Six people were injured in Russian attacks on Kherson Oblast. Russian forces targeted critical and social infrastructure facilities as well as residential areas across the oblast. A high-rise residential building, a house and cars were damaged.
Three people were injured in Kharkiv Oblast: a 12-year-old girl in Kharkiv and two men in Cherkaski Tyshky.
Another four people were suffering from shock: three in Kharkiv, including a 13-year-old boy, and a woman in Blyzniuky.
Medics also treated a nine-year-old girl who had been injured in Izium on 22 October.
According to the Oblast Military Administration, Russian forces attacked Kharkiv and 15 other settlements in the oblast over the past day, using missiles, guided aerial bombs and drones, among other weapons.
Background: Russian forces attacked Ukraine with 126 Shahed and Gerbera attack drones, S-8000 Banderol/Dan-T drone- and air-launched cruise missiles and decoy UAVs on the night of 23-24 October. Strikes were recorded at 14 locations.
