articles.title: China’s Liaoning carrier: 10 years from training ship to warship
articles.body:
- China’s Liaoning carrier group completed its second Western Pacific training deployment of 2026, ten years after the carrier’s first such voyage.
- Japan’s Joint Staff observed fighter takeoffs and landings about 250 km south of Ishigaki-jima on Oct. 13, and Japanese fighters scrambled in response.
China’s Liaoning carrier group has carried out its second far-seas training deployment to the Western Pacific this year, a decade after the carrier’s first such voyage in 2016, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported on Oct. 24, describing the ship’s path over those 10 years as a three-step climb from training ship to combat ship to the command core of a carrier group.
Japanese forces first spotted the carrier on Oct. 13 with Renhai-class destroyers 103 and 104 and Luyang III-class destroyer 123. The group sailed southeast between Okinawa and Miyako-jima into the Pacific on Oct. 14, and the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force observed carrier-based fighters taking off and landing in waters about 250 km (155 miles) south of Ishigaki-jima, Japan’s Joint Staff said. Japan Air Self-Defense Force fighters scrambled in response. On Oct. 15, the four ships were confirmed sailing toward the South China Sea.
China’s Ministry of National Defense confirmed that a naval task group led by the Liaoning was training in the Western Pacific, Stars and Stripes reported. The carrier’s flight operations came days before Keen Sword, a U.S.-Japan exercise running from Oct. 19 to 29.
CCTV said the Liaoning’s Western Pacific deployments are routine training organized under the navy’s annual plan and are not aimed at any specific country or target. Military commentator Du Wenlong told the broadcaster that the training complies with international law.
“If we do not train, our level cannot improve and our readiness cannot be maintained,” said Du Wenlong.
Du traced the change in how Chinese state media describe the navy’s carrier drills. In October 2024, the Liaoning and the Shandong held China’s first dual-carrier exercise in the South China Sea, which was described as a joint drill. When the two carriers operated together again in June 2025, the wording shifted to “real combat confrontation,” with each side looking for the other’s weaknesses and building strike plans without a script.
“In future naval battles, no one will tell you what they will do next,” said Du Wenlong.
The Liaoning began life as the Soviet Kuznetsov-class carrier Varyag, laid down in 1984 at a shipyard in what is now Ukraine. China rebuilt the unfinished hull, and Du said the work taught Chinese engineers the basic principles of carrier design. After further upgrades, he said, the ship moved from simply being able to go to sea to being able to fight, with improved command and weapons systems and a major step up in its carrier aviation. With new information and command systems installed, the Liaoning now serves as the flagship at the center of its carrier group.
“Over ten years, the Liaoning has completed its ‘three steps,’ and in just ten years our overall capability has made a huge leap,” said Du Wenlong.
The October voyage follows a 40-day deployment from May to June, when the Liaoning group, including cruiser Wuxi (104), destroyer Kaifeng (124), frigate Luohe (545) and supply ship Hulunhu (901), trained in the South China Sea and the Western Pacific. Japan’s Joint Staff counted about 170 aircraft takeoffs and landings over three days in late May, and the group held joint drills with an amphibious assault ship group before returning to Qingdao on June 22.
China now operates three aircraft carriers: the Liaoning, the Shandong and the Fujian, which was commissioned in November 2025.

articles.title: The great divorce: Why Russia must turn away from Europe
articles.body:
The great divorce: Why Russia must turn away from Europe
In Russia, many people, driven by lingering Europhilia and habits formed during the second half of the 20th century, when Western Europe enjoyed a period of relative peace following its defeat, continue to look for signs of its ‘recovery’ and ways to restore relations.
There are forces within Russia that would advocate overcoming the current hostility and there are decent people in Western Europe, too, even if they are increasingly marginalized. But the causes of this outbreak of desperate Russophobia run deep and cannot easily be remedied and overcoming them may require the complete defeat and dismantling of much of the current European elite. But achieving that goal could come at too high a cost.
I shall attempt to analyze the causes of the almost unprecedented hostility towards Russia among the elites of most European countries and offer recommendations for Russian policy towards Western Europe.
I have written more than once that Peter the Great’s journey towards the rest of Europe, which initially brought many benefits, including helping to create some of the world’s greatest literature and music and modernizing the armed forces, continued for a century and a half longer than was necessary or beneficial.
For many centuries, Europe was the principal source of evil in the world, offering endless wars, including two world wars within a single generation, repeated genocides, colonialism, racism and other calamities.
For Russians who grew up in the shadow of Peter the Great and Catherine the Great, and who internalized a love of Europe, it’s not easy to acknowledge this simple truth and act accordingly.
Russian Europhilia was greatly reinforced when Western Europe, having been overwhelmed by the torrent of evil it had unleashed, became relatively peaceful for a time during the second half of the 20th century. In the USSR, Europhilia was fueled by the everyday hardships of Soviet socialism, contrasted with the far greater material prosperity of the western part of the half-continent.
There are many reasons for the current anti-Russian hysteria. The main one is the all-encompassing, multi-layered crisis that has gripped the western part of Europe and this crisis is particularly painful after decades of relative prosperity and, above all, the euphoria of victory that swept the West following the collapse of the USSR.
That euphoria temporarily obscured the mounting signs of crisis in European economies and societies, which had already become apparent by the end of the 1960s, when a mood of protest was beginning to take hold. And then a miracle happened as the collapse of the Soviet Union and the Eastern Bloc provided hundreds of millions of eager new consumers and millions of cheap workers.
From the 2000s onwards, these problems resurfaced with renewed force. A decade later, most Western European countries had fallen into stagnation as inequality began to worsen once again. Living standards for much of the population began to decline, while competitors started pulling ahead, not only the US and China, but also many countries of the Global South.
Euphoria gave way to a sense of failure and European elites are now trying to drown out that feeling by fueling hostility towards Russia.
At the same time, from the end of the 20th century, the consequences of the anti-colonial revolutions of the 1950s and 1960s began to make themselves felt. The flow of resources that Europe had extracted from the rest of the world since the 16th century, and upon which its prosperity and cultural, military, scientific and technological leadership had largely been built, began to dry up.
An unusually long period of relative peace and prosperity brought to the surface some of the worst traits of the European character and heritage as Western Europe began to turn its back on humanism and the desire to serve the common good.
Decades of development in a climate of peace and formal democracy have led to the degradation of the ruling elites because democratic political systems are anti-meritocratic. The majority elect those who resemble themselves, or even those who are worse, and in the best cases, they elect shrewd manipulators.
One of the most significant causes of Western Europe’s current decline, and to a lesser extent, that of other parts of the collective West, is the rejection of faith.
This began with the Age of Enlightenment, which created the conditions for the decline of people who, consciously or unconsciously, set about rejecting the divine, the best within themselves.
I finally realized that Western Europe had taken a sharp and irreversible downward turn in the early 2000s, when following lengthy debates over the European Union’s proposed constitution, it was decided not to mention Christianity as its spiritual foundation.
Losing its footing and falling behind in economic and spiritual competition, Western Europe is reverting to one of the worst traits of its civilization, which is militarism.
The militarization of the economy is seen as one of the principal ways out of economic decline and militarization requires an enemy. As so often before, that enemy has been identified as Russia as the image of the enemy is being inflated practically out of thin air.
We must tell ourselves firmly, we are not Europeans, but an independent northern Eurasian civilization whose external spiritual roots lie in the south and east.
Our traditional religions came to us from the south, from Byzantium, Palestine, and the Arab and Buddhist worlds. Our political culture stems from the east, from two and a half centuries of interaction and conflict with the Great Mongol Empire, of which the territory of modern-day China was historically a part.
The Mongols plundered, but they didn’t suppress religion, language or culture and we would never have become Great Russia, the world’s largest and one of its most culturally, nationally and religiously open countries, united through a rigid vertical hierarchy of power centered on the Russian people and the Russian language, had it not been for the Mongol political and ideological legacy.
From Western Europe, which, relying on its military superiority, took the lead in education during the 17th and 18th centuries, we sought to adopt the European Bologna system.
Yet that system is increasingly anti-meritocratic as it churns out poorly educated people on a mass scale, many of whom are now coming to power. Let me remind you that some of the earliest institutions of higher learning were established in North Africa and Byzantium.
Some of our more affluent fellow citizens still send their children to study in Europe, ‘abroad’, where as I have seen time and again, they often lose more skills and talents than they acquire.
Our military doctrine contains a clear directive and in circumstances of extreme necessity, provides for the possibility of nuclear strikes against key European countries that are fueling anti-Russian hysteria while simultaneously supporting the war in Ukraine.
Our restraint and peacefulness over recent decades have proved counterproductive. They have contributed to the resurgence of the worst aspects of European political culture so Western Europe must therefore face firm deterrence.
But at the same time, we must remember that we are a country of Pushkin, Tchaikovsky, Dostoevsky, and Tvardovsky, as well as Goethe, Dante, Shakespeare, Mozart and countless others.
Culturally, we must not cut ourselves off from Europe. Rather, we must develop and nurture our Asian roots, of which we have foolishly been ashamed.
The main direction of our internal spiritual, economic and political development must be a shift towards Siberia as there, in the east and north, lies Russia’s future.
We must finally acknowledge that we are not an Eastern European civilization, but a northern Eurasian one, among the most open to the world.
We must also recognize, however difficult it may be, that ‘European-ness’, in the present circumstances, is increasingly becoming a sign of intellectual narrow-mindedness and moral duplicity.
And given the current orientation of European elites, it is simply harmful to us, the representatives of the great multinational, multi-confessional and multicultural Russian people.
Our country-civilization must at last become, for all of us, Russian Yakuts, Russian Buryats, Russian Ossetians, Russian Tatars, Russian Belarusians, Russian Great Russians and others, an independent northern Eurasian civilization.
Europe, in its present and foreseeable future condition, must end at our borders.
This however, is not a call for a new Iron Curtain, but for a rational, modern policy directed towards the future.
This article was first published by Russia in Global Affairs, translated and edited by RT.

articles.title: Houthi missiles target Aden airport, coastguard
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Houthi missiles target Aden airport, coastguard
Rocket attacks launched by Yemen's Houthi rebels targeted several locations in the city of Aden on Saturday afternoon, including the vicinity of Aden International Airport and two coastguard facilities, according to official statements and local sources.
Government media outlets reported that the group had launched three ballistic missiles, two of which struck the airport, while the third landed in al-Tawahi near the port. However, the General Directorate of Moral Guidance and Public Relations at the Interior Ministry said that the first two missiles targeted the coastguard headquarters at the ministry’s premises, while the third struck the coastguard building in al-Tawahi.
Sources told The New Arab that the attacks had once again affected the vicinity of the airport, coinciding with explosions heard in al-Tawahi, the main stronghold of the separatist Southern Transitional Council (STC).
No confirmed information was available regarding the extent of the damage or any casualties. Yemen’s government-affiliated Interior Ministry said that the relevant authorities were gathering information and evidence to assess the damage.
The ministry added that the latest attacks were part of a series of strikes targeting civilian and critical infrastructure in Aden, including Aden International Airport, which, according to its statement, has been attacked multiple times with ballistic missiles and drones.
The city has experienced further attacks during October, targeting the airport and its surrounding area, as well as other locations, including the vicinity of the presidential Maashiq Palace on 7 and 16 October. The area around Maashiq was also attacked on 15 October.
These attacks have raised concerns about the safety of civilian infrastructure and air traffic, as Aden Airport serves as a major air gateway for areas under the control of Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
For their part, the Houthis claimed to have targeted what they described as “Saudi military build-ups at al-Nasr Camp and the naval military base in Aden".
The group’s military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said that “Saudi officers are overseeing the preparation of these sites”, accusing Riyadh of preparing military operations against the Houthis. He provided no independent evidence to support the allegations.
Saree urged Yemenis not to join these military build-ups.

articles.title: Trump’s Iran pause is for November
articles.body:
President Trump’s pre-midterm pause on strikes against Iran landed as a claim of diplomatic momentum, not a concession of failure. The pause was framed as proof that negotiations are working. Look closer, and a different mechanism appears. The war meant to project strength has become an electoral liability, and the president’s response is to bury its most visible costs until voters have finished deciding. Then the option can reopen.
The White House insists Washington is negotiating from strength. Military options remain on the table. The blockade stays in force. The administration has not ended the war, only hidden its sharpest edges from the campaign season. That sequence matters. It allows Republican candidates to campaign without the immediate risk of new strikes or another energy-price spike, while preserving the argument that renewed action may be warranted later. Nothing has been settled. Everything has been postponed.
Trump’s political identity rested on rejecting costly, open-ended foreign interventions. His appeal to swaths of the MAGA movement included the claim that American leaders had squandered resources and neglected domestic problems chasing overseas conflicts. “America First” was a promise about priorities as much as power.
The Iran war has strained that promise to its breaking point.
Back in February 2026, it looked like a pressure campaign: force Tehran to accept Washington’s terms. Months later, it’s a drawn-out confrontation with no clear settlement. Rising fuel prices, stubborn inflation, and the uncertainty over how long the war will last have turned it into a domestic political problem.
Consumer sentiment has fallen close to a record low, dragged down by rising living costs linked to the conflict.
This creates a tension the Republican coalition cannot easily absorb. Some supporters prioritize nationalist strength and a confrontational stance toward Iran. Others were drawn by pledges to avoid costly wars and focus on economic grievances at home. An extended conflict makes satisfying both impossible. Pausing attacks before the midterms offers a way to postpone the reckoning.
The question is whether this pause is a genuine step toward peace or simply an attempt to protect Republicans from the political costs of an unpopular war. The attacks may have stopped, but the naval blockade remains in place, economic pressure on Iran continues, and neither side appears any closer to a lasting agreement. Trump has ruled out further strikes before 3rd November. What he has not ruled out is a return to military action once the election is over. This sequence allows the administration to present the pause as controlled progress, lets Republican candidates campaign without the immediate risk of new strikes or energy-price spikes, and preserves the option of arguing later that renewed action may be warranted.
The reports tell a different story than the public messaging. The Pentagon has been instructed to prepare for a potential resumption of large-scale operations. Discussions involving Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have touched on a major new operation before elections in both countries. The White House calls such reports false. But the military remains on alert, and preparations are being finalised.
For many MAGA voters who supported Trump in part because he promised to reject endless wars, a purely electoral pause represents a significant contradiction.
An unpopular foreign war won’t turn MAGA loyalists into Democrats. The real hazard for the GOP is exhaustion: an endless conflict paired with painful pump prices gives frustrated voters every reason to leave their ballots on the kitchen table.
By removing the immediate threat of renewed attacks, Trump can try to prevent the war from becoming the dominant symbol of Republican failure and shift attention toward negotiations. If the conflict remains relatively quiet until November 3, Republican prospects improve. If Democrats gain control of one or both chambers, congressional scrutiny of military spending and presidential war powers would intensify.
This is where the powerless ballot enters the picture. Elections are meant to give citizens influence over decisions made in their name. That relationship weakens when a president can temporarily reduce the visibility of a policy’s costs until after ballots are cast, then resume the same course. Trump’s approach could turn the midterms into a debate over whether he appears willing to pull back from the war, rather than whether his Iran policy has actually changed. Americans are already feeling the strain of higher living costs, and consumer confidence has fallen sharply. A brief pause in the fighting will do little to ease that burden, much less resolve the underlying conflict. What is needed is a lasting diplomatic settlement, not a temporary break that leaves the same problems unresolved.
Neither a Republican nor a Democratic outcome automatically resolves the strategic problem. Iran has its own calculations.
Iranian officials continue to demand sanctions relief and an end to the blockade while Washington insists on further concessions. A pause that leaves these disagreements unresolved may simply delay the next confrontation.
The bigger question is not whether Trump keeps his promise before the election, but what he plans to do once the votes are counted and the political pressure has eased. If the coming weeks bring a verifiable agreement backed by credible safeguards, the pause could be a genuine first step toward ending the war. If instead November 3 is treated as the moment political restraints disappear, then the restraint will have functioned primarily as an electoral maneuver.
In that case the danger is clear. Voters are being asked to endorse the appearance of an ending while the means to continue the conflict remain intact. The ballot becomes a ratification of a decision already made elsewhere.
If the fighting resumes after the votes are counted, the question will no longer be whether Trump delivered peace, but whether his supporters were ever given a genuine choice between peace and a war that had only been postponed.
The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Monitor.

articles.title: Chinese navy flotilla returns after record 378 days at sea
articles.body:
- China’s 48th naval escort task force returned to Qingdao on Oct. 23 after a record 378-day mission in the Gulf of Aden.
- The destroyer Tangshan, frigate Daqing and supply ship Taihu sailed more than 150,000 nautical miles and escorted 423 vessels.
China’s 48th naval escort task force returned to a military port in Qingdao on Oct. 23 after 378 days away, the longest deployment in the history of the Chinese navy’s anti-piracy missions in the Gulf of Aden and the waters off Somalia, China’s Ministry of National Defense said.
The task force, made up of the guided-missile destroyer Tangshan (Hull 122), the guided-missile frigate Daqing (Hull 576) and the supply ship Taihu (Hull 889), sailed more than 150,000 nautical miles (about 278,000 km) during the mission and escorted 423 Chinese and foreign vessels, according to the ministry.
The three ships left Qingdao on Oct. 11, 2025, to take over from the 47th task force, carrying two helicopters and dozens of special operations personnel, Xinhua reported at the time. Before departure, the crews trained on weapons use, convoy escort procedures and replenishment at sea.
The deployment extends a run of successively longer missions. The 46th escort task force spent 339 days on deployment and the 47th spent 368, China Defense Blog noted, putting the 48th task force’s 378 days at the top of a steady climb in time on station across three consecutive rotations.
“Incremental progress, repeated often enough that one day it no longer looks incremental at all,” China Defense Blog wrote.
Beyond escort duty, the task force took part in the “Will for Peace 2026” joint maritime exercise in South Africa and the China-Pakistan “Sea Guardian IV” naval exercise in Pakistan. It joined a parade marking the 50th anniversary of Seychelles’ independence, paid visits to Bangladesh, Myanmar and Malaysia, and made technical stops in Oman, Kenya, Singapore and other countries, the ministry said.
China began sending warships to the Gulf of Aden and the waters off Somalia in December 2008, after a surge in piracy attacks on commercial shipping in one of the world’s busiest sea lanes, which links the Indian Ocean with the Red Sea and the Suez Canal. Each task force typically pairs combat ships with a supply vessel and an embarked special operations team, and hands over the mission to the next rotation on station.

articles.title: Labs that design U.S. Navy reactors get $2.4B more
articles.body:
- The U.S. Navy awarded Fluor Marine Propulsion a $2.4 billion modification for naval nuclear propulsion work at the Naval Nuclear Laboratory.
- The laboratory designs and supports reactors for U.S. Navy submarines and aircraft carriers, with work in Pennsylvania, New York and Idaho.
The U.S. Navy has added $2.4 billion to Fluor Marine Propulsion’s contract to run naval nuclear propulsion work at the Naval Nuclear Laboratory, the network of government labs that designs and supports the reactors powering every U.S. Navy submarine and aircraft carrier.
Naval Sea Systems Command awarded the $2,409,077,590 cost-plus-fixed-fee modification on Sept. 24, 2026, according to a Department of War contract announcement. Work will be split among the laboratory’s main sites near Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania (47%), Schenectady, New York (45%), and Idaho Falls, Idaho (8%). The announcement lists $582,062 in fiscal 2026 Navy operations and maintenance funds and $15,838 in fiscal 2026 shipbuilding funds obligated at the time of award, with the shipbuilding portion expiring at the end of the fiscal year.
The Naval Nuclear Laboratory is owned by the Department of Energy and overseen by Naval Reactors, a joint Energy Department and Navy program. It includes the Bettis Atomic Power Laboratory in West Mifflin, Pennsylvania, outside Pittsburgh, the Knolls Atomic Power Laboratory in Niskayuna, New York, near Schenectady, the Kenneth A. Kesselring Site in West Milton, New York, where sailors train to operate naval reactors, and the Naval Reactors Facility at the Idaho National Laboratory.
The labs develop new nuclear propulsion systems, provide technical support to keep the fleet’s reactors safe and reliable, and train the sailors who run them at sea. Knolls is the lead design laboratory for the Virginia-class attack submarines and is leading reactor design work for the Columbia-class ballistic missile submarines, while Bettis supports the Nimitz-class aircraft carriers and Seawolf-class submarines. The laboratory employs more than 7,500 engineers, scientists, technicians and support staff.
Fluor Marine Propulsion, a wholly owned subsidiary of Fluor Corporation, took over management of the laboratory from Bechtel Marine Propulsion Corporation on Oct. 1, 2018. The Navy-funded portion of its contract started with a cost-plus-fixed-fee base of about $1.2 billion and options that could bring its total to about $13 billion, alongside a separate Energy Department contract for the same laboratory. Earlier modifications have included a $1.78 billion award in March 2020 and a $1 billion option in 2021.
The new modification covers continued naval nuclear propulsion work across all three regions, and the Department of War contract announcement did not list a completion date for the effort.

articles.title: Normalization of attacks on nuclear sites unacceptable
articles.body:
“Nuclear facilities shall never, under any circumstances, be subjected to attack or threat of attack,” the countries said in a joint statement delivered at the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly’s First Committee on Friday.
According to Press TV's report, the statement was issued by Belarus, Burkina Faso, China, Cuba, Eritrea, Iran, Nicaragua, Niger, Pakistan, Russia, Tajikistan and Zimbabwe, addressing the prohibition of attacks and threats against nuclear sites dedicated to peaceful purposes.
The countries reaffirmed “the inalienable right of all states to develop research, production, and use of nuclear energy for peaceful purposes without discrimination.”
They underscored that attacks or threats against nuclear facilities violate the principles of the UN Charter, international law and the IAEA Statute, adding that such actions are “profoundly inconsistent with the objects and purposes of the NPT,” referring to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons.
The statement also recalled UN Security Council Resolution 487 (1981), which strongly condemned a military attack against nuclear facilities, as well as relevant decisions and resolutions adopted by the IAEA General Conference.
The 12 countries warned that attacks against nuclear facilities have “grave implications for nuclear safety, nuclear security” and pose a serious threat to the credibility and effectiveness of the IAEA safeguards system and the wider global non-proliferation framework.
They also cautioned that such attacks could undermine the peaceful use of nuclear energy and international cooperation, potentially triggering radioactive releases with severe consequences both inside and beyond the affected country.
MNA

articles.title: Three days before election, Netanyahu warns Iran is preparing to destroy Israel
articles.body:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned Saturday evening that Iran has resumed its nuclear program and intends to destroy Israel, describing the final days before Tuesday's election as "a fateful week" in a new campaign video.
"Iran has restarted its nuclear program, and it wants to destroy us within a short time," Netanyahu claimed, framing the October 27 vote as a decision with consequences for Israel's survival.
The prime minister also claimed that all of Israel's enemies want him to lose the election. Echoing U.S. President Donald Trump's public support for his reelection bid, Netanyahu declared that "the very existence of the State of Israel and the prevention of its destruction are at stake."
His remarks came as the Wall Street Journal reported Saturday that Trump was leaning toward renewed military action against Iran, although he had not made a final decision. According to the report, the president has been briefed on several Pentagon options, including strikes against Iranian nuclear facilities and infrastructure, as well as operations to seize islands controlled by Tehran. 
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, meanwhile, struck a different tone Saturday, calling for a renewed attempt to finalize an agreement with Washington. In remarks broadcast on Iranian state television, Pezeshkian blamed the United States for the collapse of previous negotiations.
"We were having negotiations, the cowards [Americans] messed everything up. I still think we should go and conclude it," he said, according to Reuters. 
The developments follow reports in recent days that Israel has been pressing for renewed military action against Iran, potentially even before the election. The Financial Times reported that Netanyahu had planned a major attack for the weekend of October 10 but was blocked by Trump, who opposed restarting the fighting before the U.S. midterm elections.
Netanyahu rejected the report, calling it biased and untrue. IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir has warned that another war so close to the October 27 election could force its postponement, adding another layer of uncertainty to the final days of the campaign.

articles.title: Houthis claim Saudi airstrikes targeted Yemen's Sanaa, Mokha
articles.body:
Mohammed Sami and Serdar Dincel
24 October 2026•Update: 24 October 2026
Yemen’s Houthi group claimed on Saturday that the capital Sanaa and the city of Mokha in Taiz governorate had come under a series of airstrikes by Saudi Arabia.
The Houthi-run Yemen News Agency quoted an unnamed local source as saying that “Saudi aircraft carried out a series of airstrikes on various areas of Mokha, west of Taiz governorate.”
The source said aircraft were still flying over the area but provided no further details on the outcome of the attacks.
Separately, the agency said Saudi aircraft carried out a series of airstrikes on Sanaa, targeting the areas of Asr and Hamdan.
It claimed that civilians were killed and wounded in the strikes, but did not provide casualty figures.
There was no immediate response from Riyadh on the claims by the rebel group.
Earlier on Saturday, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki, spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen, said two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis toward the Saudi cities of Taif and Yanbu had been intercepted and destroyed.
The Houthis have controlled Sanaa and other parts of the country since 2014.
Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting Yemen's government against the Houthis since 2015.
Recent escalation between Yemen's government forces and the Houthis began in July as a 2022 ceasefire collapsed. The group has also targeted Saudi Arabia's energy and civilian sites.

articles.title: Ballistic missile attacks rock Yemen's Aden
articles.body:
ADEN, Yemen, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- Loud explosions were heard in Yemen's southern port city of Aden, the seat of the internationally recognized government, on Saturday following a ballistic missile attack, a local security official told Xinhua.
The official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the Houthi group fired nearly four ballistic missiles at the city, with some striking near Aden International Airport and key military facilities in the Khormaksar district, and another hitting the Coast Guard Troops headquarters in Al-Tawahi district.
The blasts shook buildings across parts of Aden, residents told Xinhua, with plumes of smoke seen rising from the targeted areas. Casualties and damage were not immediately known.
The attack marked the latest in a series of Houthi missile strikes on Aden. On Wednesday, the Houthis claimed a ballistic missile strike on a Saudi military operations room at Badr military base near Aden International Airport.
Earlier this month, strikes hit the airport grounds, a military base in the Al-Buraiqa district, and the Al-Ma'ashiq Presidential Palace compound. The government said the Oct. 15 attack on the palace compound killed five people and wounded 16 others.
The renewed strikes come amid intensified fighting between the Houthis and government forces backed by the Saudi-led coalition. Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, prompting the coalition to intervene in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government. ■

articles.title: Russia running sabotage campaign across Europe
articles.body:
Russia is conducting a campaign of hybrid attacks and sabotage across Europe, and Britain is working with the United States to deter and contest activity that threatens Euro-Atlantic security, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Jim Shannon, the Democratic Unionist Party member for Strangford, had asked what steps are being taken to work with the United States to reduce the Russian threat to both home territories.
Louise Sandher-Jones, the Minister for the Armed Forces, said: “As our closest defence and security partner, we engage and collaborate with the US regularly on a range of issues. We know Russia is conducting a campaign of hybrid attacks and sabotage across Europe. The UK does not seek confrontation with Russia, but we will continue to deter and contest activity that threatens Euro-Atlantic security.”
Answering a separate question from Shannon on support for Poland and Lithuania, Sandher-Jones said: “The UK stands ready to defend every inch of Allied territory, with NATO remaining the cornerstone of the UK’s defence and security. This is reflected in our commitment to reach NATO’s defence spending target of 3.5% of GDP by 2035. Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty makes clear that an armed attack against one NATO Ally is considered an attack against the entire NATO Alliance.
“As the third-largest cash spender on defence in NATO, the UK contributes significantly towards the security of NATO’s eastern flank, which includes Poland and Lithuania. This is demonstrated through rotational air policing, troop deployments, and joint exercises, including maritime surveillance in the Baltic region. NATO is a defensive alliance and does not seek confrontation with Russia, but Russia should understand that any attack on a NATO ally would be a grave miscalculation.”
Wes Streeting told the Defence Committee this month that hybrid activity of this kind amounts to state backed terrorism. European governments have attributed arson, parcel bombs, rail sabotage, cable damage and drone incursions over airports and military sites to Russian intelligence services or to proxies recruited through messaging apps.

articles.title: Iran vows to block US warships from Gulf amid Trump threats
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran vows to block US warships from Gulf as Trump threatens fresh attacks
Iran said on Saturday that US military ships would never be allowed to enter the Gulf "under any circumstances" and that President Donald Trump would "take that dream to his grave".
The remarks came amid mounting US and Israeli threats of renewed attacks on Iran, as US ambassador to Turkey Tom Barrack warned that Washington could "absolutely" strike Iran as soon as this weakened.
"We will not allow US military ships in the Persian Gulf under any circumstances and at any time," said Iran's armed forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi, according to Iranian state television.
"The US president must dream of seeing the armed forces enter the Persian Gulf. He will take that dream to his grave."
Iranian forces have restricted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital energy conduit and gateway to the Gulf, since the war with the United States broke out on 28 February.
In retaliation, the United States has imposed a counterblockade on Iranian ports and ships.
Tehran has required vessels to seek permission to transit, and repeatedly targeted ships attempting to pass through Hormuz via a southern route close to the Omani coast.
According to the Guards, several tankers attempting to transit Hormuz through the route Tehran considers "illegal" were hit by mines in recent days.
On Friday, the Guards said two supertankers carrying more than 4.5 million barrels of crude oil have been abandoned at sea after hitting mines in the strategic waterway.
"Their engine rooms were disabled by an explosion and a fierce fire," the Guards said in a statement carried by their Sepah News website.
In peacetime, around a fifth of the world's oil and gas passed through Hormuz.
US spy chief warns Iran has ramped up efforts to target Americans
Iran has "substantially increased" its efforts to target Americans in the Middle East and beyond, US national intelligence chief Jay Clayton warned on Friday.
The warning comes after Washington ordered non-essential US embassy staff and their families to leave Saudi Arabia this week, following increasing attacks from Yemen's Houthis.
The kingdom has come under near-daily attacks this month from the Iran-backed group, including a strike on Riyadh's international airport that was the kingdom's deadliest in years.
"We have received intelligence that Iran has substantially increased efforts to target US personnel," Clayton said in a memo sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, according to a US official.
"The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against US citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," said the memo, which was first reported by Axios.
Washington previously ordered non-essential staff to leave the Gulf ahead of the start of its war against Iran and again in July before Trump called off a new wave of strikes.
The US official said: "When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment."
"The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting US officials are informing our decisions," the official added.
Trump suggested on Friday that the US might launch renewed military operations against Iran.
"We may do another little Epic Fury", Trump said, referring to the US name for its attacks on Iran. He gave no indication of timing.

articles.title: Iran slams US-Israeli attacks on peaceful nuclear facilities, condemns double standards
articles.body:
Iran slams US-Israeli attacks on peaceful nuclear facilities, condemns double standards
TEHRAN– Iran’s ambassador to the United Nations has condemned US and Israeli attacks on Iran’s peaceful nuclear facilities, accusing Western countries and international nuclear authorities of applying double standards and politicizing global non-proliferation efforts.
Addressing the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York on Friday, Gholamhossein Darzi, Iran’s ambassador and deputy permanent representative to the United Nations, reaffirmed Iran’s inalienable right under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) to develop nuclear energy for peaceful purposes, including uranium enrichment.
Darzi said the United States was challenging the rights of NPT member states by questioning their entitlement to pursue the full nuclear fuel cycle. He argued that denying countries access to uranium enrichment technology while claiming to support peaceful nuclear energy was incompatible with Article IV of the treaty.
“No State can unilaterally rewrite the Treaty or impose its own political veto on the legitimate rights of other States Parties,” he said, warning against the use of non-proliferation concerns as a means of exerting political pressure on sovereign nations.
The Iranian envoy said the United States and Israel had launched two wars of aggression against Iran in 2025 and 2026, targeting its peaceful nuclear facilities under International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) safeguards. He described the attacks as violations of international law, the UN Charter, the IAEA Statute, relevant IAEA General Conference resolutions and UN Security Council Resolution 487 (1981).
According to Darzi, the attacks caused extensive destruction and claimed thousands of lives, including that of Iran’s Leader, whose religious decree, or fatwa, rejects nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction.
Iran criticizes international response
Darzi strongly criticized the IAEA’s governing bodies, its director general and the UN Security Council for failing to condemn the attacks on safeguarded nuclear facilities. He said the absence of a clear response had exposed the selective application of international non-proliferation standards.
“Instead, pressure is directed against the victim while the aggressors escape accountability,” he said.
The envoy contrasted the treatment of Iran, an NPT member since 1970, with that of Israel, which he described as the only nuclear-armed state in the region and whose nuclear facilities are not subject to comprehensive IAEA safeguards.
He argued that continued political and military pressure on Iran, alongside 'impunity for Israel,' undermined the credibility of the international non-proliferation regime. He also criticized the withholding of technical cooperation that, in his view, deprived Iran of the benefits of peaceful nuclear development that the IAEA is mandated to promote.
Safety conditions remain central to inspections
Addressing calls for the resumption of inspections, Darzi said Iran had neither abandoned nor formally suspended its safeguards obligations. However, he stressed that the military attacks had fundamentally changed the physical and security conditions under which verification activities could take place.
He noted that the IAEA’s own reports acknowledged that verification activities had ceased and inspectors had been withdrawn for safety reasons. Such concerns, he said, could not be disregarded when demands were made for their return.
“No country can reasonably be expected to provide access amid military operations and persistent threats without adequate safety guarantees,” Darzi said, adding that responsibility for creating these conditions rested with the countries that carried out the attacks.
He concluded that Iran remained prepared to cooperate with the IAEA to the extent permitted by prevailing circumstances, but emphasized that such cooperation must not compromise the safety of the Iranian people, nuclear facilities or agency inspectors.
Darzi also insisted that the IAEA’s reporting must remain professional, objective and free from political influence, arguing that the agency’s credibility depended on technical integrity and impartiality.

articles.title: Iran has "increased efforts to target U.S. personnel," intel chief warns
articles.body:
Iran has "increased efforts to target U.S. personnel," intel chief warns
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Friday that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" abroad, with plots to kill Americans reaching "advanced stages" in the Middle East and other countries.
The warning, contained in an unclassified memo that was sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and obtained by CBS News, comes as the State Department adjusts staffing at diplomatic posts across the Middle East, and the U.S. military pares back its footprint in the region, amid concerns about direct threats from Iran and threats from the Iranian-backed Houthi movement in Yemen.
"The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," Clayton wrote.
The memo, which was issued as the Trump administration weighs resuming military strikes against Iran, does not identify specific targets or countries where the alleged plots are underway, or indicate whether attacks may be imminent.
Clayton said the U.S. intelligence community is working to downgrade sensitive intelligence — received through various channels — so it can be shared more broadly with State Department personnel. CIA Director John Ratcliffe was copied on the memo.
Axios was first to report on the memo.
The warning follows a series of precautions at U.S. diplomatic facilities across the region. Earlier this week, the State Department ordered non-essential U.S. embassy personnel and their families to depart Saudi Arabia. Several other American embassies in the region adjusted their staffing under "restricted operations" status, which allows them to reduce the number of personnel without formally going on ordered departure, CBS News previously reported.
"When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment," a U.S. official told CBS News on Friday. "The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting U.S. officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on RO [Restricted Operations] Status in the region."
A U.S. official and a senior U.S. military official also told CBS News this week that the military has been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing threats.
Houthi militants have stepped up drone and missile attacks against Saudi Arabia, targeting oil infrastructure and airports. One strike on Riyadh's King Khalid Airport earlier this month killed at least a dozen people, including a U.S. citizen, and injured hundreds more.
Last weekend, U.S. embassies in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and other countries warned Americans to exercise caution due to Houthi attacks.
Although the U.S. and Iran have refrained from striking each other in recent weeks, President Trump has not ruled out restarting hostilities after next month's midterm elections. Iran has also continued to take responsibility for attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.
At a campaign rally in Florida on Friday, Mr. Trump suggested the U.S. could launch another operation against Iran if Tehran failed to reach an agreement.
"We may do another little Epic Fury, or they'll agree," the president said, invoking the name of the U.S. military campaign launched in February.

articles.title: Saved wounded soldiers since 2015: Journalist and veteran Olena Sharhovska dies
articles.body:
Journalist and veteran Olena Sharhovska, who began saving wounded soldiers in 2015, dies
Olena "Jane" Sharhovska, a veteran of the Hospitallers medical battalion who worked as a translator and journalist in civilian life, has died. Olena began saving wounded soldiers in 2015.
Source: Yana Zinkevych, commander of the Hospitallers medical battalion; Sharhovska's former colleagues at Novynarnia
Details: Olena had extensive experience in the media, working as a journalist, translator, editor and social media specialist. Over the course of her career, she worked in television and print media, as well as on projects for Ukraїner and Osvitoria.
From 2015 onwards, she dedicated herself to saving others. Olena, alias Jane, volunteered on the front line with the First Volunteer Mobile Hospital named after Mykola Pyrohov. She later joined the Hospitallers.
Quote from Zinkevych: "Having mastered tactical medicine, Jane went to evacuate the wounded from the hottest sections of the front line, snatching the lives of our soldiers from the jaws of death as they were on their way to stabilisation points."
Details: In addition to helping the wounded, the paramedic and her fellow servicewomen campaigned for women to have the right to serve in the Armed Forces of Ukraine on an equal footing with men.
She was a co-organiser of the Invisible Battalion March held in Kyiv in 2016, in which participants called on the authorities to allow women to hold military positions that had previously been only open to men.
Olena was in Portugal when Russia launched its full-scale invasion. An injury prevented her from returning to Ukraine immediately, but she supported the country as a volunteer.
On 10 September 2022, her birthday, Olena joined the military. Serving with the International Legion of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, she was deployed in Bakhmut, Toretsk and Kharkiv Oblast.
In addition to carrying out medical evacuations, "Jane" provided tactical medicine training to other service members and, as a member of the Women's Veteran Movement, campaigned for female defenders to receive proper equipment.
She was discharged from military service in August 2024 for health reasons.
Quote from news agency Novynarnia: "Olena was a person of words and travel, with a deep interest in the world and in people. [...] Despite all the difficulties and trials, she held onto her love of words and people, and continued to help her brothers- and sisters-in-arms by fundraising and buying vehicles for the front.
Her motto in life was: 'Do what you believe needs to be done, come what may'."
Details: Olena's former colleague Bohdan Lohvynenko, a serviceman, journalist, writer and founder of Ukraїner, also shared his memories of her.
Quote from Lohvynenko: "We lived in neighbouring buildings in Vynohradar and would often sit and discuss editorial matters in your kitchen or mine. You were an enormous source of support and a driving force behind many processes, while at the same time remaining quite harsh towards the unknown. I would always remind you of what you had once said about those whose ranks you later joined. And we often laughed about it."
Previously: Earlier, we reported that Yaryna Nishtuk, a defender from Lviv who served as a strike drone platoon commander, had been killed in action.

articles.title: Twelve countries condemn any attack or threat against nuclear facilities
articles.body:
Twelve countries condemn any attack or threat against nuclear facilities
TEHRAN – Twelve countries, including Iran, Russia, China and Pakistan, have issued a joint statement declaring that nuclear facilities must never, under any circumstances, be subjected to attack or the threat of attack.
On Friday, the 12 countries — Belarus, Burkina Faso, China, Cuba, Eritrea, Iran, Nicaragua, Niger, Pakistan, Russia, Tajikistan and Zimbabwe — issued the joint statement during the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly’s First Committee. The statement addressed the prohibition of any attack or threat of attack against nuclear sites and facilities that are under the safeguards of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and dedicated to peaceful purposes.
According to IRNA, the statement was read out by Gholamhossein Darzi, Iran’s ambassador and chargé d’affaires to the United Nations. It contained eight points, as follows:
1. We reaffirm the importance of the full and effective fulfilment of the objectives of the International Atomic Energy Agency, particularly its statutory mission to accelerate and enlarge the contribution of atomic energy to peace, health and prosperity throughout the world. We also reaffirm the inalienable right of all states to develop research into, produce and use nuclear energy for peaceful purposes without discrimination.
2. We recall United Nations Security Council Resolution 487 (1981), which strongly condemned a military attack against nuclear facilities. We also recall the relevant decisions and resolutions of the IAEA General Conference — documents GC(53)/DEC/13, GC(XXIX)/RES/443, GC(XXIX)/RES/444 and GC(XXXIV)/RES/533 — which clearly reflect the longstanding position of the international community opposing any attack or threat of attack against nuclear facilities under IAEA safeguards and dedicated to peaceful purposes.
3. We reaffirm that an attack or threat of attack against nuclear facilities violates the principles of the United Nations Charter, international law and the Statute of the International Atomic Energy Agency, and is fundamentally incompatible with the objectives and purposes of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT).
4. We emphasize that attacks against nuclear facilities have serious implications for nuclear safety and security and pose a grave threat to the integrity, effectiveness and credibility of the IAEA safeguards system, as well as to the broader global non-proliferation framework.
5. We emphasize that attacks against nuclear facilities would adversely affect the peaceful uses of nuclear energy and international cooperation, and could result in the release of radioactive materials, with severe consequences both within and beyond the affected country, including serious impacts on civilian populations and long-term environmental damage.
6. We emphasize that silence in the face of attacks against protected nuclear facilities undermines established international norms, erodes confidence in the international legal order and increases the risk of such attacks becoming normalised.
7. We therefore reaffirm that nuclear facilities must never, under any circumstances, be subjected to attack or the threat of attack.
8. We call on all member states to stand united in preserving the integrity and credibility of the IAEA safeguards system, strengthening nuclear safety and security, and protecting the peaceful uses of nuclear energy and international cooperation by expressing their clear and unequivocal opposition to any attack or threat of attack against nuclear facilities.

articles.title: Ukraine-Russia war sees more strikes in occupied territories as Starlink speeds return to normal
articles.body:
A Ukrainian strike in part of the northeastern Kharkiv region held by Russia killed at least three people and gravely wounded another on Saturday, according to the Moscow-backed authorities.
"Three civilians were killed and a woman was seriously wounded as a result of a strike by a Ukrainian drone on a car in the village of Pisky in the Kharkiv region," Vitaliy Ganchev, a local Russia-installed governor, wrote on Telegram.
Russia's defence ministry reported having shot down a total of 616 Ukrainian drones during the night across more than 20 regions of the country.
Several people were wounded as a result of falling drone debris, which also started fires, according to local Russian authorities.
Another drone barrage damaged industrial infrastructure in Togliatti, on the Volga river in southeastern Russia, said the city's mayor, Ilya Sukhikh.
Three bodies were pulled from the rubble after a Friday night attack on a factory in Oryol, about 370 kilometres (230 miles) southwest of Moscow, the Russian authorities said.
Five people were also seriously wounded and are in intensive care, according to the emergency services.
On the Ukrainian side, the air force said that Russia had launched at least 126 drones at Ukraine overnight, of which 101 were shot down.
Two people were wounded in the capital, Kiev, according to the emergency services.
Ukrainian attack cuts water, power in occupied Crimea
Meanwhile, a separate Ukrainian attack led to water and power cuts in occupied Crimea on Saturday, when a drone barrage hit southeastern Russia, according to the Russian authorities.
"As a result of an incident that occurred on the main power grids outside our region, caused by an enemy attack using a drone, restrictions on the supply of electricity and water have been put in place," Sergei Aksyonov, the Moscow-installed head of the Crimean peninsula, wrote on Telegram.
He did not specify the number of households affected in Crimea, which is home to more than 2.5 million people.
The peninsula, which was seized from Ukraine by Russia in 2014, is a regular target for Ukrainian attacks.
Ukraine says Starlink and Starshield operating at 400 kph after week of throttling
The Starlink satellite communications system and its military version Starshield are operating again at speeds over 400 km per hour, Kiev's defence minister said on Saturday, after over a week of service restrictions that slowed connections and disrupted military operations.
"The Ministry of Defence's monitoring systems are recording a return to normal speed for Starlink/Starshield. We are recording a speed of over 400 kph. The connection is stable," Evhenii Khmara told reporters.
The Ukrainian military does not disclose the systems' maximum operating speeds, and the defence ministry did not say whether service had been fully restored.
"Monitoring systems had previously recorded disruptions to the Starlink/Starshield service. The speed metrics have now returned to normal," the ministry said.
The restrictions, first reported on October 14, undermined Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian attack drones and disrupted frontline communications, Ukrainian officials said.
Sources said connection speeds had been reduced to about 160 kph or less.
Ukraine's problems with SpaceX-owned Starlink came after US President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel and waived new sanctions on Moscow while pressing Ukraine to stop striking Russian oil refineries.
Neither SpaceX boss Elon Musk nor the US government has acknowledged responsibility for restricting Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine. Both have said publicly that any such decision could only have been taken by the other.

articles.title: Iran blames US for deal failure, urges new try amid fear of new attacks
articles.body:
Iran blames US for deal failure, urges new try amid fear of new attacks
Tehran warns that even limited strikes would trigger a response ‘several times greater’.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has blamed Washington for the unravelling of an interim deal aimed at ending the war with the United States and Israel, amid growing fears that the fighting could resume imminently.
In comments broadcast by Iranian Press TV on Saturday, But Pezeshkian also said that both sides should return to the deal and “conclude it”.
His remarks come amid growing fears that military action could resume as soon as this weekend, after US President Donald Trump said on Friday that he “may do another little Epic Fury”, using the codename of the US-Israeli war against Iran that started on February 28.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has warned that even limited strikes would trigger a response “several times greater”, according to comments reported by the semi-official Fars News Agency.
Iranian Armed Forces Chief of Staff Ali Abdollahi said on Saturday that the US military would not be allowed in the Gulf “under any circumstances and at any time”. Abdollahi said Trump could only “dream” of seeing US forces enter the Gulf, adding that he would take his dream to the grave.
Trump has suggested he could take further military action against Iran, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said he remains committed to overthrowing the country’s government.
Both leaders face elections, with Israelis set to choose their next government on Tuesday. Meanwhile, Trump’s Republican Party faces crucial midterm elections on November 3, with Democrats potentially winning control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate. Such an outcome would be a major blow to Trump, who still has more than two years left in his final term in the White House.
Iranian government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani said on Saturday that Tehran would not “wait for permission to defend itself”, adding that the country “seeks peace but will respond to any aggression with severe consequences”.
“Our position is clear: we do not flee from dialogue for peace, and we do not hesitate in defending the country. Those who harbour the illusion of destroying Iran must correct their calculations,” Mohajerani wrote in a memo.
Her comments came as Iranian judiciary chief Gholamhossein Mohseni Ejei met Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. The pair discussed how to tackle corruption and pursue compensation for Iranians affected by the US-Israeli war, among other issues.
Khamenei replaced his father as supreme leader after the latter was assassinated during the opening strikes of the war on February 28. He has not been seen in public since assuming the position in early March.
Parliament Speaker and chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf was reported to have met Khamenei earlier this week.

articles.title: Yemen's Houthi rebels claim new attacks on oil facilities and airports across Saudi Arabia
articles.body:
Yemen's Houthi rebels claim new attacks on oil facilities and airports across Saudi Arabia
Yemen’s Iran-allied Houthi rebels said they launched attacks at Saudi oil facilities and airports on Saturday while Yemen’s Saudi-backed government said the group also fired three ballistic missiles at coast guard sites in the port city of Aden.
There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi authorities on the Houthi reports, and it was not immediately clear if the reported attacks had hit their targets in the kingdom or been intercepted.
Houthi rebel spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, an Aramco facility in Yanbu, the Rabigh oil refinery, crude oil pumping stations and the East-West Pipeline.
He also said the group targeted King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, an airport in Najran and an airbase in Khamis Mushait.
The Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed two ballistic missiles fired by Houthis towards Yanbu and Taif on Saturday.
The renewed fighting has shattered a 2022 UN-brokered truce that largely halted cross-border attacks between the Saudi-led coalition, which backs Yemen’s internationally recognised government, and the Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa.
The escalation has opened another front in the US-Israeli war on Iran.
In Yemen, the Interior Ministry of the internationally recognised government said two of the Houthis’ missiles had struck a coast guard headquarters, while a third hit a coast guard building in the Tawahi district.
Houthi spokesman Saree said the group’s forces had targeted Saudi-backed military gatherings at what he called Al-Nasr camp and a naval military base in Aden, saying Saudi officers were overseeing the mobilisation there.
There was no immediate comment from the Saudi-led coalition on that assertion.
Earlier on Saturday, Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defense briefly issued alerts warning residents of potential danger in Taif and Yanbu, as well as in the holy city of Mecca and the kingdom’s second-largest city, Jeddah.
About 10 minutes later, the agency said the threat had passed.
The Houthis warned airlines earlier this month against using Saudi airspace, exempting only the airspace over Mecca and Medina, as they intensified attacks on the kingdom.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

articles.title: Houthi militia launches multiple missile attacks on Yemen's Aden
articles.body:
Yemeni authorities have said that the Houthi militia targeted Aden International Airport, a port in the city’s al-Tawahi district and two coast guard facilities with ballistic missiles.
The information ministry reported renewed ballistic missile attacks on the airport and port in a post on X on Saturday, without providing details on casualties or damage.
Separately, the interior ministry said two ballistic missiles targeted the coast guard headquarters at the ministry’s compound, while a third targeted a coast guard building in the al-Tawahi district. 
Saudi Arabia and the internationally recognised Yemeni government have come under sustained attack from the Houthi militia.
The Saudi-led coalition said earlier it intercepted two missiles targeting the western Saudi cities of Taif and Yanbu before explosions were heard in Aden.
The Houthi militia quickly claimed responsibility for the attack, saying it had targeted a naval base and a military camp overseen by Saudi forces.
Houthi militia military spokesperson Yahya Saree said its forces targeted Saudi troops at Al-Nasr camp and the naval base in Aden.
His statement did not mention Aden International Airport or specify the weapons used.
The interior ministry said the strikes came after previous attacks on civilian and vital facilities in Aden, including repeated ballistic missile and drone attacks on the international airport.
It warned that targeting vital facilities and public infrastructure threatened the city’s security and stability, endangered civilians and affected institutions providing security and public services.
The Yemeni government and its allies hold Aden and large parts of the country’s southern and eastern provinces, while the Houthi militia control the capital Sanaa and much of northern and western Yemen.
Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting Yemen's government against the Houthi militia since 2015.
Recent escalation between Yemen's government forces and the Houthi militia began in July as a 2022 ceasefire collapsed. 
The group has also targeted Saudi Arabia's energy and civilian sites.

articles.title: Inside the Trump-administration campaign to return Brazil’s Bolsonaro clan to power
articles.body:
By Gabriel Stargardter
SAO PAULO, Oct 24 (Reuters) - Two US State Department officials led a campaign to restore the right-wing Bolsonaro clan to power in Brazil and successfully pushed for sanctions aimed at tilting the election in their favor, according to 10 current and former US officials with direct knowledge of the matter.
Their plan faces a reckoning on Sunday, when Senator Flavio Bolsonaro faces leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in a tight run-off. Lula has warned Washington against encroaching on Brazil’s sovereignty and accused his opponent of plotting with the Trump administration.
The two officials were Darren Beattie, a Senior Advisor for Western Hemisphere Affairs who oversees Brazil policy, and Ricardo Pita, another senior advisor promoted this year to Deputy Assistant Secretary for North America. The details of their campaign to return the Bolsonaros to power haven’t been previously reported.
Beattie and Pita, both political appointees, operated with wide latitude to manage Washington’s relationship with the second most-populous country in the Americas, the people said.
In the months before election campaigning began, they instructed US diplomats in Brazil that it was US policy to restore former President Jair Bolsonaro as Brazil’s leader – even though he had been disqualified from office for plotting a coup in 2022, when he lost the presidential election to Lula, three of the people said.
After Bolsonaro received a 27-year sentence in September 2025, the two men pivoted to supporting the candidacy of his son, right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the three sources said. Beattie and Pita told embassy staff not to interact with other conservative presidential contenders who could challenge the younger Bolsonaro, they said.
Since last year, the two men have successfully advocated for punitive US government measures on Brazil designed to weaken Lula and boost the Bolsonaros, the 10 people told Reuters. The policies included designating Brazilian gangs as terrorist groups and imposing US sanctions against the Brazilian Supreme Court Justice who was spearheading the investigation into Jair Bolsonaro.
Reuters could not determine the extent to which the two men were acting on orders from the White House or Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Trump, a vocal defender of Bolsonaro since his election defeat in 2022, hasn’t publicly endorsed any candidate.
The White House declined to comment and referred questions to the State Department.
State Department Spokesman Tommy Pigott didn’t answer questions about specific measures and directives involving Beattie and Pita but said in a statement: “All actions taken by the United States against narco-traffickers and to protect free speech are to defend the rights and lives of the American people. The Brazilian people have the right to choose their leaders through free and fair elections.”
Lula’s office did not respond to comment requests.
Orna Blum, one of the officials who spoke to Reuters about Beattie and Pita’s efforts, led the State Department’s Brazil and Southern Cone office until retiring last year over her opposition to the Trump administration.
Washington “has every right to pursue its economic and strategic interests,” she said. “But when American foreign policy instruments are used to pressure another democracy over the legal fate of a political ally, the line between diplomacy and political intervention has been crossed.”
SANCTIONS ON A SUPREME COURT JUSTICE
Beattie is a former White House speechwriter fired in 2018 after addressing an event frequented by white nationalists. He’s also the architect of “free speech diplomacy,” a policy advocated by Trump allies that seeks to punish nations they accuse of censoring right-wing speech by US citizens, companies and global right-wing allies.
The United States has accused Brazil Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes of violating free speech rights by jailing Brazilians for political social-media posts and by censoring content of US social-media companies. Moraes has argued he was ridding social media of fake news that undermined public faith in Brazil’s democratic institutions.
Moraes did not respond to a comment request.
Pita, a conservative Venezuelan-American, is among many in Rubio’s orbit who view Lula as a threat to US interests in Latin America. Rubio has been a key leader in the administration’s aggressive policy in the region, which has included an invasion of Venezuela to oust its president, an oil blockade of Cuba, and military attacks on suspected drug boats from Latin America.
Beattie and Pita were drawn to the Bolsonaro family’s right-wing politics, their antipathy towards Lula, and the idea that Jair Bolsonaro was a victim of abuses by Brazil’s Supreme Court.
Like Trump in the 2020 US election, Bolsonaro refused to concede he lost Brazil’s 2022 presidential vote, triggering riots by supporters who stormed government buildings. The Supreme Court convicted him in September 2025 of plotting a coup to remain in power.
Before the conviction, in early 2025, the Bolsonaros were aggressively lobbying Washington for sanctions under the Global Magnitsky Human Rights Accountability Act against Moraes, who had led criminal investigations into Jair Bolsonaro. The act is a 2016 federal law allowing US sanctions against foreign individuals responsible for human-rights abuses or severe corruption.
Around April 2025, Jair Bolsonaro’s younger son, Eduardo, visited Beattie in his State Department office in Washington DC, according to two former US officials. Eduardo Bolsonaro had been making the public case for Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes since at least 2024, and in March 2025 he said in a livestream that it was “practically certain” the Trump administration would do so.
Eduardo Bolsonaro did not respond to requests for comment.
Beattie made calls to the US Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control to appeal for Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes, said a former US official with direct knowledge of the matter.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, whose department administers Magnitsky sanctions through OFAC, offered no opposition, the former official said.
The US announced Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes in July 2025, citing his alleged violations of free-speech rights by censoring anti-government social-media posts.
A Treasury official said Bessent and Rubio are “fully aligned on the administration’s foreign policy.”
TERRORIST DESIGNATIONS
The Bolsonaro family was also pushing for Washington to designate Brazil’s top gangs – the Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) and Comando Vermelho (CV) – as terrorist organizations. They believed such a designation would hurt Lula, who some opponents have criticized for failing to control crime.
Eduardo Bolsonaro had become friends with Pita through US conservative circles, and both supported the effort to designate the gangs as terrorist groups.
In May 2025, Pita joined a US delegation that visited Jair Bolsonaro at his residence in Brasilia as he awaited his trial, according to public announcements at the time. Also in the group: David Gamble, the State Department’s top sanctions official at the time.
Back in Washington, Pita asked State sanctions officials to explore how terrorist designations like those announced against Mexican cartels in February 2025 could be used in Brazil, one former official said.
Nearly a year later, in May 2026 – after Pita was promoted to a new job that pulled him out of Brazil affairs – presidential contender Flavio Bolsonaro met with Beattie and Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau in Washington to discuss “the urgency of designating the PCC and the Comando Vermelho as foreign terrorist organizations,” according to an X post by right-wing influencer Paulo Figueiredo that included photos of the attendees.
The State Department announced the designation the following day.
Reuters could not determine the extent of Pita or Beattie’s influence in securing the final decision.
BACKFIRES AND SETBACKS
In July 2025, Washington also announced a series of other measures against Brazil, including the revocations of eight Supreme Court justices’ visas and 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods, citing the “persecution” of Jair Bolsonaro.
Reuters could not determine what, if any, role Beattie or Pita played in the additional measures. But if they were intended to undermine Lula, many of them backfired, according to political analysts in Brazil.
Measures targeting the court did nothing to stop it from proceeding with Bolsonaro’s trial, while the tariffs boosted the Lula government’s poll numbers, the analysts said.
Major US and Brazilian firms reliant on bilateral trade – including meatpacking giant JBS - controlled by Brazilian billionaires Wesley and Joesley Batista – also pushed back on the tariffs, which Washington eventually watered down.
Beattie and Pita’s campaign also hit setbacks. Without an official explanation from the Treasury Department, the US removed Justice Moraes from the Magnitsky sanctions list in December, and in March Brazil barred Beattie from entering the country to visit Bolsonaro in prison.
Mario Braga, a Latin America analyst at risk intelligence firm RANE, said Trump may have decided to withhold a public endorsement of Bolsonaro to avoid being seen as meddling in Brazil’s election – a perception that could boost Lula’s popularity.
Still, after Flavio Bolsonaro narrowly outperformed Lula in the first-round election earlier this month, Trump called it a big victory.
“Close, but a very, very big victory,” he told reporters. “Amazing, actually.”
(Reporting by Gabriel StargardterAdditional reporting by Gram Slattery in Washington, Luciana Magalhaes in Sao Paulo, Lisandra Paraguassu in Brasilia Editing by Brad Haynes and Richard Valdmanis)

articles.title: Russian embassy denies reports of staff leaving Iran’s Bushehr nuclear power plant
articles.body:
Russian embassy denies reports of staff leaving Iran’s Bushehr nuclear power plant
TEHRAN – The Russian Embassy in Tehran has dismissed reports that Russian diplomatic staff and specialists working at Iran’s Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant are leaving the country, stressing that activities are continuing as usual.
In a statement, the embassy said it was aware of reports published by certain hostile media outlets alleging that an evacuation of Russian embassy personnel and specialists at the Bushehr facility was underway.
“We would like to clarify that neither embassy staff nor Russian specialists at the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant are leaving Iran,” the statement said.
The embassy emphasized that operations were proceeding as normal, describing contrary reports as false information and saying their origins were entirely clear.
Located on Iran’s southern coast along the Persian Gulf, the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant is Iran’s first commercial nuclear power facility. Although construction at the site was initially undertaken by the German company Siemens in the 1970s, Russia took responsibility for completing the plant’s first reactor unit under an agreement signed with Iran in the 1990s. The first unit was connected to Iran’s national electricity grid in 2011 and reached full capacity in 2013.
Russia has continued to cooperate with Iran on the development of the facility, including the construction of additional reactor units. The project forms part of broader cooperation between Tehran and Moscow in the peaceful use of nuclear energy.
